Description: Brigade REAP, the Brigade Real Estate Accelerator Program, is an UrbanTech accelerator backed by the Brigade Group. It works with early-stage founders building across the built world and runs from the Brigade Gateway Campus on Dr. Rajkumar Road in Malleswaram, Bangalore. Its own pages describe it in two ways that do not fully agree: the programme page and homepage call it "India's pioneering accelerator" for UrbanTech founders, while its about and investments pages call it "Asia's first UrbanTech accelerator". Both are its own claims. What they support Brigade REAP backs founders building across the built environment rather than real estate alone. Its programme page describes the scope as PropTech and ConstructionTech, Smart Buildings and IoT, sustainability in real estate, urban mobility and infrastructure, cleantech for the built world, retail tech and hospitality, and cross-sector ideas at the intersection of real estate with finance, retail or health. It looks for founders who have built an MVP or have early transactions and are ready to scale. Programmes Brigade REAP runs a single accelerator programme over 16 weeks. It brings together mentorship, pilot opportunities, investor access and go-to-market and fundraising support. Mentorship is one-to-one, covering product, go-to-market, capital and strategy, and comes from REAP coaches and industry leaders. Selected startups get the chance to pilot with developers, including the Brigade Group, and curated introductions to venture investors, family offices and corporate partners who work in UrbanTech. The programme also offers market-access introductions to decision-makers across real estate, government and infrastructure, and support across go-to-market, fundraising, brand and PR. Founders join an alumni community that the programme page puts at more than 80 UrbanTech startups. Track record Brigade REAP's about page reports its own numbers for the programme: 82 startups mentored, 1,752 formal applications received, and 4,572 initial conversations. It also reports an average monthly growth rate of 4.2 times across its portfolio. These are the programme's own figures. Who runs it Brigade REAP is a programme of the Brigade Group, and its about page lists Nirupa Shankar, Joint Managing Director of the Brigade Group, among its people. The programme is based at the Brigade Gateway Campus in Malleswaram, Bangalore. How to apply Applications are open year-round. The programme page routes applicants to a third-party application platform, where the current intake is handled. For general queries, Brigade REAP publishes the address info@brigadereap.com. Its office is on the third floor of the new Library building. The centre started around technology start-ups in ICT and electronics, and it still describes SMAC and IoT as its main areas. Its recent calls reach wider: the 2025-26 incubation call names agritech, cleantech, healthtech, SaaS, AI/ML, deep-tech software and product, edtech, greentech, electronic design and manufacturing, aerospace and defence tech, sports tech, e-commerce, fintech, IoT, robotics and social innovation. How programmes work CEDI describes a three-step pipeline. Pre-incubation takes an idea to an MVP over six to twelve months. Incubation takes the MVP to market. Acceleration covers scale-up and mass production over six to twelve months. The two sources give slightly different lengths for the middle step: the incubation services page says CEDI commits to 24 months with a 12-month extension, while the pre-incubation call's chart gives 24 to 36 months. Either way, the agreements are described as flexible and a startup can leave earlier. NAVIYA is the pre-incubation programme. It runs in two stages, Srijan then Virutcham, each within six months. The first is for validating the idea, building a prototype and writing a business model canvas; the second is for turning that into a working MVP and a venture. Teams that finish are onboarded into the main CEDI incubation programme. NAVIYA also reimburses MVP development expenses for selected teams. Alongside its own programmes, CEDI issues calls under MeitY's GENESIS scheme. Three have run recently and all have closed: Entrepreneur in Residence, which offers a startup grant to early-stage teams; a Pilot programme for startups with a working prototype and a purchase or work order in hand; and a Matching Investment component that matches private investment raised, one to one, as equity. All three are aimed at electronics design and manufacturing, deep-tech software and product, and ICT, using AI/ML, IoT, VLSI and semiconductors, blockchain, cybersecurity, quantum computing and AR/VR. The EiR track has reached a third cohort. Who can apply It depends on the programme, and the difference matters. The 2025-26 CEDI incubation call is open beyond the campus — it invites students, faculty, early-stage founders, alumni and innovators, so an outside founder with no NIT Trichy connection can apply. NAVIYA is not: its call limits it to NIT Trichy faculty members and UG, PG and PhD students. The GENESIS calls carry their own gates. The Pilot call asked for full-time founders, an MVP or working prototype, a valid purchase or work order from an eligible buyer, DPIIT registration, and incorporation in a tier-2 or tier-3 city. The Matching Investment call asked for market-ready or revenue-generating startups incorporated in tier-2 or tier-3 cities, that are not already beneficiaries of TIDE 2.0 scale-up or SAMRIDH, and preferred startups with granted patents. Facilities CEDI provides office space in the Central Library building along with office equipment — PCs, laptop access points, phones and standard office furniture — for eligible applicants. Its own facilities page adds work space, communication and computing facilities, equipment labs, a library and information centre, and training and conference rooms. The bigger draw is the host institute. Incubatee companies are given access to NIT Trichy's common infrastructure, its departmental laboratories and its other resources for product development, and they can take on NIT Trichy students as interns. CEDI's facilities page also lists NIT Trichy centres it is well connected to, including ISRO's Space Technology Incubation Centre for the southern region, a Siemens Centre of Excellence in Manufacturing, and centres of excellence in transportation engineering, corrosion and surface engineering, AI and machine learning, energy harvesting, and energy and environmental science. Those belong to NIT Trichy, not to CEDI. On services, CEDI runs monthly group mentoring plus individual sessions, with a mentoring team drawn from alumni and faculty, and reviews progress quarterly. It keeps a pool of corporate-sector experts, runs networking sessions, and helps with raising money, reaching markets and managerial skills. Track record The numbers on the site do not line up, so read them carefully. The About page says CEDI had incubated ten businesses in the previous three years, with no date on the sentence. The startup tables list more than that: thirteen graduated companies, nine ongoing ones, and five student or faculty startups. The ongoing table's own numbering skips from six to eleven. Named graduates include Silicic Innova Technologies, Navriti Technologies, Blaer Motors, GMetri Studio, SENZWIZ Technologies, Fixyard Technologies and Bolt 3D Printers. Ongoing incubatees include Greenerg Mobility Solutions, Trawello Healthcare Services and Recubitech. Who runs it and who backs it G. Krishnan is listed as Chief Executive Officer. Dr. M. Umapathy handles overall administration, with Dr. R. Leela Velusamy on industry and alumni relations, Dr. G. Lakshminarayanan on finance, incubation and outreach, and Dr. S.R. Balasundaram on skill training and development. A long list of NIT Trichy faculty associates is attached to the centre across ICE, production engineering, EEE, computer applications, civil, ECE, mechanical, energy and environment, and management studies. MeitY funds CEDI's TIDE project, which is the centre's core government backing, and CEDI issues the GENESIS calls under the same ministry. Sonata Software is a long-standing corporate partner; the joint CEDI-Sonata Entrepreneurship Fund has co-sponsored competitions run by NIT Trichy's E-Cell, including Ventura. CEDI has also worked with EDII Ahmedabad on DST-sponsored faculty and entrepreneurship development programmes, and with the Asia Foundation on a women entrepreneurship project, though the pages describing that work are dated 2014 to 2017 and nothing more recent is published. Where it is and how to reach it CEDI is at NIT Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu 620015, on the third floor of the new Library building. There is one office and no other locations. General enquiries go to cedi@nitt.edu. Staff and intern openings — a CEO post, an incubation executive, engineering and management interns — are posted as notices on the same page as the funding calls rather than on a careers page, and past events and workshops are listed under the events section.

Name: CIE IIIT Hyderabad
Description: The Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (CIE) is the technology business incubator of IIIT Hyderabad, set up in 2008 and based on the university's campus at Vindhya C4, Gachibowli, Hyderabad. It was recognised as a Technology Business Incubator by the Department of Science and Technology's National Science and Technology Entrepreneurship Development Board in 2012, and today runs three named incubators under one roof: the Deeptech Incubator (its oldest, from 2008), the OJAS MedTech Incubator (launched in 2018 with BIRAC's BioNEST support), and the AIC Social Tech Incubator (set up in 2019 with the Atal Innovation Mission). What they support CIE's core focus is deep tech seeded out of university research — startups working in AI, machine learning, computer vision, NLP, robotics and AR/VR. Alongside that, OJAS supports medtech, life sciences, biotechnology, diagnostics and wellness startups, and AIC supports technology startups built around social impact. A separate accelerator backed by the Department of Science and Technology works with AI-powered mobility startups (ADAS, road safety, freight), and CIE also runs a women-entrepreneur track, the FLO Incubator, with FICCI FLO Hyderabad. Most accelerator tracks ask for a working MVP with some customer validation; the fellowship and grant programmes described below reach earlier, idea- and prototype-stage founders as well. Programmes Avishkar is CIE's six-month deep tech accelerator, open to startups registered in India with a full-time founder and a validated MVP; a cohort runs twice a year, applicants pitch to a panel at IIIT-H, and selected startups get mentoring, lab access, cloud credits and are eligible for seed funding. OJAS-MedTech Acceleration runs on the same six-month, twice-a-year cadence for MedTech and life-sciences startups, and requires taking up at least one incubation seat. Sitting above the OJAS accelerator is the OJAS MedTech BioNEST incubator itself, for companies building at the intersection of technology and medicine, and a separate OJAS PEP fellowship gives researchers and medical professionals a year-long entrepreneurial track into healthcare. AIC-IIITH runs a flagship incubation programme for tech-based social enterprises that ends with a pitch for seed funding. The FLO Incubator offers FICCI FLO members a two-day Idea Validation Bootcamp capped at twenty participants, followed by a month of weekly one-on-one mentorship for those who complete it. On the research side, the DST NIDHI Entrepreneur-in-Residence programme and the MeitY TIDE 2.0 EIR both let founders co-create a deep tech product with IIIT-H labs, paying a monthly fellowship and a milestone-linked seed grant; NIDHI-PRAYAS separately funds prototyping work and Fab Lab access for individual innovators and young startups, and TIDE 2.0 also runs a standalone three-to-six month grant track for early-stage deeptech startups moving from prototype to pilot. CIE has also run the HDFC Bank Parivartan: AI for Social Good Challenge, a grant competition for research-driven, socially-focused deep tech startups — its most recent round closed in February 2025. Research Connect groups four lighter-touch tracks — Research Cafe and Rootnode (advisory sessions and office hours with IIIT-H faculty), a two-week CV Labs workshop, and Deeptech CoWorkz, a coworking space for AI and deeptech founders to build alongside IIIT-H's research labs. Facilities and support Startups can take a desk under CIE's Launch Pad plan or a dedicated cabin under Propel, both with round-the-clock access, mentoring, industry connects and cloud credits, or opt for fully remote Virtual Incubation. The NIDHI-PRAYAS Fab Lab gives prototyping grantees access to 3D printing, cutting and welding machines and an electrical lab. AIC-IIITH runs its own co-working space, conference room and meeting space for its incubatees, separate from the main CIE floor. Mentoring across the programmes draws on IIIT-H faculty and a roster of resident mentors with backgrounds spanning venture investing, healthcare and enterprise technology. Track record CIE's own pages give inconsistent figures for its history — its homepage states one set of startup, funding and jobs numbers while its About page states different ones for the same claims, so we have not repeated the specific counts here. What its pages agree on: DPIIT awarded CIE a grant under the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme in November 2021 to support early-stage technology startups, and CIE has been recognised by TiE Hyderabad. Named startups that have come through CIE's programmes include Logy.AI, an AI oral-health startup that partnered with Colgate-Palmolive in Nigeria; Saukhyam, maker of banana-fibre reusable menstrual pads, recognised by NITI Aayog; and Avishkar founders Xmachines, Dave.ai and Mashinga. Who runs it CIE is led by C. V. Jawahar as CEO, who is also Dean of Research and Development at IIIT Hyderabad, with Ramesh Loganathan as COO. The Social Tech Incubator, AIC-IIITH, has its own leadership under CEO Ravi Sarkunan. A governing council and executive council — drawing on IIIT-H faculty, resident mentors and outside investors — oversee the centre. How to apply CIE's apply page routes founders by track — its Deeptech, MedTech, Social (AIC-IIITH) and Women (FLO-IIITH) incubators, its Avishkar and OJAS accelerators, and its bootcamps, workshops, mentoring and research programmes each link to their own application form. General incubation and partnership queries go to CIE's incubation inbox, and OJAS-specific questions go through a dedicated outreach address.

Name: CII Centre of Excellence
Description: CII Centre of Excellence for Innovation, Entrepreneurship & Startups (CII CIES) is a centre of the Confederation of Indian Industry, based at T-Hub 2.0 in Madhapur, Hyderabad. It connects growth-stage startups with large companies through corporate pilot and market-access programmes, and runs a paid affiliation scheme that certifies startups. Its programmes are built around what a corporate partner wants to solve, and the programme pages do not publish a fixed intake calendar. How programmes work CII CIES runs two standing programmes and a series of partner-specific calls. The Corporate Accelerator Program is a sixteen-week market access programme in which growth-stage startups demonstrate or pilot their innovations inside large corporates. The Corporate Innovation Program runs for thirty-two weeks and is aimed at startups that want to co-create solutions with a corporate business unit and solve specific domain problems alongside it. Neither programme page states dates, a fee or any equity terms, so confirm those with the team before you plan around them. Alongside these, CII CIES publishes one-off calls built around a single corporate partner's problem statements. Recent ones include the FutureSites Innovation Program (retail technology, with an oil and gas company's retail business unit), the NextGen Procurement Programme (a procurement platform for MSMEs buying metal cutting tools), the SmartMFG Innovation Programme (manufacturing safety, efficiency, sustainability and quality) and the ICONN NINJA India Programme (Indian startups matched with Japanese corporates, run with JICA and Deloitte Tohmatsu Venture Support). All four have closed, and ICONN NINJA has run for at least two cohorts. Together they show the kinds of corporate problems CII CIES takes on. Who can apply The two standing programmes are for growth-stage startups with proven product-market fit and existing clients. CII CIES looks for a high level of innovation and differentiation, a product or service validated in the market with measurable traction, a committed and skilled founding team with at least one co-founder working full time, and compliance with all regulatory requirements, including the permits the business needs. For the Corporate Innovation Program, startups must also be ready to work closely with corporate business units and adapt their solutions to the corporate's requirements. The one-off calls set their own bar. SmartMFG welcomed early or growth-stage ventures with deployable, scalable solutions for heavy manufacturing. ICONN NINJA wanted Indian startups with at least a proof of concept or early market validation. FutureSites wanted scale-ready startups with a tested product or early deployments, ready to run a pilot within six to twelve months, and said international startups could apply if they could operate or deploy pilots in India. Sectors vary with each corporate challenge; the affiliation scheme itself is open to all sectors. Startup Affiliation Programme The Startup Affiliation Programme recognises Indian startups and serves as the gateway to the CII CIES network. Affiliated startups receive an official affiliation certificate and a digital badge, valid for 24 months, along with a public profile on the CII CIES platform, networking, masterclasses and policy consultations. It is a paid annual affiliation, with the fee set by the startup's annual revenue, and only startups recommended by the expert panel pay. To qualify, a startup needs to have been operating for at least two years, be registered and incorporated in India, have a dedicated founding team able to execute and scale, and have a commercially available product or service with customer adoption or market validation. The review is stated to take 30 days from the date of application. CII CIES describes this scheme in two ways. Its home page groups it with the market-access programmes that let startups pilot inside corporates. The affiliation page itself describes a certificate and network, and says access to programmes is subject to each programme's own eligibility. Treat affiliation as a credential and a way into the network, not as a promise of a corporate pilot. Locations CII CIES operates from the 6th Floor, T-Hub 2.0, 20, Inorbit Mall Road, Vittal Rao Nagar, Madhapur, Hyderabad, Telangana 500081. Its own site does not describe workspace or desks for startups. A March 2023 news report on the opening of the centre said it had a 200-seat facility with workspaces, ideation labs and mentoring rooms, set up with the Government of Telangana and Pratiksha Trust. We have not been able to confirm from CII CIES's own pages that this space is open to startups, so ask before assuming it. Who runs it The centre describes itself as a Centre of Excellence of the Confederation of Indian Industry, set up to bridge the gap between corporates and startups. The same news report said CII launched the CIES initiative in 2020 and opened the Hyderabad centre in 2023, and that agreements for corporate accelerator programmes were exchanged at the launch with Apollo Hospitals, Elico, Skoda Auto and Vedanta. Its own site gives no founding year. Other activities CII CIES also organises international delegations. Its site lists past trips to Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Australia and Singapore, including a UAE delegation to Dubai, Ras Al Khaimah and Abu Dhabi from 13 to 16 October 2025. It also runs capacity-building work aimed at family offices, senior corporate executives, government officials and academia. Neither of these has a stated way for a startup to apply, so we have not listed them as programmes. For any question, the general inbox is info@ciicies.in.

Name: Change Engine
Description: Change Engine, also written Changengine, is an accelerator for non-profits and social enterprises in India. Its flagship is the ACE programme, a nine-month, hybrid programme that sets out to take founders from where they are to clear pathways to scale. The site is run by Big Bets, and its privacy policy gives a registered office at Karol Bagh, New Delhi. Change Engine describes itself as founders at heart. Its three founders are Varun Aggarwal, who founded Aspiring Minds, Shubham Bansal, who founded Leapclub, and Shailendra Nath Jha, a product leader. It says it has built and scaled organisations itself and has distilled lessons from more than 30 non-profits into a report called The Playbook for Non-profit Unicorns. How the ACE programme works ACE is sector agnostic but picks organisations by how they plan to scale. There are two cohorts. The Tech for Impact cohort is for teams that use recent developments in AI and digital infrastructure as the core drive for scale. The Policy and Community cohort is for teams that use government partnerships to reform or improve public programmes, or that mobilise communities and self-help groups to change behaviour. What selected organisations get is a co-founding team for the nine months, unrestricted seed capital to spend on research, pilots, hiring or anything that helps them scale, weekly one-to-one office hours, off-the-record talks from non-profit founders and funders, and access to a network for follow-on capital, board members and government partnerships. The 2026 programme runs in hybrid mode. In-person working sprints were set for 1 to 10 July, 3 to 14 August, 5 to 9 October and 7 to 11 December. Between sprints there are weekly group office hours and cohort check-ins, mentor talks on Thursdays, readings and discussions, and formal strategic reviews in September, November and January. Who can apply Change Engine says it does not care about legal structure: non-profit, for-profit, Section 8 or private limited are all fine. What it asks for is that founders are domain experts with deep insight into their problem, have a strong hypothesis for using technology, government or community to scale, and care about data, execution and measurable outcomes. It also says the programme is not only for early-stage organisations. It partners with organisations at all levels of funding and maturity, including late-stage ones exploring pathways to systemic impact at India scale. Founders must be ready to commit time to strategic work that can mean redesigning the model and even the organisation. Application timeline for ACE 2026 The 2026 page set submissions for 5 April 2026, rolling interviews until 15 April 2026, an in-person bootcamp for 10 organisations from 4 to 8 May 2026, a final decision on 20 May 2026 and the cohort start on 6 July 2026. The same page also says applications are rolling and to apply early. Because the dates have passed, check the site or write to the programme inbox before assuming an intake is open. Past cohorts and portfolio The site has pages for the 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 cohorts and says it has completed three cohorts and backed more than 10 organisations. These are its own undated figures. Organisations named on its cohort pages include Jaljeevika, Farmers for Forests, Safe School, Vardhishnu, CLIC, Saarthi Education, Project DEEP, Scholarlify and Sajhe Sapne. Their work spans fisheries, agroforestry, school safety, schooling for marginalised children, support for care-leavers, practice-based learning and cash transfers to families. Mission Billion Summit and resources Change Engine also hosts the Mission Billion Summit, an annual one-day convening for founders, funders and policymakers aimed at India's next 100 non-profit unicorns. The 2027 edition is announced for 12 February 2027 in New Delhi. For the 2026 edition the site reports more than 300 attendees, more than 40 speakers and more than 150 organisations. The site also carries a Parivartan Dialogues video series for early-stage founders, a blog, and the playbook, which can be downloaded after leaving a name, email and organisation. Mentors and advisors The site lists mentors from entrepreneurship, investing and operations, and an advisory board of leaders from business, philanthropy and the social sector. Mentors include founders of Agami, Samagra, iDreamCareer and Avanti Fellows. Contact The programme inbox is ace@changengine.in. The registered office is 24 Pusa Road, Karol Bagh, New Delhi 110005.

Name: Cisco LaunchPad
Description: Cisco LaunchPad is an accelerator for technology startups, run by Cisco Systems and based in Bengaluru. Cisco's own profile gives 2016 as its launch year, and Cisco publishes it on its Cisco for Startups website. What they support The programme is for technology and technology-enabled startups. A Cisco-hosted report describes it as open to mid-to-late stage startups, while a 2016 news report described the first intake as open to early-stage startups. The two accounts differ, so confirm the stage before you apply. The programme focuses largely on Cisco's core technology areas, and startups work with Cisco technologies. Programmes Cisco LaunchPad is the accelerator itself. Startups in it get co-working space within the Cisco campus, work with Cisco technologies, and connections with angel investors and venture capitalists. After graduation they join an alumni programme focused on use-case integration and go-to-market. The site does not say when the next intake opens. Cisco STEP is an enablement platform for Cisco-accelerated startups. It lets them collaborate with mentors, investors and ecosystem partners, and it is a platform rather than a separate intake. The India Technopreneurship Series is a series of workshops that blend business and technology. It ends in a pitch day, where emerging startups and innovators present to corporate leaders. It can be run in individual cities or states, and the site gives no dates for its editions. Facilities and support Startups in the programme work from co-working space within the Cisco campus. Support after graduation includes go-to-market work through the alumni programme. Track record Cisco's startup website reports 100 or more mentors, 100 or more investor connects, 30 or more pilots, 30 or more startups onboarded as Cisco solution partners, and 3,000 or more jobs created. These figures cover Cisco's startup work as a whole, not this programme alone, and the site gives no dates for them. The startup count is not consistent across Cisco's pages. The homepage gives 70 startups, while Cisco's profile of the LaunchPad programme gives 41 startups supported. Both are undated. The startups page also features SatSure, which the site says has seen more than 2 million farmers receive loans through its product. How to apply The site does not say how to apply to LaunchPad or when its next intake opens, and it does not state whether the programme charges fees or takes equity. STEP is for startups Cisco has already accelerated. To bring the India Technopreneurship Series to a city or state, get in touch with the team. Who runs it Cisco Systems, Inc. runs the programme, which is based in Bengaluru.

Name: CoE-IoT
Description: CoE-IoT is the Centre of Excellence for IoT and AI in India. It is a Digital India initiative led by MeitY and NASSCOM, and its Bengaluru brochure describes it as a joint initiative that also involves the Karnataka state government and industry. It helps startups building IoT, AI, machine learning and other deep-tech products move from a working prototype towards a market-ready product. The main centre is in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, with further centres in Gurugram, at IIT Gandhinagar and in Visakhapatnam. How the programmes work The centre runs two startup routes. Incubation gives a startup a seat at the Bengaluru centre for six months, renewable for up to two years based on progress and need. Virtual acceleration is for startups that do not want a seat. It follows the same application route and offers similar support, and it is charged per startup per year. Incubation seats are charged per seat per month, plus GST, at a government subsidised rate. Neither route runs fixed-date cohorts. Startups apply at different times, and the centre takes them on as they are accepted. Who can apply Startups focused on IoT, AI, ML, deep tech or other emerging technologies can apply, and they need at least a prototype. The centre says it is sector agnostic but names AgriTech, HealthTech, Industry 4.0, Energy, Water, CleanTech, Automotive and Smart Cities as preferred areas. Founders should check the current intake on the centre's startup page before applying, because the intake form is hosted by a third-party platform. Facilities The InnovateLab at the Bengaluru centre holds test and measurement equipment, including oscilloscopes, digital multimeters, DC power supplies, waveform generators, logic analysers, vector signal analysers and generators, a power meter and a DC power analyser. Development kits from TI, Bosch, Intel, Qualcomm and Cisco are available for prototyping, and the team gives technical help with building a secure Big Data infrastructure. The Bengaluru site is air-conditioned and covers 9,000 sft, including a 2,500 sft ESD-protected floor. It has 144 seats for startups across open desks, ESD lab tables and cabins, along with a 150-seat seminar hall and meeting rooms. Locations Bengaluru is the main centre, at KEONICS in HSR Layout. Gurugram, Haryana is a second centre. The Gujarat centre sits in the academic block of IIT Gandhinagar, and the Visakhapatnam centre is on the North Campus of Andhra University. The centre's pages do not say which programmes run at each site, so confirm this before applying to a centre outside Bengaluru. Support on offer Startups get mentorship, market access and enterprise connects, including co-create work with enterprise partners and central and state government entities. The centre also lists funding connects and sessions, strategic fundraising through a curated community of investors, cloud credits from curated providers such as AWS and GCP, help with manufacturing partners and product certifications, and support on intellectual property. The centre describes its model as FAME, which stands for funding, incubation, acceleration, mentor support and enterprise connect. Its in-house team also works with incubated startups on hiring, business model refinement, startup metrics and workshops. Incubated startups also get deals and credits from service partners that the centre has vetted. Who runs it Sanjeev Malhotra is the CEO. His background spans hardware and software, and he has set up and led many multinational development centres and operations in India and the US. Archana Kulkarni is the Programme Director and manages the startup programmes. The centre's governing council includes senior officials from MeitY and state governments as well as industry leaders. Contact General enquiries go to coe-iot@nasscom.in. Enterprises that want to join as partners write to co-innovate@nasscom.in.

Name: Conquest
Description: Conquest is a student-led accelerator run by the Center for Entrepreneurial Leadership at BITS Pilani. It takes early-stage, MVP-ready startups through a 6+1 week programme that mixes online mentoring with one in-person week, and it ends with a Demo Day pitch to investors. The programme takes no equity and charges founders nothing. How the programme works The programme opens with a Bootcamp phase in June. For six weeks, cohort founders join online learning sessions and have one-on-one calls with mentors. Small pod sessions bring founders together for peer discussion, and online workshops build practical skills. The final week is an offline phase in Bangalore. It brings founders together for networking events, in-person workshops led by investors, operators and industry experts, and knowledge sessions on problems that early startups commonly face. Coworking space is provided during this week. The programme closes with Demo Day. The top startups of the cohort pitch on stage to a jury made up of venture capital and angel investors. Who can apply Conquest is built for early-stage startups that are actively building and preparing to scale. It is sector-agnostic, so founders from any industry can apply. The programme describes itself as nationwide. Startups are assessed by evaluation partners who are VCs and angel investors. What founders get The programme is equity-free, so founders keep full ownership of their startups during and after the programme. It says it has disbursed non-dilutive grants to startups over the last three years, and it says some selected founders receive grant support. Its network includes over 150 mentors, 50+ investors and operators across domains, by its own count. Founders also get access to resource credits from partners including AWS, Notion and Freshworks. Who runs it The programme is run by students at BITS Pilani, with the Center for Entrepreneurial Leadership as its parent. Alumni named on the site include Atlan, formerly SocialCops, which the site describes as a global data collaboration platform; Sarla Aviation, which works on electric air mobility; and Thinkerbell Labs, which builds learning devices for visually impaired students. Dates and history The site gives two founding markers that do not match. Its home page says Conquest was founded in 2004. Its about page says the programme began in 2002 as a B-Plan competition in BITS Pilani classrooms and grew from there. Both are the programme's own statements. Where it runs The Bootcamp runs online. The in-person week is in Bangalore. The programme's timeline also names a launch event held in Gurugram, which marks the start of the accelerator.

Name: Cultiv8
Description: Cultiv8 is a technology business incubator based in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu. It is the technology business incubator of the Coimbatore Institute of Engineering and Technology (CIET), its host institution, and it describes itself as powered by the Government of India. Its coworking base, Cultiv8 Coworks, is on Gurusamy Nagar, Codissia Road, Peelamedu, Coimbatore. Cultiv8 works with founders across the spectrum, from idea and early-stage teams to more mature startups looking for their next stage of growth. It runs a standing incubation offer alongside a set of accelerator programmes, and channels government seed support to its startups through two schemes: NIDHI-SSS, supported by the Department of Science and Technology, and the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme. What they support Cultiv8 does not restrict itself to a single sector. Its newest sprint, LaunchLite, names a focus on legal tech, real estate tech and agri tech, while its accelerator track has at various points worked with industrial deep-tech teams. Across its programmes it supports founders at idea, prototype and early-traction stages, and its accelerators step in once a startup is validating product-market fit and working on go-to-market. Eligibility is set programme by programme rather than through a single published list. The standing incubation programme is open to startups from idea stage to mature growth-stage ventures. LaunchLite selects on founder attributes — commitment, coachability and an execution mindset — rather than on how polished an idea is. The past Overseas Accelerator batch was open only to startups based in Tamil Nadu. Programmes Cultiv8's standing offer is its Incubation Program, which gives startups coworking space in Coimbatore, mentoring and technical expertise, partner software credits, community networking, and access to government seed support through NIDHI-SSS and the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme. LaunchLite is the newest live programme: a four-week, venture-studio-led execution sprint for idea-stage and very early-stage founders, run as an operator-led founder sprint rather than a taught course. It has an open registration form. Several accelerator batches are run as closed cohorts between intakes. The Overseas Accelerator Program 2024 equipped a group of Tamil Nadu startups with a global entrepreneurial lens, facilitated by Jumpstart Studio in Australia in partnership with Payirgal. Accelerator 2.0 focused on product-market-fit validation and go-to-market execution with hands-on mentorship, and Accelerator 1.0 accelerated eleven startups, three of which expanded into global markets, with over 250 hours of mentoring and go-to-market support. Cultiv8 also describes an Intrapreneurship Accelerator for industrial deep-tech solutions and an Idea to Business programme for aspiring entrepreneurs, though neither states a current intake. Facilities and support Cultiv8 offers its startups coworking space in Coimbatore, at Cultiv8 Coworks in Peelamedu. Its incubation offer also includes mentoring and technical expertise, a startup community to network and learn in, and partner software credits. Track record On its own counters Cultiv8 reports more than 150 startups supported, more than 60 products released and more than 8 patents filed. These are the incubator's own self-reported figures. Its pages give different totals for the seed and follow-on funding its startups have drawn, so those are best read as orders of magnitude rather than settled counts. How to apply Applications are made programme by programme through an online form. The Incubation Program and LaunchLite each have their own application form on the Cultiv8 site, and LaunchLite's selection weighs founder commitment and execution over idea maturity. The past accelerator batches are shown as completed cohorts without an open intake, so founders interested in those should check the accelerator page for the next round. General queries go to business@thecultiv8.com.

Name: DDTII
Description: The Defence Design and Technology Incubator of India (DDTII) is an incubator for startups that want to build or sell technology in the aerospace and defence sector. Karnavati University set it up to nurture innovation and research in defence, space and allied industries, and it operates as a not-for-profit section 8 company. How programmes work DDTII runs a set of programmes that follow a startup's path from idea to market. The earliest programme, Startup – Xcite, supports early-stage green-field startups that are still exploring an idea. Its mentoring and funding help a team build a working prototype and show proof of concept. Startup – Xpand Seed takes teams that have already proven the concept and need help finishing a full product and building a minimum viable product. Startup – Xcelerate Growth sits between them as a traction-stage programme for early-stage green-field startups. Startup Xcavate is an outreach effort that scouts and engages defence-domain startups, and Startup – Xpert connects startups with aerospace and defence mentors through DDTII and allied programmes under SSIP. DDTII also runs defence innovation challenges with Karnavati University and the Indian Army. The second edition, Defence Innovation Challenge 2.0, ran applications in 2023 and has closed. Who can apply DDTII supports startups that want to explore or venture into the aerospace and defence sector. It accepts both green-field startups, which are new ventures, and brown-field startups. The programme pages describe the stage a team should be at, from an exploration-stage idea to a prototype that shows proof of concept, so check the stage before you apply. Challenges set their own eligibility. The most recent published challenge rules limited entry to DPIIT-recognised startups and MSMEs with a product in one of the listed defence categories. Who runs it DDTII is an incubator of Karnavati University, Gandhinagar. The university describes the incubator as one of its initiatives for defence innovation, and it works with Karnavati Innovation and Incubation Foundation (KIIF) on the same agenda. DDTII describes itself as a not-for-profit section 8 company. Locations DDTII's office is at Uvarsad-Vavol Road, Uvarsad, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. The site lists this as its only address.

Name: DERBI Foundation
Description: DERBI Foundation is a healthcare-focused incubator in Bengaluru, run as the Dayananda Sagar Entrepreneurship Research and Business Incubation Foundation. It grew out of the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Centre set up for Dayananda Sagar Institutions in 2009, and was created as a foundation in 2015 with financial and other support from NSTEDB, the Department of Science & Technology's entrepreneurship board. It sits on the DSU Innovation Campus at Kudlu Gate on Hosur Road. How programmes work DERBI runs a ladder rather than a menu, and it is worth reading in order. PACE is the entry point: a 16-week hands-on programme for founders who need to validate a problem, build a first proof of concept and get to a pitch. Completing PACE gives direct entry to GALLOP, so the 16 weeks are themselves a route into incubation rather than a separate application. GALLOP is the two-year incubation programme, for healthcare startups already working on a proof of concept or an MVP. EMERGE sits at the top of the ladder for later-stage healthcare startups with something ready to deploy or trial, though its published timeline has not moved since 2022, so treat it as between intakes and ask. Alongside the ladder, DERBI runs a BIONEST bio-incubation track under BIRAC, and five named funding schemes: NIDHI EiR, NIDHI PRAYAS and NIDHI SSS from DST, MeitY TIDE 2.0, and the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme. On its Current Programs page DERBI lists BIONEST, the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme and DigiKey events as what is running now. Everything goes through one form. The Pitch To Us page asks which programme you want, which funding scheme you want, your problem statement, your innovation, your stage, and a pitch deck upload. A sample deck is downloadable from the same page. Who can apply PACE is open to early-stage startups or individual founders with a clear problem statement, across India, with hybrid participation from Bengaluru encouraged. The constraint that will decide it for most people is stated up front: at least one founder must be available full-time for the whole 16 weeks. Building alongside a job will not work here. PACE takes medtech and healthtech, wellness and sports tech, sustainability and greentech, and space tech. GALLOP is narrower — startups in healthcare and allied areas, working on proof of concept and MVP development. The funding schemes each carry their own national eligibility rules, and DERBI publishes them. NIDHI EiR is for Indian citizens with a science or engineering qualification who are willing to go full-time, and the recipient must register for DERBI's pre-incubation programme for the whole period of support. NIDHI PRAYAS is for individual innovators aged 18 or over, teams of innovators, or existing incubatees of a PRAYAS centre whose company is under two years old with no significant revenue. PRAYAS has real exclusions worth reading before you start: the project must involve physical product development, so software-only and pure academic research projects are not eligible; doctoral students on long-term research projects and teaching academics are not supported; and ideas whose intellectual property would vest with an institution are out. MeitY TIDE 2.0 takes idea-to-proof-of-concept technology startups, working professionals, aspiring entrepreneurs and students. Facilities The reason to look at DERBI is the Prayas Shala lab, co-named with DigiKey. Most incubators say "lab access" and stop there. DERBI publishes an instrument-by-instrument list with model numbers, an equipment list with charge details, a components bank list and an online sample-submission form. What is on the bench points squarely at medical devices. Alongside the spectroscopy you would expect — confocal laser RAMAN, FTIR and UV/VIS — it holds a Fluke ProSim 3 vital-sign simulator for ECG, pacemaker, arrhythmia, respiration, blood pressure and cardiac output testing, and an ESA609 electrical safety analyser. Electrical safety testing is a mandatory gate for a medical device and normally means booking an external test house, so having it on the bench during development rather than at the end is a real advantage for a hardware team. The rest supports the same story: a PCB and SMT line with a prototype milling machine, pick-and-place and reflow oven, Tektronix oscilloscopes and test gear, NI CompactDAQ sensor rigs, a Stratasys uPrint SE 3D printer and an Artec Eva Lite scanner, a small machine shop with a benchtop lathe and laser cutter, and a DELL 5820 workstation with LabVIEW and MATLAB. DERBI's promoter director also describes a route to approved clinical trials through CDSIMER, the group's medical school, on top of pilot trials at Sagar hospitals. Scale DERBI's homepage counters report 185 startups supported, 1,400 startups reached, 32 startups invested in, 84 given grants or fellowships, 1,080 jobs created and 200 sector experts. The Director's Message repeats the 185, 84 and 32 figures. Other pages do not agree with each other: the PACE page's counter strip claims 220+ startups incubated and 120+ grants and fellowships, and the three pages give mentoring hours as 1,500+, 2,400+ and 14,175. All of these are self-reported and undated, and we have not verified any of them. Who runs it Sathyanarayana B V is CEO. The team page names Bhavani G as Incubation Manager, Dr. Santhiya Sasidharan as Innovation Lab Coordinator and Dr. Adithya Hande as Associate Manager for Clinical Research. The Governing Council is chaired by Mr. Vidyashankar M N and includes Rohan Prem Sagar as promoter director, Samir Kumar of Inventus Capital India, Anand Kumar of Bugworks, A Vijayarajan of InnAccel Technologies, Dr. Vishal Rao of HCG Cancer Centre, Dr. Nandakumar Jairam and T R Anand. DERBI also runs a Clinical Mentor Forum of practising doctors from HCG, Sagar Hospitals, NU Hospitals and others. Locations The main address is the DSU Innovation Campus at Kudlu Gate, Hongasandra Village, Hosur Road, Bangalore 560068. The host campus is at Shavige Malleshwara Hills, Kumaraswamy Layout, Bengaluru 560078, and there is an off-Bangalore site at CDSIMER in Devarakaggalahalli, Harohalli, on Kanakapura Road in Ramanagara district. DERBI lists one careers opening, for a Lab Manager in Bangalore, though that posting is dated 2024. Its events page is currently empty.

Name: Deshpande Startups
Description: Deshpande Startups is the working name of the Foundation for Sandboxstartup Initiatives (FSSI), a technology business incubator on a six-acre campus on Gokul Road in Hubballi, Karnataka, near the airport. It describes itself as a two-state, government-recognised Technology Business Incubation centre established under DST-NSTEDB, and says it has been building for non-metro India since 2016. Its second campus is KREST, the Kanwal Rekhi Rural Entrepreneurship and Startup Centre, in Nizamabad, Telangana. The organisation is one of several under the Deshpande name. This page covers the incubator only. Deshpande Foundation and the Deshpande Skilling campus next door are separate bodies; the incubator names them as routes to a rural network and to local hiring, not as things it runs. What they support The incubation programme is sector agnostic. Across the site the portfolio is sorted into agritech, cleantech, consumer tech, edtech, food tech, hardtech, healthtech, media and internet, mobility, online services, recruitment, SaaS and SME tech. Two of the government programmes are narrower: the MeitY GENESIS schemes want technology-led work in electronics design and manufacturing, IT, ICT and deep tech, and they are restricted to founders based in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. Deshpande Startups groups its own programmes by how far along a founder is. Student founders start at YUVA Validate. Idea-to-prototype founders go to Grind2Growth, MeitY EIR, NIDHI EIR or NIDHI PRAYAS. Prototype-to-MVP founders go to the Incubation programme or the MeitY GENESIS Pilot. Early-revenue founders go to Acceleration or the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme. Founders past product-market fit go to Bridge2Bharat Hubballi or the MeitY Matching Fund. How programmes work Incubation runs for twelve months and is described as a lab-to-market programme for startups past the prototyping stage. It takes 2 per cent equity. After the twelve months, founders keep alumni benefits and access to the ecosystem for a further two years. Selection runs through a pitching contest: you apply, email your business deck, a committee of experts shortlists, shortlisted startups pitch virtually to a panel, and selected startups are onboarded. Acceleration is a sixteen-week cohort programme for early-revenue and market-ready startups. It covers growth and productivity training, marketing and promotion mentoring, peer networking and partnership building, and sessions with investors and financial institutions. Selection is a call for applications, screening, a jury pitch, due diligence, then an agreement and onboarding. Three named acceleration cohorts are shown on the site, all closed: Agri and Food Acceleration, run with I-Venture @ISB, Elevate Women Acceleration, and We Enable Bharat Acceleration. YUVA Validate is a five-week hybrid programme for student founders and is free for those selected. Most of it is self-paced, with live sessions on Saturdays and a few mandatory days on campus. Cohorts run through the year, applications are open year round, and you pick your cohort on the form. Grind2Growth is a six-month entrepreneurship development programme for early-stage and pre-revenue founders from North Karnataka. Each month covers one theme, from entrepreneurial foundations through business fundamentals, product and finance, storytelling, sales and finally funding readiness, delivered as live workshops, recorded content, community events and mentoring. The rest are government schemes that Deshpande Startups delivers as a host or implementing agency. NIDHI EIR and NIDHI PRAYAS come from the Department of Science and Technology; the incubator says it has been an approved NIDHI PRAYAS centre since March 2020. The MeitY GENESIS programmes come from MeitY Startup Hub and cover an entrepreneur-in-residence track, equity-based pilot funding for startups holding a work order from a large corporate or PSU, and a matching investment for startups that have already raised private money. On all three you apply on the MeitY portal and name Deshpande Startups as your first implementing agency preference. The Startup India Seed Fund Scheme is applied for on the Startup India portal, where the incubator is listed under its legal name. Facilities Infinity Innovation Labs is the hardware side of the campus, backed by IESA, the Government of Karnataka and DST. It has four labs. The Mechanical Lab has CNC, conventional and hand-tool zones, with metal laser cutting and bending, a CNC lathe and welding. The ESDM or PCB assembly lab covers 2,700 sq ft with an ESD-safe floor, a Fuji SMT line and sand-dust, rain, vibration and environmental test chambers. The 3D lab runs FDM, SLA and SLS printing across more than 1,500 sq ft. The electronics lab, 1,500 sq ft, holds spectrum analysers, oscilloscopes, development boards and multimeters. Each lab lists technical consultation alongside the machines. The campus also rents space. Co-working comes as daily, weekly and monthly passes, with a team pass for startups under ten people on a minimum three-month agreement. Dedicated private offices total 4,271 sq ft. Beyond the offices there is an industrial shed of 11,510 sq ft, currently full, and 87,120 sq ft of experimental land for field trials, agritech and prototype testing, most of it available. Event space runs to a 500-seat open amphitheatre, a 110-seat auditorium and a conference room for ten to fifteen people. KREST in Nizamabad has a 3,000 sq ft prototyping lab, 4,000 sq ft of dedicated incubation space, a 100-seat co-working area and room for more than thirty startups. Scale The incubator's own counters report 521 or more startups supported, more than 3,100 jobs created and more than 120 patents granted. It says it connects founders with over 40 mentors who have given more than 200 hours of guidance, and puts its community at more than 500 founders, entrepreneurs, experts and investors. The labs report more than 549 prototypes executed and 179 innovators, startups and SMEs supported. These are self-reported figures published on the site, and some of the per-programme counters elsewhere on the site do not line up with them. Named portfolio companies include NanoPix, which builds cashew grading machines, Sonic Lamb from Rapture Innovation Labs, the water intelligence company FluxGen, Mitti Cafe, Local Narratives, WeMakeScholars, the drone logistics company Airbound, LinkEz Technologies, Widemobility Mechatronics and Safehands 24x7. Who runs it Raju Reddy chairs the board, alongside directors Ramanathan N, Rachit Parekh and Manish Jaiswal. Manish Jaiswal is also the chief executive. Jaishree and Gururaj Desh Deshpande are named as the founders behind it. The careers page carries the incubator's own openings, and a separate board lists jobs going at portfolio startups. Where they are The Hubballi campus is on Gokul Road, Hubballi 580030. The KREST campus is in Nizamabad, Telangana. Community events, the Founder's Dialogue and the Startup Dialogue run from both regions.

Facilities Infinity Innovation Labs is the hardware side of the campus, backed by IESA, the Government of Karnataka and DST. It has four labs. The Mechanical Lab has CNC, conventional and hand-tool zones, with metal laser cutting and bending, a CNC lathe and welding. The ESDM or PCB assembly lab covers 2,700 sq ft with an ESD-safe floor, a Fuji SMT line and sand-dust, rain, vibration and environmental test chambers. The 3D lab runs FDM, SLA and SLS printing across more than 1,500 sq ft. The electronics lab, 1,500 sq ft, holds spectrum analysers, oscilloscopes, development boards and multimeters. Each lab lists technical consultation alongside the machines. The campus also rents space. Co-working comes as daily, weekly and monthly passes, with a team pass for startups under ten people on a minimum three-month agreement. Dedicated private offices total 4,271 sq ft. Beyond the offices there is an industrial shed of 11,510 sq ft, currently full, and 87,120 sq ft of experimental land for field trials, agritech and prototype testing, most of it available. Event space runs to a 500-seat open amphitheatre, a 110-seat auditorium and a conference room for ten to fifteen people. KREST in Nizamabad has a 3,000 sq ft prototyping lab, 4,000 sq ft of dedicated incubation space, a 100-seat co-working area and room for more than thirty startups. It says it connects founders with over 40 mentors who have given more than 200 hours of guidance, and puts its community at more than 500 founders, entrepreneurs, experts and investors. The labs report more than 549 prototypes executed and 179 innovators, startups and SMEs supported. These are self-reported figures published on the site, and some of the per-programme counters elsewhere on the site do not line up with them. Named portfolio companies include NanoPix, which builds cashew grading machines, Sonic Lamb from Rapture Innovation Labs, the water intelligence company FluxGen, Mitti Cafe, Local Narratives, WeMakeScholars, the drone logistics company Airbound, LinkEz Technologies, Widemobility Mechatronics and Safehands 24x7. Who runs it Raju Reddy chairs the board, alongside directors Ramanathan N, Rachit Parekh and Manish Jaiswal. Manish Jaiswal is also the chief executive. Jaishree and Gururaj Desh Deshpande are named as the founders behind it. The careers page carries the incubator's own openings, and a separate board lists jobs going at portfolio startups. Where they are The Hubballi campus is on Gokul Road, Hubballi 580030. The KREST campus is in Nizamabad, Telangana. Community events, the Founder's Dialogue and the Startup Dialogue run from both regions.

Name: Encubay
Description: Encubay is a platform that connects founders, investors, financial institutions and innovation hubs. It runs programmes for founders in India, and its pages describe activity in other countries too, although the list of countries differs from page to page. How programmes work Most of Encubay's founder programmes run through introductions and invitations rather than an open application. Its pages describe a small number of named programmes, and a wider set of gatherings and networks. The Fempreneurs Accelerator Program is a four-month programme for women founders, designed to prepare them for fundraising. Its sessions cover vision, scaling, networking, personal branding and fundraising, and are led by industry experts. The partner is named differently across the site: the homepage names the US Department of State, while the Our Work page names the US Consulate. The site describes one completed cohort of 30 members and gives no open intake date. The Tech FoundHER Challenge is run with Prosus and VAIA Climate. It is a challenge-based accelerator for women-led tech startups in India, offering equity-free grants, mentorship and access to an investor panel. The case study says 30 startups were shortlisted from more than 500 applications. The challenge is described as completed, and no open call is stated. Influence Lab is a curated programme that helps founders shape their narrative and visibility. Encubay also offers fundraising support through warm introductions to investors, narrative refinement and process discipline. Both are by introduction or invitation. The Encubay Angel Network was launched so that women and men can fund female-led startups together. The About page does not give its current status, cheque size or entry route. The site also describes dedicated programmes that connect early-stage founders with funders through pitch sessions, mentorship and direct investor introductions. It describes structured conversations between vetted founders and investors, invite-only roundtables for growth-stage founders, and invite-only gatherings for senior leaders. Its events calendar lists invitation-only international delegations for founders, investors and family offices, including upcoming events in Singapore and Davos. Fees, dates and entry routes are not stated for most of these. Who can apply The Fempreneurs programme is for women founders. The Tech FoundHER Challenge is for women-led tech startups in India. The Angel Network's focus is female-led startups. The pitch, roundtable and fundraising offers are for early-stage and growth-stage founders. Several gatherings are for investors, family offices and senior leaders rather than founders, and the site does not state eligibility for most of them. Scale The homepage says Encubay has accelerated more than 10,000 founders through its initiatives. It also lists over 600 investment partners, over 100 ecosystem partners and seven countries. The About page gives different figures: 1,000+ investors, 30+ countries, and 10,000+ ecosystem members across founders, investors and corporates, which it reports for 2024. It also says it has engaged 100+ corporate partners, and its Our Work page lists 30+ institutional engagements. These are the organisation's own figures, and its pages do not agree with each other. They are reported here as claims, not verified totals. Partners and collaborations Its pages name collaborations with DIFC, Hub71, ADGM, HSBC, DBS and Barclays, and list EDB, the US Consulate and the Dubai Chamber as trusted partners. Case studies on the Our Work page cover work with Google for Developers, with OneValley, and a NETWORK HER conference with DBS, supported by Microsoft for Startups. Who runs it The About page credits Deeksha Ahuja with launching its ecosystem initiatives, including the angel network and a mentoring programme with the US Government. The About page gives 2020 as the founding year. A third-party directory gives 2019. Locations The site does not give a street address, so none is published here. Its pages describe operations across India, the UAE, the United States and Europe. The homepage also lists Singapore, which the privacy policy omits. Two third-party directories place the organisation in Pune, India; neither is the organisation's own statement.

Name: Evolvex Accelerator
Description: EvolveX Accelerator is a cohort-based startup accelerator that invests in early-stage startups in exchange for equity and runs a structured programme of mentorship for the founders it selects. The site brands the programme as EvolveX by WFC, part of WeFounderCircle, and lists its main office in Surat, Gujarat, with additional offices in Bengaluru and the National Capital Region. EvolveX describes itself as sector-agnostic, and names Fintech, SaaS, AI, D2C, CleanTech, AgriTech and EdTech among the areas it backs. It is built for founders raising their first cheque at pre-seed or seed stage, and it takes equity in the startups it selects rather than running on fees. How the programme works The EvolveX Accelerator Program runs as a cohort over roughly three months, with training sessions led by industry experts and CXOs. The accelerator invests in selected startups in exchange for equity, and alongside the investment it provides mentorship across the course of the programme. EvolveX's pages do not describe the delivery format consistently: one page calls the programme hybrid, with both online and in-person sessions, while another describes it as conducted online, so a founder should check the current programme page for how a given cohort will run. The accelerator has been inviting applications for its eighth cohort. Who can apply The programme is aimed at early-stage, India-based founders who are seeking their first cheque at pre-seed or seed stage. EvolveX asks that applicant startups be recognised by DPIIT. It is open to teams at ideation, proof-of-concept and MVP stage, and startups that are already generating early revenue can apply as well. Scale EvolveX's own pages do not agree on how many startups it has backed or how many cohorts it has run. One programme page states it has invested in a certain number of startups across its past cohorts, while other pages give a lower count across fewer cohorts, and the portfolio page separately lists cohorts running from January 2022 through to a cohort that began in January 2025. Because these counts conflict, they are best read as rough orders of magnitude rather than a settled total. EvolveX says it typically selects a handful of startups in each cohort. Locations The site's footer gives the main office as The Financial Supermarket on Ring Road in Surat, Gujarat, and lists further offices in Bengaluru and in the National Capital Region. Founders researching EvolveX by its parent brand will also see it referred to as EvolveX by WFC, under WeFounderCircle. How to apply Applications are made through an online application form linked from the EvolveX for-founders page, and the accelerator also accepts enquiries by email. EvolveX describes an evaluation process that runs over several weeks and several rounds of discussion before shortlisted founders pitch to its investment committee; its pages give different estimates for how long that evaluation takes, so treat the timeline as approximate. The current for-founders page indicates that a new cohort is open for applications.

Name: Fibonacci X
Description: Fibonacci X is a Gurugram-based venture accelerator that also describes itself as a global M&A and holding company. Its home page says it offers three things: acceleration, mergers and acquisitions advice, and investments. On the investing side it says it is a syndicate made up of founders, HNIs and family offices, and that it invests in promising early and growth-stage ventures. For acceleration it says it works closely with founders through a high-touch, non-cohort model tailored to each company's growth journey, so there is no batch to apply to and no fixed programme calendar. The firm says it is built for Bharat and reaches global markets, with India as home base and Dubai, New York and London named as its wider corridor. Its thesis page is explicit about what it looks for. It says it wants business models that fit India's diversity and changing consumer landscape, and it names four themes: middle India, Gen Z and Gen Alpha consumers, a productivity layer built on India's skilled but underemployed workforce, and employment, including hiring, skilling and workforce management. It lists its principles as curiosity, first principles, dharmic capitalism, Bharat first, patience with market cycles and integrity. The portfolio page shows what that looks like in practice. The companies listed span food and wellness, specialty coffee, pet care, on-demand services, agritech, fintech, AI and analytics, edtech, mental wellness, hospitality, enterprise technology and lab-grown jewellery, including names such as Groww, OYO and InCred. That is a consumer-leaning mix with fintech and technology alongside it, rather than one narrow sector. The home page also says the firm takes in 6–8 startups a year, which tells you it is selective. The way in is the Pitch to us page. It asks for your name, mobile number, email, LinkedIn profile and company name, and says the team reads every submission and replies to the ones that fit its thesis. You can also write to the general inbox listed on the site. The site does not publish eligibility rules, a deadline, a fund size or a cheque size, so expect an investor conversation rather than a programme with set steps. It also lists a mentor and advisor network spread across investment, product and customer, and a library of videos, reports and press coverage that is worth reading before you pitch.

Description: First World Accelerator (FWA) is a startup and investor accelerator that works online from firstworldaccelerator.in. What they support FWA's offerings fall into three groups. For investors, corporates and organisations, it runs a paid Enterprise Membership that opens access to its pool of startups and innovators so members can identify teams to invest in or collaborate with. For founders, it offers a mentoring service that runs from ideation through to marketing, including design and prototype exercises, industry collaboration and connections across countries. For companies looking to hire, it runs a talent-pipeline programme that pairs them with students from partner colleges and universities who work on company-related problems before being hired. FWA presents itself as sector-agnostic, open to innovators and startups across fields rather than tied to one industry. The site does not publish eligibility criteria, intake dates or selection rounds for most of what it offers, so founders should confirm current terms directly with the team. How the mentoring works The mentoring service is reached through FWA's sign-up path for startups and innovators. As described on its pages, mentoring moves a venture from early ideation to marketing through a series of design and prototype exercises aimed at building new revenue streams, and it draws on FWA's cross-country network to help with industry collaboration, reducing production cost, and export and import opportunities. The pages do not set out a cohort structure, a duration or a selection process. Partnerships and reach FWA says it operates through strategic alliances with organisations in several countries, naming the United States, the United Kingdom, Western Europe, India, Malaysia and Japan among them, and describes its purpose as helping investors, startups and enterprises collaborate and grow across that network. These are the platform's own descriptions of its reach; the site does not name specific partner organisations in a way that can be independently confirmed here, so treat the network as reported rather than verified. How to apply There is no single application. Investors and organisations sign up through the Enterprise Membership path and pay a registration fee to join. Founders enter through FWA's sign-up route for startups and innovators to reach the mentoring service. Companies interested in the talent-pipeline programme, and the colleges and universities that supply students to it, follow their own sign-up paths on the site. Because the pages do not state deadlines or cohort dates, anyone interested should check the current status with FWA before applying.

Name: Flipkart Leap
Description: Flipkart Leap is the startup accelerator run by Flipkart, the Indian e-commerce company. It is a corporate programme rather than a separate incubator: there is no campus, no office space and no registered incubation entity behind it, and Flipkart's own people run it. It works online, and startups from anywhere in India can apply. The programme is split into two tracks that do quite different things. Flipkart Leap Ahead, shortened to FLA, is the investment track. Flipkart Leap Innovation Network, shortened to FLIN, is the pilot track. A founder can apply to one or to both, and the site is clear that they have different objectives. How programmes work Leap Ahead is built around Flipkart taking equity. Flipkart Leap says the track exists to find early-stage startups that could disrupt the digital ecosystem, and to back them with investment and growth acceleration. The investment is made by Flipkart Ventures, Flipkart's investment arm, and Flipkart Leap describes it as financial rather than strategic. Selected startups then go through a sixty-day programme meant to set them up for faster growth, ending in a demo day with invite-only investors. Alongside the money, startups get a curriculum built with founders and operators, mentoring from senior Flipkart people, introductions inside the Flipkart ecosystem and to the wider investor community, and help co-developing the core product and the strategy around it. Leap Innovation Network works the other way round. Instead of investing, Flipkart buys. Selected startups get paid pilots, deploy their solution on Flipkart, and work directly with Flipkart product and engineering teams. A pilot that goes well can turn into a commercial partnership, and Flipkart Leap says startups may also be considered for investment afterwards. Startups keep sole ownership of the intellectual property they already have and of anything they build during the programme; Flipkart Leap notes that ownership may be revisited only if both sides go on to sign a deeper partnership. Both tracks share a curriculum. The modules are delivered with Bain and cover business strategy, being a founder, performance and finance management, engineering strategy, finding product-market fit and knowing when to pivot, and fundraising, down to practical sessions on compliance and on startup finance. Cohort pages also list named Flipkart senior vice-presidents against the subject each one mentors on, from supply chain and marketplaces to data, growth, corporate affairs and finance. Who can apply There is no fee for either track. Flipkart Leap states plainly that startups do not need to be based in Bengaluru and that any startup can apply. For Leap Ahead, the published criteria are that the startup is based in India, is tech-first and uses GenAI in its core solution or product, and is preferably between seed and Series A. Its application form asks which country the company is registered in, so an incorporated company is assumed. The sectors named on the Leap Ahead page are fintech, healthtech, logistics and supply chain, AI and machine learning, consumer tech across social, content and new commerce models, retail SaaS, sustainability, gaming, native AI, quick commerce enablement and drone tech. An older answer elsewhere on the site describes the same track as backing pre-seed and seed startups and lists a slightly different sector set, including edtech and Web3, so the two do not agree. For Leap Innovation Network, the bar is a working business rather than a stage label: Flipkart Leap says the track suits startups that have a viable product and are already shipping to consumers in its areas of focus. Those areas are rewritten for each cohort. The ones currently published are next-generation logistics and hyperlocal intelligence, next-generation AI infrastructure and compute efficiency, and autonomous systems with continuous quality evaluation — in practice, deep-tech teams working on last-mile delivery, large GPU and CPU fleets, and self-monitoring production systems. Selection is the same shape on both tracks. Startups fill in the application form, applications are evaluated, and shortlisted startups are called for an interview before the final cohort is picked. Flipkart Leap says the cohort is not capped at a set number of startups and that selection is merit and opportunity based. Applying today This is the part to check before you spend time on it. Leap Ahead is not accepting applications: its own application page says entries are closed, and the site still promises that dates for the next Leap Ahead cohort will be announced. Leap Innovation Network's apply link points at a sixth cohort on an external application platform, and its themes were rewritten recently, so that call looks live — but no closing date for it is published, and the announcement bar across the top of the site is out of date, still advertising the fifth cohort and a deadline that has passed, even though the fifth cohort's startups are already named on the site. If the timing matters to you, write to the programme inbox and ask which cohort is open before you start the form. Track record Flipkart Leap has been running since at least 2021, when its inaugural cohort of eight startups was announced. It has since published five Innovation Network cohorts and three Leap Ahead cohorts. Named alumni include ANS Commerce, Entropik, Fashinza, Gully Network, Piggy, Tagbox, Unbox Robotics and Wolkus Tech from the first batch, Expertia.AI, Factors.ai, Visa2Fly and Tune from the third Leap Ahead cohort, and Bureau, Warebee, Nudgebee, AccelData, Adaptive6, Ayudo and Keploy from the fourth and fifth Innovation Network cohorts. Flipkart Leap's home page also claims it has partnered with more than twenty-five startups globally, but that sentence sits next to a line saying the network is in its third edition, which the rest of the site contradicts, so treat the count as out of date. Where it runs The programme runs primarily online. Flipkart Leap says startups may be asked on site for some pitching or co-working sessions where that is feasible, but that startups arrange their own travel and stay and do not work from Flipkart premises. There is no published postal address for the programme; queries go to its shared email inbox.

Name: FounderX
Description: FounderX is a 12-week startup fellowship run by Inc42, the media and research company operated by Ideope Media Private Limited. It is a cohort-based programme that aims to take aspiring founders from an early idea to a launch-ready startup, ending in a Demo Day. Ideope Media's registered office is at 59/16, 3rd Floor, R.D. Marg, Kalkaji, New Delhi 110019, and FounderX runs as a hybrid programme, mostly online with a smaller in-person component. What they support FounderX is built for working professionals rather than for founders already running a company full-time. Its stated eligibility is a minimum of two years of work experience, and it describes its intake as including corporate professionals, solopreneurs, traditional business owners, early pre-revenue founders and people returning to entrepreneurship. The programme is open to applicants across India. Because it is a time-boxed, paid cohort that ends in a Demo Day rather than an open-ended residency, it reads as an accelerator-style fellowship rather than an incubator: there is no coworking or incubation space, and the in-person element is limited to a small number of events. The programme FounderX runs over 12 weeks, which the programme also describes as three months. The format is hybrid, with the large majority delivered online and a smaller share in person. The curriculum is built around a set of hands-on sessions and workshops that walk a founder through the stages of starting up, taught by a faculty drawn from startup founders, investors and operators. The programme states it has more than 30 such mentors and faculty on its panel and more than 25 hands-on sessions and workshops across the cohort. The programme closes with a Demo Day, where founders pitch to investors. One founder, judged on the strength of the pitch, receives an equity-free grant, and participating founders are given the chance to raise pre-seed funding from investors. FounderX is a paid programme: there is an application fee, which it states is fully refundable if an applicant is not selected, followed by an enrolment fee for those offered a place. Scale FounderX describes an alumni network of more than 100 founders. These are the programme's own figures rather than independently audited numbers. The exact live cohort number is not stated consistently across the site, so the current intake is best confirmed on the application page itself. Who runs it FounderX is a product of Ideope Media Private Limited and carries the Inc42 brand. The same company operates Inc42's media and research work, and FounderX is its founder-education programme. The in-person touchpoints are split across cities: an orientation is held in Bengaluru and the convocation in the Delhi-NCR region, with founders meeting the rest of the programme online. How to apply Application is a staged process. A founder first submits the application form and pays a refundable application fee. The FounderX curation team then reviews applications, and shortlisted candidates are invited to an interview. Those who are offered a place complete enrolment by paying the remaining programme fee. Intake runs in rounds with their own deadlines, so the open round and its dates are best checked on the FounderX site before applying.
