Name: Invention Engine
Description: Invention Engine is a founder-led accelerator for early-stage AI and deeptech startups. It runs one programme, a six-month accelerator called ACE, and its published address is at 91 Springboard, Udyog Vihar, Sector 18, Gurugram, in the Delhi NCR region. The footer of its site names the operating entity as Big Bets Accelerator LLP. The accelerator describes itself as a co-founding partner rather than a mentor panel. Its own words are that it embeds like a co-founding team and works side by side with entrepreneurs for six months, and that it was built by AI entrepreneurs rather than consultants or academics. Three people are listed as its founders: Varun Aggarwal, Shailendra Nath Jha and Shubham Bansal. How ACE works ACE runs for six months and is described as high-intensity and based in Delhi NCR. The accelerator invests in each selected company, gives more than 120 hours of one-to-one time with its own founders, and handles recruiting, finance and legal work so the team can stay on product and go-to-market. The programme is laid out as six stages. It starts with backing high-agency, technically strong founders, then moves to nailing the Ideal Customer Profile and sharpening user segmentation, iterating the product through user feedback and hands-on product sprints, running tight feedback loops to get closer to product-market fit, shaping a fundraising and scale strategy with investor-ready narratives and models, and finally crafting a focused go-to-market strategy and testing real traction channels. Cohort companies also get early access to a Global Customer Advisory Board. This is a group of senior operators based in the US, Europe and Singapore who help founders validate products, sharpen positioning and work out how to sell abroad. The site lists more than twenty of them, in product, engineering, sales and consulting roles at companies including Meta, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, AMD and McKinsey. Alongside it are an AI advisory group of researchers and practitioners, and a set of ACE mentors drawn from product leadership and founder backgrounds. Two anonymised case studies on the ACE page show the kind of work involved: repositioning a niche edtech video tool as a creator-first AI video platform, and helping a horizontal voice AI company pick BFSI as its wedge, close its first large enterprise contracts and raise seed capital through the accelerator's investor syndicate. Who can apply Invention Engine states four things it looks for. The startup should have been operating for the last six to twelve months and have a product or an MVP, preferably with a few users. The team should be able to move to Delhi NCR for most of the six months. It is aimed at people who have worked in product-based companies and want to build in AI, and at anyone keen to build products from zero to one, including people still in college, provided they have a working product. The accelerator says it typically works with startups from prototype or MVP stage through early traction and early scale, and that it stays open to exceptional teams at an earlier stage if the problem, approach and ambition are compelling. There is no stated incorporation requirement, no state or category restriction and no minimum funding bar. The only hard condition on the page is the relocation one. The sector focus is narrow and explicit: AI and deeptech. The accelerator says plainly that it is not a scouting platform for funds. How to apply Applications run through an online form reached from the Apply for Cohort button on the home page and the ACE page. The published timeline has four steps: an invitation for applications, one-to-one nurturing sessions with the accelerator's founders, a one-week in-house evaluation programme ending in an offer, and then the cohort start. The current call on the site is for the 2026 cohort, with no closing date published. Portfolio The cohort page names Cheerio, an AI CPaaS platform for no-code messaging automation; Desible AI, an agentic voice AI platform for BFSI; SuperStars AI, a fantasy cricket platform built around creator-driven gameplay; Flowbee AI, an assistant for growing on LinkedIn; Rapture Innovation Labs, working on personal audio; Magicroll.ai, which transforms video using AI; and Callprep, which prepares sales teams before customer calls. The accelerator's news strip also features Sonic Lamb, a deeptech audio company that appeared on Shark Tank season four and was incubated in the 2024 cohort, and Magicroll.ai winning the AI, DeepTech and Cyber category at the Startup Maharathi Challenge during Startup Mahakumbh after the 2023 cohort. Callprep was selected for WTFunds. In March 2026, Indian startup press reported that four of its portfolio companies — Sonic Lamb, Cheerio AI, Desible.ai and Magicroll — had together closed a new funding round. Invention Engine publishes no total for startups supported, no cohort size and no founding year, so the scale of the programme cannot be stated from its own pages. Beyond the accelerator Outside ACE, the team publishes free material for founders who are not in a cohort. There is a podcast featuring AI practitioners, a blog of articles on AI products and startup practice, recorded talks and presentations, and an India's State of AI Research report that measures India's output at the main AI research conferences and sets out recommendations for improving it. These sit on the Resources section of the site and need no application. Invention Engine does not run a campus, labs or coworking space, and it claims no government or scheme recognition on any of its pages.

Who can apply Invention Engine states four things it looks for. The startup should have been operating for the last six to twelve months and have a product or an MVP, preferably with a few users. The team should be able to move to Delhi NCR for most of the six months. It is aimed at people who have worked in product-based companies and want to build in AI, and at anyone keen to build products from zero to one, including people still in college, provided they have a working product. The accelerator says it typically works with startups from prototype or MVP stage through early traction and early scale, and that it stays open to exceptional teams at an earlier stage if the problem, approach and ambition are compelling. There is no stated incorporation requirement, no state or category restriction and no minimum funding bar. The only hard condition on the page is the relocation one. The sector focus is narrow and explicit: AI and deeptech. The accelerator says plainly that it is not a scouting platform for funds. How to apply Applications run through an online form reached from the Apply for Cohort button on the home page and the ACE page. The published timeline has four steps: an invitation for applications, one-to-one nurturing sessions with the accelerator's founders, a one-week in-house evaluation programme ending in an offer, and then the cohort start. Name: Ipreneur Accelerator
Description: Ipreneur Startup Accelerator is a privately run accelerator in Bengaluru, operated by Infopace Management Pvt Ltd. It takes startups that are already past the idea stage, already earning revenue, and puts them through a fixed-length cohort aimed at making them ready to raise. It is not a government or university incubator: selected startups pay a participation fee to join, and Infopace takes a small equity stake in the company. How the cohorts work The accelerator runs numbered cohorts, currently Cohort 8.0, alongside two cohorts built for particular audiences: a Women Cohort for women founders and female-led ventures, and an MSME Cohort for small and medium enterprises looking to expand. Each runs the same way. There is a short bootcamp to open, then structured modules on go-to-market, business strategy, operations, finance and investment readiness, one-on-one mentor sessions, milestone reviews, and a demo day where startups pitch to investors and ecosystem partners. Work on the pitch deck, financial model, valuation and due-diligence paperwork runs through the whole programme. The length of a cohort is stated two different ways on their own pages. The Cohort 8.0 page calls it eight weeks; every other page, including the cohort overview page and the answers to common questions, calls it twelve weeks and describes it as three stages named MVP, Growth and Investment. Treat the length as something to confirm with them before you commit. Founders are asked to plan on roughly eight to ten hours a week for sessions, workshops and investor meetings. Who can apply Idea-stage companies are explicitly not accepted. Applicants are expected to be MVP-ready or to have a live product with market traction, to be generating revenue, and to have been operating for at least six months. The company must be a registered entity, listed variously as a Private Limited Company, an LLP, a registered Partnership Firm, or an MSME. Cohort 8.0 adds that the company should be under ten years old and that at least one founder must be full-time in the business, and asks for a commitment to attend and to sit the milestone reviews. The requirement founders should check first is recognition status, because the site says two different things. The site-wide selection criteria list DPIIT registration as something the startup must obtain. The Cohort 8.0 eligibility list instead says Udyam registration or DPIIT recognition is preferred. Cohort 8.0 also carries a minimum valuation bar stated in only one place on the page, well below the eligibility list, so it is easy to miss. Ask about both before applying. Whether the accelerator is open to any sector is also stated inconsistently. Their general material describes the programme as domain agnostic and says innovation can come from any industry, while the Cohort 8.0 page describes the accelerator as sector-focused and says applications are invited only from startups in that cohort's focus sectors. The current Cohort 8.0 is promoted on their home page as being for AI in agriculture. Startups based outside Bengaluru can apply. They say participants can take part remotely through their learning platform and travel to Bengaluru only as needed. Cost and equity This is the part of the offer a founder should understand before anything else, because it is unusual among the incubators and accelerators listed here. Participation is not free. Startups that clear selection pay a participation fee before the programme starts, and the fee is set at one of three levels according to how much investment the startup is seeking. Infopace also takes a small equity stake, with the exact amount decided case by case according to how much support the startup received. Some services around due diligence, valuation and business model work are charged on top. None of these figures are reproduced here; read them on their own pages and get them in writing. On funding, they say they facilitate tranche-based investment through Infowise Startup Catalyst, which they describe as their in-house fund, with money released against milestones, and that selected startups get to pitch to it directly. They also state plainly that joining a cohort does not entitle anyone to investment, and that any investment depends on jury evaluation, due diligence and the startup's own performance. Their pages give two very different sizes for that in-house fund, so neither is repeated here. How selection works Applications go through a five-step ladder: an application form, screening against the programme criteria, an interview, a selection pitch, and a final decision by a panel. They say application deadlines for each cohort are enforced strictly and that seats are limited. By their own account past cohorts drew between two hundred and a thousand applications each. The cohort overview page is unusually specific about what "investment ready" means to them. It publishes a stage ladder running Research, Launch, Growth and Ideal, and a table of thresholds at each level for annual recurring revenue, month-on-month growth, customer acquisition cost against lifetime value, gross and EBITDA margin, monthly burn, runway, customer growth, retention, churn, customer base, average revenue per user, payback period, net promoter score, team strength, defensibility and exit potential. Only companies that reach the Ideal stage are considered investment ready. It is worth reading before applying, because it is effectively the scorecard. Facilities and where they are They provide cubicle space for a participating team for meetings in their Bengaluru office, which they describe as seven thousand square feet of floor area, and say co-working space is part of what the programme provides. Accommodation is not provided to visiting teams. Two addresses are published, both on Sankey Road in Sadashiva Nagar, Bengaluru. Their contact page also shows a row of overseas city names under a worldwide heading, with no address or contact given for any of them. Who runs it The accelerator is led by Kishor Jagirdar as Chairman and Managing Director, with Yogesh Makam as Vice President. A core team of around eleven people is listed, most without job titles, along with a separate management team covering HR, operations, sales and marketing. Infopace Management Pvt Ltd, the company behind it, describes itself as working in change management and innovation and as having supported startups across Karnataka with mentorship, investment, co-working space and government liaison; those are the parent company's claims rather than the accelerator's own track record. They list partner organisations including FICCI, FKCCI, TiE Global, TiE Bangalore, BCIC, AIMO, Rotary, KSCST and eMERG India, and a set of investor networks and funds. An Angel Investor Accredited Program for investors rather than founders is advertised on their site as coming soon. They also run a careers page and publish blogs, case studies and past events.

Name: JioGenNext
Description: JioGenNext is Reliance Industries Limited's startup engagement platform, connecting startups with the Jio and Reliance business units for pilots, proof-of-concepts and commercial deployments. It calls itself a "scalerator, not an accelerator": it does not run pitch days or make investments, and its focus is on getting a startup's product used inside Reliance rather than funded by it. The programme is hybrid, with selected startups expected to attend some sessions in person at Reliance Corporate Park in Navi Mumbai. How the programme works JioGenNext's one standing programme is the Market Access Program (MAP). A startup that applies and is approved is matched with an internal sponsor inside Reliance who owns the business problem the startup solves, rather than being handed a generic mentor. From there the programme works to get the startup a proof-of-concept with a relevant Reliance business unit, matched to a real need rather than whichever pilot slot is open. If the proof-of-concept works, JioGenNext runs a structured process to move it toward a commercial contract, and continues to help the startup expand into other Reliance business units after that first win. Startups also get testing environments, cloud resources and data access as needed for the pilot, plus feedback when an engagement does not progress rather than being left without an explanation. Alongside the pilot track, the programme connects founders with a pool of internal and external mentors and helps them sharpen their pitch and value proposition for Reliance stakeholders. JioGenNext no longer runs the programme in fixed cohort batches. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, and once a startup is approved, the aim is to schedule its first pitch to a business user within two to three weeks. How long the engagement itself lasts is not fixed either — some resolve in a few months around a single pilot, others turn into a multi-year relationship as the startup expands across more of the Reliance ecosystem. Who can apply JioGenNext prefers startups that are past the MVP stage and already have a few enterprise customers using the product, and it has also worked with startups past product-market fit. It is not aimed at idea-stage founders. Its stated focus areas are enterprise SaaS, AI/ML, fintech, healthtech, logistics and supply chain, media and content, IoT, edtech, retail and e-commerce, and new energy. Startups from outside India can apply as long as their solution is relevant to the Indian market. The programme takes no equity and charges no fees, and it does not invest in the startups it works with — its own value proposition is market access rather than capital. A startup can also be referred by writing to the programme's general inbox instead of applying directly. Who runs it and what startups get access to Because JioGenNext sits inside Reliance, the business units a startup can potentially work with span Jio's telecom and digital platforms, Reliance Retail, Reliance Industries' oil-to-chemicals and energy businesses, new energy initiatives, financial services and other group companies — the specific unit depends on where the startup's solution fits. The programme also gives founders access to a roster of senior Reliance and Jio executives and outside mentors as part of its stakeholder-interaction sessions and events. Track record JioGenNext's own startup directory currently lists 247 startups that have gone through the programme since its first cohort, across 23 cohorts, with the most recent labelled Cohort 23 (MAP 2026) and running 20 startups. Of the 247, the directory tags 161 as active, 48 as inactive and 38 as acquired. Separately, the programme states it has run 84 pilots, resulting in 31 deployments across more than 15 Reliance business units. Among the startups it highlights: Fynd, whose platform was integrated with Reliance Retail for real-time inventory sync across more than 20,000 stores and which was later acquired by Reliance Retail; Expertia AI, an AI recruitment platform deployed across more than 14 Reliance business units; and Jiny, a digital-adoption platform deployed across Jio's apps that was later acquired by Whatfix. Other startups that have come through the programme include Headspin (later acquired by PartnerOne), GUVI (later acquired by HCL Technologies), Dozee, Flytbase, Signzy, and, from its earliest 2014 cohort, LogiNext. How to apply A startup applies by filling out JioGenNext's online application form. There is no fixed application window — the team reviews submissions on a rolling basis rather than against a cohort deadline.

Name: Kerala Startup Mission
Description: Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM) is the Government of Kerala's nodal agency for entrepreneurship development and incubation, and the body that implements the Kerala Technology Startup Policy. It was founded in 2006, having started as T-TBI, a business incubation centre set up by Technopark. Its head office is at Thejaswini, Technopark Campus, Kariyavattom, Thiruvananthapuram, with offices in Kochi, Kozhikode, Kasaragod and Palakkad. What KSUM offers falls into three groups: money, a programme, or space and equipment. The money is a ladder of grants and loans a Kerala-registered startup climbs as it grows. The programmes are stage-based incubation and acceleration cohorts, plus separate pipelines for women founders, students and researchers. The space is a network of coworking centres, fablabs and startup complexes across the state. How the funding ladder works KSUM sorts its funding page into grants, loans and reimbursements, and labels every scheme state funded or centrally funded. That label matters: the two are decided by different committees. The state-funded grants run in sequence. The Idea Grant is for innovators at ideation, design or proof-of-concept stage. The Productisation Grant takes a validated prototype to a market-ready product. The Women / Transgender Productisation Grant adds further support on top of that for startups where women or transgender founders hold at least 51 percent. The Market Acceleration Grant is for startups already earning revenue and expanding their market. The Scaleup Grant is for growth-stage startups with proven traction. The BCDD Grant, run with the Backward Classes Development Department, combines an idea and a productisation component for OBC graduate founders aged 23 to 40. The grants stack rather than repeat: take the Idea Grant and the Productisation Grant gives you only the balance you have not claimed, and the same rule applies further up. Grants are paid in milestone tranches, generally half up front and the rest after a progress review and a utilisation certificate, and the later schemes ask you to bring margin money of your own. The state-funded loans are separate. The Seed Fund lends against a purchase order, and was marked as not yet open when we last checked. The Scaleup Seed Fund is collateral-free debt or convertible instruments for revenue-stage startups, on soft-loan terms with a twelve-month moratorium and repayment over 36 months. The Soft Loan Scheme for Women Entrepreneurs is working capital against purchase orders from Kerala government departments and public sector undertakings, capped at 80 percent of the order value. Three schemes on the page are central, not state: the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, NIDHI PRAYAS and the NIDHI Seed Support Programme. KSUM channels these rather than funding them, and describes itself as a designated PRAYAS Centre for the Department of Science and Technology. Two further state schemes, patent reimbursement and technology transfer, are listed as coming soon. Programmes Incubation and acceleration run in three stages. Pre-incubation lasts 45 days to three months and covers idea validation, problem-solution fit, rapid prototyping and founder preparedness; the named tracks are SparkX, SparkX Creative Tech, delivered with Kalamandalam for creative and cultural industries, and SparkX: AI & IT for students and first-time founders. Incubation runs three to six months and covers mentoring, infrastructure, customer discovery and go-to-market; GrowthX supports Productisation Grant recipients, KERA works on agriculture and rural livelihoods with the World Bank, and Bio-AI sits at the intersection of AI, biotechnology, Ayurveda, spices, biodiversity and life sciences. Acceleration is a three-month intensive for revenue-generating startups, with LeapX for B2B SaaS and LeapX AVGC XR for animation, gaming and immersive technology. Women founders have their own pipeline. WE Start is a three-month hybrid pre-incubation programme from idea to MVP; WE Grow is a five-month hybrid incubation programme from MVP to revenue that ends in a Demo Day. Alongside them sit a co-incubation with NSRCEL at IIM Bangalore, She Builds Tech for women student innovators, the LeadHER Talk series and an annual Women Startup Summit. A programme handbook is published in English and Malayalam. Students reach KSUM through IEDCs, the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Centres set up in colleges, medical institutions, polytechnics and universities. The Idea Box is a three-month student pre-incubation programme, Idea Fest lets student teams pitch projects to an expert panel for development support, and IEDC NEST is the student community around it. Researchers go through RINK, the Research Innovation Network Kerala, which offers an R&D grant for deep-technology startups, exposure visits to research institutions, demo days where institutions show commercialisable technology, a one-to-one Researchpreneurship validation programme, a technology transfer catalogue, an instrumentation portal mapping scientific equipment across the state, and IPR support through partner institutions. On the investment side, KSUM runs a Fund of Funds that invests as a Limited Partner in SEBI-registered Category I and II alternative investment funds backing Kerala startups; it launched in 2018 and has partnered with 16 venture capital funds. A Creative Economy Fund is proposed under the same framework and is not yet live. For founders there is a VC 101 bootcamp, Pitch Day, Investor Cafe and the annual Seeding Kerala investor meet; for investors, Ignite. Facilities KSUM's infrastructure timeline lists the Integrated Startup Complex at the Kerala Technology Innovation Zone in Kalamassery, Kochi, from 2019, the Super Fablab from 2020 and the Digital Hub from 2021. Coworking runs under the LEAP brand — Launch, Empower, Accelerate, Prosper — across KSUM's own centres, partner incubation centres and IEDCs. There is also an Emerging Tech Hub, Startup Pod workspaces at scenic locations, and Freedom Square, a 24x7 space supported by Kerala Tourism. FabLab Kerala describes itself as part of the MIT-affiliated Fab Lab Network and runs machining, fabrication and PCB work alongside Fab Academy, Fab D-Lite, workshops, internships and a Creator Residency Fellowship. Mini fablabs sit across the districts. Scale and network KSUM counts ten lakh square feet of incubation space, 550 IEDCs, 63 incubators, more than 15 coworking spaces and 720 ideas supported. Its district explorer lists associated incubators across Kerala, among them Maker Village and BIONEST in Kochi, Amrita TBI in Kollam, IIMK LIVE and NIT TBI in Kozhikode, SCTIMST TIMED and ICFOSS in Thiruvananthapuram, and Care Keralam in Thrissur. Its flagship events are Huddle Global, Seeding Kerala and the IEDC Summit. Who runs it The Chief Executive Officer is Anoop Ambika. The Executive Committee is chaired by the Special Secretary of the Electronics and IT Department, Government of Kerala. The Board of Governors combines state secretaries for IT, industries, science and technology, agriculture, higher education and finance with university vice chancellors and members from industry and investing. KSUM publishes a careers page, which had no open positions when we last checked. How to apply Every state grant follows the same route. You apply on the KSUM website during an official call, KSUM officials screen the application, shortlisted startups pitch to an Expert Committee, and successful applicants sign an agreement before money is released in tranches. A KSUM Unique ID is required — at application for most schemes, and before disbursal for all of them — and your company must be incorporated as a private limited company, LLP or OPC with active MCA status before funds move.

Name: Kolkata Ventures
Description: Kolkata Ventures is a private startup incubator that works entirely online. It describes itself as an Indo-US collaboration set up to support entrepreneurship in India through virtual incubation, seed funding and startup resources. Avelo Roy is its Managing Director, and he personally runs the investor-readiness mentorship. It is a commercial business, not a government-backed or university-hosted incubator: nowhere on its site does it claim recognition, accreditation or funding from any ministry, department or state government. The important thing to understand before you apply is that its incubation is paid. Every track charges a registration fee, and the site says the fee falls due only once you have been selected. On top of that, each track states that equity of between zero and five per cent is to be mutually decided, so equity may or may not be taken depending on what is agreed. Kolkata Ventures also says it will take equity in exchange for deeply discounted services. If you are looking for grant funding or free incubation, this is not that. How programmes work There are four incubation tracks, all delivered virtually. Idea Stage Incubation runs three months and is for people who are about to start or have only just started working on a business; its stated goal is to move you from an idea to consistent revenue on a business model that holds together. Growth Stage Incubation runs four months and is for startups already earning revenue that want to restructure the business model, remove bottlenecks and lift sales and profitability. Startup To Scaleup runs five months and is for startups with a settled business model and consistent revenue that want to enter new markets, through access to investment, mentorship and specific resources. Make Your Startup Investor Ready is the shortest, at around two months, and is built around six one-hour sessions with Avelo Roy over sixty days. The investor-readiness track is the most precisely described of the four. Sessions run over phone or video. You are given tasks after each session to finish before the next one, and you can ask for help on WhatsApp in between, with a stated response time of anywhere from a few minutes to forty-eight hours. The package includes introductions to three potential investors, depending on your stage and how ready you are to pitch. The outcomes it commits to in sixty days are a complete business plan, a complete pitch deck, a one-page executive summary, a use-of-funds document, and the ability to pitch and answer the questions investors usually ask. If those are not reached in sixty days, three further sessions over a month can be booked at additional cost. Professional pitch-deck design is a separate paid add-on. The page also says plainly that whether you actually get investment depends on you and on the investor, and that Kolkata Ventures gives no guarantee about it. Who can apply The tracks are separated by how far along you are, not by sector, and no sector focus is stated anywhere. Idea Stage is for people at or just past the idea; Growth Stage and Startup To Scaleup both require that you are already generating revenue consistently. The site sets no incorporation requirement, no state or city restriction and no category restriction, and nothing on it limits applications to Kolkata or to West Bengal. On the investment side the application form asks whether you are pre-revenue or post-revenue and marks post-revenue as preferred. Funding and investment Separately from the paid programmes, Kolkata Ventures says it gives access to startup investment in three forms: equity for cash, convertible debt that can convert to equity at a trigger point, and deeply discounted services taken in exchange for equity. What it says it looks at is a capable founding team, the size of the market opportunity, the strength of the business model, an unfair competitive advantage and whether the business can scale with technology. Applications go through a form on its funding page, and it says it will come back to you within seven days. Mentors and support The mentor panel is named on the incubation page and spans India, the United States and Hong Kong. Alongside Avelo Roy it lists Neeraj Krishna G, an IIT Kharagpur and ISB Hyderabad alumnus who has built products for clients including Siemens and AIWA; Dr David Pistrui, who teaches entrepreneurship in US universities; Nik Rokop, who leads entrepreneurship development at the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago; Gary Dollinger, a technology executive working with private equity firms; Rajiv Ghosh, chief executive of the outdoor advertising company Selvel; Leon Leong, who has run a design and manufacturing company in China and Hong Kong; Sarbajit Das, a Kolkata software and UI/UX entrepreneur; and Naveen Kejriwal, a sales professional who has worked with food startups. Beyond the programmes, Kolkata Ventures brokers startup services from outside providers at rates it says are below market because of the volume it buys. The request form covers company registration as a private limited company, LLP or one-person company, GST and professional tax, annual accounting and legal compliance, trademark and patent work, web and app development, social media marketing, graphic design, pitch deck review and design, and food, fire and trade licences. It also says startups it backs get benefits from Google, Amazon Web Services and PayTM. There is a free request-mentorship form on the site that lets you ask up to three questions at no charge, which is a sensible first step before paying for anything. Track record Its own published counts do not agree with each other. The incubation page says it has helped launch more than two hundred startups from zero to revenue and more than three hundred from growth to scaleup; an older page gives just over four hundred graduates; its events page says more than five hundred revenue-generating startups and around 4,700 jobs. None is dated and none is independently verifiable, so treat all of them as self-reported. The startups it names as having come through its programmes are Brevistay, an hourly hotel booking service; Invesmate, which teaches stock market investing in regional languages; Flytant, an influencer marketing platform; ThinkAgain Lab, which builds robots and education products; and Yes Sir, an at-home men's grooming service. Locations and getting in touch Kolkata Ventures publishes no office address. Its contact page gives one phone and WhatsApp number, staffed between 10am and 10pm seven days a week except national holidays, and one email address. Everything else runs through forms on the site. There is no careers page. Its events page has a paid online masterclass format, run over Zoom with a recording and a certificate, though no upcoming date is listed at the moment.

Name: Lemon Ideas
Description: Lemon Ideas is a private, self-funded entrepreneurship company in Nagpur, Maharashtra that mentors, trains and runs contests for early-stage founders. It started in 2013 and is run by a team led by Deepak Menaria, whose title on the team page is Chief Idea Farmer. Its corporate office is on Pratap Nagar road at Mate Square in Nagpur, and it lists regional offices in Nagpur, Vadodara, Gwalior, Bhopal and Udaipur. It is not a government-funded incubator. Lemon Ideas names no parent body and no government funder anywhere on its site, and says plainly that it chose a profit model and generates its own fuel. The only recognition it claims for itself is a single line in its own timeline for 2017, reading "Startup recognition by Govt. of India" — it names no scheme, department or registration number, so treat it as the company's own undated claim rather than an incubator accreditation. What it actually runs Three brands sit under Lemon Ideas. Lemon Ideas itself does the mentoring and acceleration. Lemon School of Entrepreneurship, launched in 2015, does the training and has its own site at lemon-school.com; it states that it is not affiliated to any university or governing body and awards no recognised degree or diploma. Innopreneurs, launched in 2014, is a yearly startup contest with its own site at innopreneurs.in. Alongside those it sells two things to organisations rather than founders: professional services for startups and small businesses (accounting, legal and compliance, branding, digital marketing, recruitment, web and software development), and a consulting service for bodies that want to set up or run their own incubator. That second one has been used by a government agency, a university or a corporate looking for someone to build the thing for them; Lemon says it usually expects a new incubator to stand on its own in about two years. Who can apply, and what it costs This is the part to read carefully, because Lemon Ideas runs both free and paid programmes and they look similar from the outside. The acceleration and mentoring cohort is free. The homepage says so directly, and the application is a short form asking for your venture name and the challenges you are facing. It is selective: Lemon says it takes a small number of startups each year on the recommendation of its jury and mentors, and supports them intensively for six months as the start of a roughly two-year relationship. Name: Link Innovations
Description: Link Innovations is an innovation consultancy based in Bangalore and Paris. Its site says it enables enterprises to collaborate with startups, emerging technologies and innovation ecosystems. Its programmes page lists several calls for startups, and one of them, the GIA Bangalore Market Access Programme, is stated to be delivered by Link. How programmes work The GIA Bangalore Market Access Programme is a 12-week customised programme for startups entering the Indian market. It includes expert mentorship, market validation, strategic business connections and a one-week immersion in Bangalore, and it is supported by Enterprise Singapore. Link's programmes page describes it as 12 weeks long. Enterprise Singapore's listing is reported to describe two tracks, one of 12 weeks and one of 8 weeks, so check the current format with Link before you apply. The other calls on Link's programmes page are run by other companies. They include Volvo Group's open innovation challenge through its CampX programme, Startup Autobahn India (powered by Mercedes-Benz R&D India), OVHcloud's startup programme for cloud resources, Panasonic's Co.lab Studio by IGNITION and UST's D3 Startup Challenge. Link's own role in these is not stated, and the D3 challenge has closed to applications. Who can apply The GIA programme is aimed at startups entering the Indian market. Eligibility is not stated on Link's programmes page, so ask Link before applying. The other calls name who they are for: high-potential startups in Volvo Group's business use cases, startups that want to test and co-create products with a car manufacturer, startups registered in the DACH and APAC regions for OVHcloud, and enterprise-ready B2B startups for D3. Scale Link's website describes a network of more than 200 incubators, more than 200 corporates and more than 50,000 startups across APAC, EMEA and the Americas. Its programmes page says more than 600 proof-of-concepts have been run between startups and corporates across its programmes, and that 48% of accelerated startups raised follow-on funding within 12 months of completing a programme. Its site also says it has worked with more than 100 global corporates and runs active startup corridors across four continents. These are Link's own figures, and we have not verified them. Who it works with The D3 Startup Challenge site describes Link as a global innovation consulting company that has worked with multinational corporations in oil and gas, energy, renewables, manufacturing, automotive and aerospace. Sources give different founding dates for the company, so this page does not give one.

Name: MASA Forum
Description: MASA Forum, short for MSME And Startups Accelerator Forum, is an independent networking and advocacy platform headquartered in Kolkata, West Bengal. The organization serves as a bridge between India's micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and the broader startup ecosystem, facilitating connections with investors, mentors, industry experts, and government bodies. MASA Forum organizes events, summits, and awards ceremonies that bring together entrepreneurs, policymakers, and business leaders to discuss challenges and opportunities facing the Indian MSME and startup landscape. Role in Startup Ecosystem MASA Forum occupies a distinctive position in the Indian startup ecosystem by focusing specifically on the intersection of MSMEs and startups. While many organizations cater exclusively to technology startups or large enterprises, MASA Forum recognizes that a significant portion of India's entrepreneurial activity occurs within the MSME segment. The forum provides visibility to emerging businesses through its awards programs, industry conclaves, and networking sessions. It also serves as a platform for knowledge sharing, where founders at various stages can learn from established business leaders and peers. By organizing regional events across India, MASA Forum extends its reach beyond metropolitan centers and into Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities where many MSMEs operate. Programs and Initiatives MASA Forum is known for its flagship MASA Awards, which recognize outstanding MSMEs and startups across multiple categories including innovation, social impact, and professional excellence. The forum regularly hosts industry conclaves and business summits that address topics such as access to finance, digital transformation, export readiness, and regulatory compliance. These events feature panel discussions, keynote addresses, and one-on-one networking opportunities. MASA Forum also facilitates connections between startups seeking growth capital and potential investors, serving as an informal matchmaking platform for early-stage and growth-stage ventures. Who Benefits MSME owners, first-time entrepreneurs, and startup founders looking for networking opportunities, industry recognition, and access to a broader business community stand to benefit from MASA Forum's activities. The platform is particularly relevant for entrepreneurs in eastern India and those seeking connections beyond the traditional startup hubs of Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi. Strategic Impact MASA Forum contributes to the decentralization of India's startup ecosystem by championing entrepreneurship in regions that are often underrepresented in mainstream startup discourse. Its emphasis on MSMEs alongside startups reflects the reality that small and medium businesses form the backbone of India's economy, and their growth is integral to the country's broader economic development objectives.

Name: Maharashtra State Innovation Society
Description: Maharashtra State Innovation Society (MSInS) is the Government of Maharashtra's nodal agency for building an innovation-driven entrepreneurial ecosystem across the state. It sits under the state's Department of Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, and its General Body is chaired by the Chief Minister of Maharashtra. Who runs it MSInS's General Body is chaired by the Chief Minister, with the Minister of Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation as Vice Chairman and Dr. Raghunath Mashelkar, former Director General of CSIR, serving as Advisor. Day-to-day operations are led by CEO Shri Lahu Mali, IAS, and Joint CEO Dr. Vikas Naik. Below the General Body sits a Governing Council, ex-officio chaired by the Additional Chief Secretary of the Department of Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship & Innovation, with Principal Secretaries from the state's Industries, Higher & Technical Education, Agriculture, Urban Development, Public Health and IT departments sitting as members alongside MSInS's own CEO. This structure — a Chief-Minister-chaired body backed by a council of department secretaries — reflects MSInS's role as a cross-department coordinating agency rather than a single-sector incubator. What they run MSInS's own site currently promotes three initiatives on its homepage: Maharashtra Startup Week, a state-run competition that has previously invited startups to pitch solutions to governance challenges (past editions were covered by national press through 2018–2020); the Punyashlok Ahilyadevi Holkar Women Startup Scheme, a scheme for women-led startups with a live application link; and dedicated pages on IP support and quality testing/certification for startups, linked directly from the homepage banners. Beyond the homepage links, MSInS's programme-detail pages are served by a client-side application that this research could not fully render, so eligibility, selection process and participant benefits for these initiatives are not independently confirmed here — check the official links before relying on programme mechanics. Partners MSInS lists a number of ecosystem partners on its site, including the Indian Merchants' Chamber (IMC), AGNIi (the Government of India's innovation-matching platform), AWS Activate, Social Alpha, 100x.VC, Indian Angel Network, TiE Mumbai, CII and Acumen. Policy resources MSInS publishes a set of Government of Maharashtra policy documents on its site as reference material for founders, including the state's Startup Policy, the Maharashtra Industrial Policy, a Labour Department government resolution for startups, a 2025 Maharashtra Startup, Entrepreneurship & Innovation Policy, the state Fintech Policy, the Maharashtra EV Policy, the Shops and Establishment Act, and the Maharashtra Procurement Policy — useful background reading for any startup registering or operating in the state. How to apply MSInS does not run one common application process — each scheme has its own application link, typically hosted on an Accubate-based form linked from the scheme's page or a homepage banner, rather than a single central portal.

Name: Maker Village
Description: Maker Village is an electronics hardware incubator in Kochi, built around a 60,000 sq ft facility inside the Kerala Technology Innovation Zone at KINFRA Hi-Tech Park, Kalamassery. Its own pages describe it as a joint initiative between the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and IIITM-Kerala, with IIITM-K as the implementation agency and Kerala Startup Mission as the supporting partner. It works with teams building electronic products — electronics system design and manufacturing, IoT and robotics — rather than with software startups. How programmes work Maker Village runs a four-step incubation ladder that a founder moves along as the product matures. MV-IDEA takes an early idea and coaches the team into a concept, a business model and a pitch. MV-PROTO is the main prototyping step, and is where most hardware teams enter: it covers office space, fabrication and 3D printing, on-demand software, and training in electronic prototyping, PCB design, PCB automated testing, 3D printing and design for manufacture and assembly. MV-COMMERCE prepares a validated product for market launch and test-market validation. MV-SCALEUP is for startups that already have a market-validated product and revenue or partnerships, and want the industry-grade equipment, corporate and investor introductions and demo days that come with the facility. A separate pre-incubation programme, MV-Yentrepreneur, teaches entrepreneurship to technical college students and young graduates. Each step is offered both as resident incubation at the Kochi facility and as a lighter virtual option. None of the four ladder pages carries an application deadline, so they read as a standing intake rather than a dated cohort. Alongside the ladder, Maker Village hosts national scheme calls that open and close on dates — the MeitY TIDE 2.0 grant, the GENESIS programmes, the MeitY Startup Hub SAMRIDH accelerator and a DST NIDHI Accelerator for medical and healthcare products. Every one of those calls listed on the site had already closed when this page was checked, so treat them as recurring rather than open. Who can apply The eligibility on MV-PROTO, MV-COMMERCE and MV-SCALEUP all begins the same way: direct applicants, graduates of the previous step, or winners of any grant award. There is no Kerala residence requirement anywhere in it, and no requirement to be a student or staff member of the host institute. What the pages do require is incorporation — applications for admission are made in the name of an entity registered under the Companies Act, 2013. Beyond that they look for product and IP-based startups in the ESDM field, clear market or user validation, and high growth potential; proposals that could involve IIITM-K faculty are preferred, but that is a preference, not a gate. MV-Yentrepreneur is the one exception. It is open only to members of the MV Young Entrepreneur Club, winners of the MV Young Innovation Challenge or similar competitions, and members of the MV internship programme — so it is not a route in for an outside founder. The scheme calls carry their own tighter conditions. TIDE 2.0 was open to any Indian citizen who had completed a basic degree, as an individual innovator or as a startup under five years old, with a preference stated for women entrepreneurs. SAMRIDH and the NIDHI Accelerator both required a DPIIT-registered company with at least 51 percent Indian promoter shareholding and a working prototype at a stated technology readiness level. Facilities The Kochi facility is 60,000 sq ft: roughly 45,000 sq ft of incubation space and 15,000 sq ft of labs and equipment, with seating for around 280. Maker Village lists co-working space, conference rooms, electronics and instrumentation labs, a metal machining area, industrial 3D printing and plastics, an industrial SMT line and a PCB assembly line. There is an 80-seat amphitheatre, a 150-seat mini auditorium, meeting rooms, a library and a product showcase, along with office equipment, high-speed wifi and round-the-clock power backup. Incubatees are also helped to reach IIITM-K's own labs, including its Centre of Excellence in IIoT Sensors — that access runs through the institute and is subject to its approval, so it is the host's equipment rather than Maker Village's. Support beyond the hardware includes consultants for strategy, market research, business development, financial planning and hiring, free advisory from legal, accounting, IP and fundraising experts, corporate and investor introductions, and cloud credits. Scale Maker Village's own pages give different startup counts in different places — the startups page and the about page do not agree, and neither carries a date — so no single figure is published here. Its startups page lists companies working on underwater drones, robotics, smart eyewear, medical instrumentation, embedded systems and power management, though that listing mixes Maker Village's own incubatees with two other cohorts hosted on the same campus. Who runs it IIITM-K is the implementing institute and every published Maker Village address sits on an IIITM-K inbox. The centre is led by a professor-in-charge drawn from the institute's faculty, and its project management group includes senior figures from the state IT department and the Kerala startup ecosystem. MeitY and the Government of Kerala are the promoters and funders rather than operators. Maker Village appears in the Department of Science and Technology's own published list of incubators supported under the NIDHI Accelerator programme, listed by name for Kochi, Kerala. Locations The main facility is at KTIZ, KINFRA Hi-Tech Park, Kalamassery, Kochi. A satellite annexe operates at the IIITM-K campus in Technopark, Trivandrum, built around an IoT lab, for teams that want to be incubated in the Trivandrum region. Maker Village publishes an events page covering the workshops, demo days and industry sessions it hosts.

Name: Management Education & Research Institute
Description: MERI Startup HUB is the startup arm of the Management Education & Research Institute, part of the MERI Group of Institutions in Janakpuri, Delhi. It works with early-stage founders who have an idea or prototype, with startups that have reached the growth phase and are preparing to scale, and with investors looking for early-stage deals. The hub is based at the institute's office on Sewa Marg. How the programmes work The Pre-Incubation Program helps early-stage entrepreneurs test and refine an idea. Founders get one-on-one sessions with mentors, workshops on problem identification, prototype design and market strategy, access to tools for testing an idea, and networking events. The hub's news post on its 5.0 cohort describes a 10-week programme, but the current programme page gives no cohort number or dates. The Incubation Program supports startups with an innovative idea, a business plan and a team. Its process covers business plan refinement, financial and growth projections, market and product evaluation, help with incorporation, patents and trademarks, expert review of the plan, and regular check-ins. Corporate and government collaboration opportunities are also offered to incubated startups. The Acceleration Program is for startups in the growth phase that are ready to expand. The hub describes two stages: growth, where operations, market approach and product are refined, and scaling, where market reach and operations are expanded. Support includes mentorship, market penetration strategy, performance tracking, introductions to partners and investors, and infrastructure credits for selected startups. The programme is generally six to twelve months, and its length adjusts to progress. Who can apply Pre-incubation is for early-stage founders who have a concept or prototype. Incubation is for startups with an innovative idea, a solid business plan and a strong team, and the hub says it accepts startups at several stages, including early ones. Acceleration is for startups that have finished the growth phase, with product-market fit, an established business model and an ambitious growth plan. Domestic and foreign startups may apply to the incubation and acceleration programmes if they meet the same criteria. How selection works Applicants submit an application on the website that describes their idea, goals and current status. The team reviews submissions and invites selected candidates to a further discussion. For acceleration, the hub describes an assessment of growth potential, market readiness, scalability and team ability. Events and investor access The hub runs an Ideathon, where startups present business ideas and models to industry experts and receive feedback, and a MERI Startup Festival that gives students and startups a platform to show their projects. A student-only hackathon is hosted with CodeVerse. The hub's Investor Hub connects startups with angel investors, venture capitalists and strategic partners, and offers founders help with pitch preparation and their investment model. The hub also says it carries out due diligence on the startups it lists for investors. Event registration dates are set per event, so check the events page for the current round. Scale The hub's home page shows counters of 28 finished projects, 20 expert mentors and 15 incubation and acceleration programmes. These are the hub's own figures and carry no date, so they are shown as reported rather than verified. Costs The hub says its programmes may involve fees or equity, depending on the services a startup needs, and that costs are discussed during the application process. It does not publish a fixed price list. Location and visits The hub is based at 52-55 Sewa Marg, Janakpuri, Delhi, India. The hub encourages potential clients to visit, meet the team and learn about its services, and asks visitors to book an appointment through the website or get in touch first.

Name: Marwari Catalysts
Description: Marwari Catalysts is a startup accelerator founded in 2019 and based in Jodhpur, Rajasthan, with additional offices in Jaipur, Mumbai and Bengaluru. It sits inside the wider Marwari Catalysts Group, which also runs a venture studio for turning around existing businesses and a SEBI-registered AIF Category-I fund. The accelerator focuses on founders from Tier 2 and Tier 3 Indian cities, an audience it says is underserved by the metro-centred startup ecosystem. How programmes work The flagship programme is Thrive, a structured acceleration track that runs three to four months. It is built around monthly themes: onboarding and an ecosystem health check in month one, strategy and KPI work in month two, mentor matching and community building in month three, and pitch readiness and investor connections culminating in a demo day in month four. Founders get one-on-one mentorship from industry experts and entrepreneurs, a structured growth playbook, business workshops, pitch and KPI coaching, and access to Marwari Catalysts' investor network and co-investors. Applications for Thrive are accepted on a rolling cohort basis through the site's pitch form. Alongside Thrive, the group runs a venture studio model for businesses that need a turnaround rather than a first accelerator. Here Marwari Catalysts steps in as a co-founder, takes a stake, and works on operational restructuring and leadership gaps alongside the existing team, with funding released against milestones. This is a fundamentally different relationship from Thrive: Thrive mentors and invests in a founder's own company, while the venture studio model has Marwari Catalysts becoming a working co-founder inside the business. The group's AIF Category-I fund is the capital vehicle behind these programmes. It is positioned for family offices, HNIs, angels and institutional investors who want structured, governance-led exposure to the same pipeline of early-stage, Tier 2/3 and impact-driven businesses. Marwari Catalysts also runs Startup Exchange, an annual flagship networking event plus a rolling calendar of smaller ecosystem events through the year, bringing together founders, investors, family offices and mentors. The first two editions were held in Jodhpur, the next two in Jaipur, and a fifth edition took place in Dubai, with a further Jodhpur edition planned. Separately, the group's Foundation runs a free monthly pre-incubation session for early-stage social entrepreneurs and students, alongside elder-care initiatives, positioning community work as a second track alongside the for-profit accelerator and fund. Who can apply Thrive is open to pre-seed and early-stage, growth-ready founders across sectors, including first-time founders. The site describes support for startups from across India, with hybrid (virtual plus in-person) participation. The venture studio route is aimed at founders or business owners of an existing, often distressed, company looking for a hands-on turnaround partner rather than a first-time accelerator relationship. Facilities Marwari Catalysts' Jodhpur base sits within an IT Park that has operated since 2011, hosting more than a thousand IT professionals alongside other incubators, accelerators and small and mid-sized businesses in the same building. Who runs it Marwari Catalysts Group is chaired and was founded by Sushil Sharma, who also holds roles including Executive Director of BRICS CCI and Convenor of the Rajasthan chapter of the Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council. The core team includes a finance lead, two partners, and a vice-president for admin and government affairs, backed by an advisory board that draws on founders, investors and operators from companies including Daily Hunt, Airmeet and Myntra. Locations The group's main office is in Jodhpur, Rajasthan (Cyber Park, Heavy Industrial Area), with further offices in Bengaluru (HSR Layout), Jaipur (Durgapura) and Mumbai.
Contact Designation: Marwari Catalysts' advisory board includes operators and investors who have built or run companies such as Daily Hunt, Airmeet and Myntra, alongside finance and governance partners -- useful context for the kind of mentorship conversations to expect once you're in.

Name: Masters Union School of Business
Description: Masters' Union is a private business school in Gurugram, Haryana, whose Our Story timeline begins in 2020. It teaches undergraduate, postgraduate and executive programmes, and it also runs its own early-stage investment arm, MU Ventures, which is the part of it that an outside founder can approach. MU Ventures backs founders under 25 at what it calls the "-1 stage" — "paper-napkin stage", before day zero. Its own words are that it invests "when the idea is still on paper, your prototype isn't built, or your first customers are just a dream". It is sector-agnostic, and it says it is open to all builders under 25. That is the age gate, and it is the main thing to check before you spend time on an application. How the funds work MU Ventures describes three funds. The Dropout Fund is marked live. It is for school, undergraduate and postgraduate dropouts who want to build instead of following the script, and it comes with a twelve-month build year inside the Masters' Union ecosystem, up to 100 Founder Credits that convert into what MU Ventures calls Conviction Capital, and an academic safety net if the startup does not continue. The Founders' Fund and the Creator Fund are both marked "launching soon" and are not taking applications on their own yet. The Founders' Fund is aimed at consumer brands and deep-tech; the Creator Fund is for content-led businesses on YouTube, Instagram and similar platforms, where MU Ventures says it prefers a large following or mostly organic traffic. Beyond the cheque, MU Ventures lists six things it gives its founders: monthly one-to-one mentorship sessions, a workspace on the Masters' Union campus, tech tools and credits to design and ship an MVP, introductions across the Masters' Union network of founders, CXOs and potential customers, PR and branding support including video assets, and help preparing for the next round. Its technology partner list — the credits and infrastructure its portfolio builds on — names Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Notion, Figma, HubSpot, Slack, GitHub, Stripe, Vercel, MongoDB and OpenAI. MU Ventures says most of its funding decisions happen in under ten days. It does not publish a selection panel, scoring criteria or a decision timeline beyond that. Who can apply This is the part worth reading twice, because Masters' Union runs two very different kinds of startup activity and only one of them is open to you. MU Ventures is open to outside founders. You do not need to be a Masters' Union student, and the pitch is explicitly for people with nothing built yet — "idea-only OK" is on the page. The gate is age: under 25. The Dropout Fund adds a second gate, that you have left school, an undergraduate course or a postgraduate course. Everything the school lists under Innovation and Student Entrepreneurship is for its own enrolled students. The CEO Challenge, the Dropshipping Challenge, the Venture Initiation Programme and the Masters' Union Investment Fund are all described in terms of Masters' Union students, and the Investment Fund is run by students. The Founder Fellowship pays a monthly stipend for up to a year, but only to selected students who choose to build a venture instead of taking a campus placement. None of these has a public application route, and none of them is a way in for a founder who is not enrolled. The High School Startup League is for teenagers still at school. The school's other founder-facing offerings — the executive PGP in Entrepreneurship and Business Acceleration, for example — are fee-paying courses you join as a student, not programmes you apply to as a startup. How to apply There is one form, at the MU Ventures application page, and it covers all of MU Ventures. It runs in four steps. First your own details: name, date of birth, age, email, LinkedIn, phone, location, school and undergraduate institute. Second, your co-founders, with a one-minute video introducing them and the story of how you met. Name: NSRCEL, IIM Bangalore
Description: NSRCEL, the NS Raghavan Centre for Entrepreneurial Learning (the Department of Science and Technology lists it as the Nadathur S Raghavan Centre for Entrepreneurial Learning), is the startup incubator of the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (IIMB). It is the institute's hub for entrepreneurship and innovation, set up with the support of N. S. Raghavan, a co-founder of Infosys, and it works from the IIMB campus on Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru. Founders do not apply to NSRCEL as a whole: each programme has its own online application form and opens in cohorts, so the first step is choosing the programme that fits your stage and sector. NSRCEL does not run a single incubator programme. It runs a portfolio of them, each built for a different kind of founder: idea-stage teams, student founders, women entrepreneurs, social ventures, and revenue-stage startups looking to scale. Most programmes are delivered with a corporate or government partner, among them Kotak Mahindra Bank, Goldman Sachs, Capgemini, Maruti Suzuki, Hindustan Unilever, ALSTOM and the Government of Karnataka. How NSRCEL programmes work Programmes run as cohorts with a defined intake, rather than as open-ended residencies. NSRCEL groups them into three families: idea and prototype programmes such as Launchpad, Campus Founders and the Healthcare Incubation Program; growth programmes such as the Women Startup Program, Velocity – Kotak BizLabs, Impact Orbit and the sector accelerators for climate, circularity, mobility and renewable energy; and two Centres of Excellence, for climate and for fintech. Every programme that states a fee policy is free to join, and most state that NSRCEL takes no equity. Several offer grant support to selected startups, though selection into a programme does not guarantee a grant, and amounts differ by programme and cohort. Applications are made programme by programme, through an online application form. When a cohort is not open, most programme pages invite founders to register interest for the next intake instead. Selection usually follows the same shape: an application review, a conversation with the NSRCEL team, a pitch to a mentor or jury panel, due diligence for the growth programmes, and then onboarding. Who can apply NSRCEL's programmes are open to founders from across India, not only to IIM Bangalore students or alumni. Several accept solo founders, and most expect founders to be committed full-time. Eligibility then depends on the programme: some require a working prototype, some require revenue and existing customers, and the Velocity and mobility programmes require DPIIT recognition. The sector programmes accept only startups in their field. Scale On its homepage NSRCEL reports more than 3,657 ventures incubated, 15,901 ventures impacted and 35,792 jobs created. Its about page lists more than 100 mentors and more than 20 partners. These are NSRCEL's own figures, and its pages do not always agree with one another. Who runs it NSRCEL is led by its CEO, Rasika Prashant, and sits within IIM Bangalore's innovation structure alongside IIMB Innovations. Its board draws on IIM Bangalore faculty and on founders and executives from companies including NIRAMAI Health Analytix and Info Edge.

Name: NetApp Excellerator
Description: NetApp Excellerator is a four-month start-up accelerator run by NetApp from its campus in Bengaluru. It is the first start-up accelerator programme NetApp has deployed in India, and each cohort takes five or six start-ups at a time. NetApp runs the programme itself and takes no equity in the start-ups it works with. How the programme works Start-ups join a cohort for four months. Over that time they are mentored by NetApp technology and business experts, along with entrepreneurs, investors and other industry leaders. Start-ups also get access to coworking space, tools, platforms and investors, along with financial grants, technology support and business advisory services. The programme includes a proof-of-concept model, which lets entrepreneurs show how their solutions work in the real world. Who can apply Any start-up can apply. The programme takes start-ups from a range of technology areas, including cloud, the Internet of Things, big data and analytics, machine learning, virtualization, data security, data management and storage, and related fields. Founders must be willing to work from the coworking space at the NetApp campus in Bengaluru for a significant part of the four months. A team that cannot be on site in Bengaluru for much of the cohort should weigh that before applying. The ExcellerateHER track NetApp ExcellerateHER is the programme's track for women-led start-ups. A start-up qualifies with at least one female founder. Participants get what main-programme participants get, except the grant and the proof-of-concept work. The programme says only a few start-ups reach the main programme's top six, and that it recognises potential beyond rankings. Facilities The main facility is coworking space on the NetApp campus in Bengaluru. Start-ups also get access to tools and platforms through the programme. Scale The homepage says the programme has supported more than 90 start-ups and worked with more than 20 women-led start-ups. Each cohort takes five or six start-ups, so intakes are small. Who runs it NetApp runs the programme. Its mentors are NetApp's own technology and business experts, alongside entrepreneurs, investors and other industry leaders. How to apply Applications go through an online form. The form is available on the programme's site during each cohort's registration period, and the homepage is inviting applications for Cohort 15 now. Name: PESU Venture Labs
Description: PESU Venture Labs (PVL) is a deep-tech venture studio and micro fund, founded in 2021 by Suresh Narasimha of CoCreate Ventures in partnership with PES University in Bengaluru. It describes itself as a science-first backer of student- and researcher-led startups, working from offices on the PES University campus. What they support PVL frames itself around deep tech, backing companies where the technology is the differentiator. Its flagship programme is campus-gated to PES University engineering students rather than open to founders across India, so a founder outside the university should check eligibility before applying. Programmes The Venture Studio, which PVL also calls its Accelerator Bootcamp, is a ten-week deep-tech venture creation programme run in three phases: Discover in weeks one to three, Build in weeks four to eight, and Launch in weeks nine and ten. It is open to engineering students in their third, fifth and seventh semesters, with no GPA requirement and teams of two to six members from any year or department. All ideas are taken into the first phase, and teams are then shortlisted after three checkpoints based on evaluation by mentors and the PVL team. PVL has also run Venture City, a one-day live simulation of a startup economy held on the PES University RR Campus, where participants form teams at the event and compete through the day. Entry needed a college ID, and no prior startup experience, team or idea was required. Who runs it PVL is run in partnership with PES University, which focuses on entrepreneurship through its Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (CIE), and with CoCreate Ventures as its venture-building partner. CoCreate operates micro funds to help build deep-tech startups. Locations PVL lists two offices inside PES University: the CIE Office on the 12th floor of B Block on the Outer Ring Road campus, and the CIE Office on the 4th floor of the Main Block at the Electronic City campus.

Name: PIEDS
Description: Pilani Innovation & Entrepreneurship Development Society (PIEDS) is the Technology Business Incubator of BITS Pilani, an autonomous not-for-profit society registered in 2013 under the Rajasthan Societies Registration Act. It is based at the Rakesh Kapoor Innovation Center on the BITS Pilani campus in Pilani, Rajasthan, and also runs a separate pre-incubation track for BITS Pilani's Mumbai (off-campus) students. What they support PIEDS works with technology-first founders across a wide sector spread: AI/ML, IoT, blockchain, robotics, AR/VR, fintech, healthcare hardware, climate and sustainability, defence-tech and agritech. Its programmes span the full founder journey, from idea-stage students who have not yet registered a company through to revenue-generating startups scaling with grant support. A number of its larger funds are restricted by who the founder is rather than what they are building: some are open only to BITS Pilani students or alumni, others are reserved for women-led ventures, and one is aimed specifically at founders from Tier II and Tier III Indian cities. Programmes PIEDS runs national government schemes it is approved to disburse locally, alongside its own and CSR-funded programmes. On the government side, it hosts MeitY's TIDE 2.0 (a three-tier ladder from an entrepreneur-in-residence stipend through grants to investment for later-stage startups), MeitY's SAMRIDH accelerator, DPIIT's Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, and the DST NIDHI family — NIDHI-EIR (a fellowship paying founders directly), NIDHI Seed Support System (structured as equity), NIDHI PRAYAS (an idea-to-prototype grant for hardware) and a general NIDHI Accelerator. It also disburses a SIDBI-backed iDEX seed fund for defence-tech. Alongside these, PIEDS runs its own named schemes: the Genesis entrepreneur-in-residence fellowship for Tier II/III founders, the Srishti hardware-prototyping fellowship, and BITS-restricted funds including the Alumni Startup Seed Fund, the Mookerji Innovation Fund (run with Silicon Road Ventures) and the Smt. Rajkumari Jain Seed Fund for Innovation. Two tracks pair mentorship with company formation for students: Ideate Create runs separately on the Pilani campus and the Mumbai campus, each a six-month, mentor-driven pre-incubation programme that PIEDS says moves 70-80% of its cohort on into full incubation. A newer set of programmes is co-designed with corporate and CSR partners. Samvardhan is a six-month, design-focused accelerator for medical-device hardware startups, run with Studio Carbon and funded by Birla Carbon and the Aditya Birla Capital Foundation; PIEDS and Studio Carbon each take 1% equity per funded startup. The Sustainability Accelerator, co-designed with SusMafia, is a similar six-month format for climate and sustainability startups. The Susventures Climate Residency is shorter and more unusual: a one-month, in-person residency where a small cohort of climate founders live together in a shared villa in Bangalore. The Aarogyam Digital Healthcare Accelerator is a four-month cohort for digital-health startups that ends in a demo day, with grants for the top three teams. Navonmesh Protsahan Spardha, run with the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, is a business-plan competition that funnels students from National Skill Training Institutes through pre-incubation and incubation rounds to a final jury. Saksham and Womenpreneur For Bharat both support women-led startups, the latter now in its fourth recurring edition. The IDFC FIRST Bank IGNITE accelerator, PIEDS's newest corporate-backed programme, targets revenue-generating climate-tech and health-tech startups with a structured, multi-phase acceleration format and grant support, plus up to twelve months of support after the programme ends. Facilities and support PIEDS's labs are built for hardware and software development rather than biology. The RKIC IoT Lab is equipped with microcontrollers, sensors, communication modules and embedded development platforms for building connected devices. The NIDHI PRAYAS Fabrication Lab pairs directly with the PRAYAS grant, giving funded founders fabrication equipment and electronics workstations to iterate on prototypes. The Kiran S Bhat Computer Graphics and Computer Vision Lab offers high-performance computing for image processing, computer vision and machine-learning work. RKIC also holds meeting and conference rooms of varying sizes, from a 10-person board room to a 48-person conference room, each equipped for video conferencing. Beyond labs, PIEDS says it helps startups navigate and apply for government grants and schemes, connects them with its mentor network, and facilitates networking, investor access and pitch opportunities. Several individual programme pages describe direct, hands-on support: for example, PIEDS has connected NIDHI-EIR founders with lab access and technical experts at BITS Hyderabad, and Sustainability Accelerator founders with senior executives at UltraTech Cement for technical guidance. Track record PIEDS's own pages state more than 400 startups supported and a mentor network of more than 150 people, alongside a claim of 12 or more active programmes and 122 or more cumulative startup programmes run. Several individual schemes carry their own published outcome numbers: the NIDHI-EIR fellowship reports 11 startups supported, 67 jobs created and 3 patents filed from one completed cohort; the Samvardhan design accelerator reports 8 startups across two cohorts, more than 30 jobs and 2 patents filed with 6 more in process; and the Sustainability Accelerator reports 5 startups that between them raised further follow-on capital after the programme. Named portfolio companies with their own descriptions on PIEDS's site include Nawgati, a fuel-tech startup that built a consumer app and a station-monitoring platform for CNG and fuel stations; Cautio, which builds an AI-powered dash-cam and operating system for fleet safety; and Nexus India, which makes rechargeable batteries from crop residue. How to apply There is no single, unified PIEDS application. Each scheme has its own apply link, most commonly hosted on PIEDS's own Accubate application portal, with some cohorts instead using a partner's own application system, as with the IDFC FIRST Bank IGNITE accelerator. Programmes with an open call publish their own eligibility criteria and deadline on their individual page; several, including some of the largest available cheques, are explicitly restricted to BITS Pilani students or alumni, so a founder's first step is working out which of PIEDS's programmes their affiliation, sector and stage actually qualify them for.
