Name: PVC Partners
Description: PVC Partners has worked with entrepreneurs since 2007. It describes itself as an investment advisory firm that also acts as a venture accelerator, and it runs Accelerateam, a structured pre-acceleration programme for first-time founders based in Delhi-NCR. The programme's current intake is closed, and the site names no new cohort dates. How the programme works Accelerateam takes a cohort-based approach, so each founder learns from the experience of peers at a similar stage as well as from the team and mentors. The programme covers identifying motivations and opportunities, business modelling, design thinking, execution, sales and marketing including digital presence, finance and fundraising, and perspective development. The framework has four parts. A Knowledge Lab runs workshops exclusive to the cohort. An Experience Lab gives first-hand exposure and learning from other entrepreneurs' experience. An Application Lab offers one-to-one clinics where founders test their hypotheses on the ground. Investor Readiness work prepares founders for the questions investors ask. The team describes the approach as one that constantly challenges founders to step out of their comfort zone. The programme pairs shared workshops with individual clinics, so founders spend time on both peer learning and their own venture. The stated duration is three months or more, with two in-person sessions a week of up to three hours each. The site says the structure may change for one-on-one interactions or for support outside the cohort format. Who can apply Accelerateam is built for first-time, first generation entrepreneurs at idea to pre-seed stage. The sector focus is open. The apply page says the programme suits students, people in a job who want to explore entrepreneurship, and founders who have already committed full-time to a venture. The location is Delhi-NCR, and the personal meetings used in shortlisting are held there too. Cost and equity The site describes the programme cost as nominal. It does not say whether the programme takes equity. Co-founders from the same business who attend together get significant further discounts, and so do founders qualified as social enterprises during selection. What to expect when you apply Applicants should expect three steps before any decision: a phone or Skype conversation, a shortlist, and a personal meeting in Delhi-NCR. The site does not give timelines for these steps. How selection works Selection starts with an application form that asks about the applicant and their venture. A phone or Skype conversation follows, then a shortlist, then a personal meeting. Selected applicants are contacted after the meeting. Current intake The application form linked from the apply page no longer accepts responses. The site refers to a forthcoming programme but gives no dates for it. Founders who want the next intake should email the team. Track record and sectors The site says the companies the team has supported came from diverse sectors, including drug discovery, renewable energy, ecommerce, retail, women's enterprise, telecom innovation and social enterprise enablement. It also says the team prefers to work with first-time founders. The page does not name the companies or give a count, so treat this as a description of sectors rather than a record of results. Who runs it Devangshu Dutta and Rohit Luthra co-founded PVC Partners in 2007. The page gives each co-founder a short biography covering their entrepreneurial and investment background. The site presents a group of mentors, coaches and facilitators who work with each cohort, and a set of founder testimonials. Location The programme runs in Delhi-NCR, and the personal meetings used in shortlisting are held there too. The apply page gives rnd@pvcpartners.in for questions about the programme.

The programme pairs shared workshops with individual clinics, so founders spend time on both peer learning and their own venture. The stated duration is three months or more, with two in-person sessions a week of up to three hours each. Name: Padup Ventures
Description: PadUp Ventures is a virtual accelerator for early-stage technology startups, run by PadUp Ventures Private Limited from Star Tower in Sector 30, Gurugram, Haryana. It works with founders remotely rather than from an incubation campus, and pairs structured mentoring with a route to angel money through its own investor network. Its own framework is called the PadUp Way. How programmes work The PadUp Way has three named parts, and they run in sequence. BootUp is the pre-acceleration bootcamp: an online validation programme where founders test whether their idea has a market, work through weekly tasks with mentors, and build the result into a business plan. PadUp describes it as action learning, with weekly coaching from its Chief Mentor alongside group and one-to-one sessions with its business mentors. BootUp ends in a Demo Day, where founders pitch to the accelerator's own angel investors. The site gives BootUp's length as ten to sixteen weeks on its programme pages and as sixteen weeks on the home page. FundUp is the fundraising step that follows. Before the pitch, mentors put founders through two to three weeks of mock sessions. Once a mentor signs off, PadUp organises a virtual demo day: investors get a pre-read, then each startup gets a fifteen-minute pitch and forty-five minutes of questions in a two-hour online session, followed by a moderated discussion. Investors register their interest through a form afterwards. PadUp then appoints Singhania & Co. as the due diligence partner, a step it says takes thirty days, after which a shareholder agreement is signed and a capital call runs over two weeks. The investors are Friends of PadUp, an angel group the company describes as adjunct to itself, plus other angel networks, micro-VCs and family offices. RevvUp is the acceleration programme for startups that have taken that angel money and now need to show traction. It gives each startup on-demand mentoring, in person and remote, from a domain expert mentor, with milestones set and reviewed every month and monthly masterclasses alongside. The stated aim is to get a startup from its first customers in a niche to larger clients, and from there to a Pre-Series A or Series A round. Its length is stated inconsistently across the site: twelve, twenty-four or thirty-six months on one page, twelve to thirty-six months on the home page, and twelve to twenty-four months a few paragraphs further down the programmes page. Who can apply PadUp runs one open application form rather than dated cohorts, and no deadline or intake window appears anywhere on the site. The form asks for your name, email, phone, startup name, a short description, your sector, your stage, team size, funding status, an elevator pitch and an optional website. The sector list runs AI/ML, health tech, fintech, edtech, SaaS, consumer, e-commerce, agritech and clean tech, with an "other" option. The stage list runs idea, prototype, MVP, early revenue and scaling, so the door is open across the early-stage range rather than to one stage only. Once you submit, PadUp says its team reviews the application and comes back within 48 hours. The site sets out no eligibility bar beyond that. It names no incorporation requirement, no state or category restriction, and no student or campus tie. It also does not publish whether its programmes charge a fee, and it does not state what equity, if any, PadUp itself takes — the shareholder agreement it describes is between the startup and the investors who back it at the demo day. Ask about both before you commit. Scale PadUp's numbers are self-reported and undated, and its own pages disagree. The home page counts 3,000 startups screened, 350 mentored, 175 graduated, 120 angel or seed funded and 45 with follow-on investment; the about page instead says over 3,000 screened and 300-plus accelerated, and the programmes page says its demo days have funded over 175 startups. Treat the range rather than any single figure. Its portfolio directory lists 34 companies, among them IntelleWings, Olbrain Labs, Flixdrop, Assetchain, Innovodigm and Docturnal, several of which also have written-up case studies on the site. Who runs it The team page names Rajat Jain, Pankaj Thakar (Founder and Chief Mentor), Divyendu Kumar and Syed Safawi as the founders. Behind them sits Friends of PadUp, described as a network of 232 senior executives and business leaders from corporate, government, academia and the social sector, badged on the home page as running since 2017; the tiles beside that line count 150 mentors and 106 investors. The published directory also lists more than a hundred expert mentors and a smaller group of super mentors and investor partners, most of them long-career corporate executives rather than career investors. The site lists a wide set of partners, including university and institute partners, angel networks such as the Indian Angel Network, Lead Angels and Chandigarh Angels, and professional firms. These appear as a partner directory with no statement of what each relationship involves, so read them as an ecosystem list rather than as accreditation. PadUp claims no government recognition anywhere on its site. Locations and contact PadUp works out of one office, at 609 Star Tower, Sector 30, Gurugram, next to Star Mall on NH8. General enquiries go to info@padup.in. There is no careers page. The site does publish a resource library of articles and a short Happenings section covering events and workshops.

Name: Palava Accelerator
Description: Palava Accelerator is an acceleration programme for emerging technology startups, set up by Lodha Group with Zone Startups India in 2017. It was based at Palava City, a privately developed smart city in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. We found no sign of intakes after 2018, and the website named at launch no longer loads. How the programme works The programme was designed as a four-month acceleration. Accepted startups were to get a dedicated workspace at Palava City, mentorship from Zone Startups India and its network, and pilot opportunities in the city. Other support listed at the time included business development help, access to investor networks, networking events, and accounting, legal and tax services. The 2018 release also mentioned co-working office space and residential options. Who can apply The only stated criterion is that the programme is for emerging technology startups. It framed itself as a test-bed for pilots at Palava City. No other eligibility rules were published. Sector focus Sources disagree on sector focus. The 2019 homepage listed five focus areas: mobility, sustainability, urban healthcare, smart homes and better governance. The 2017 launch release described real estate and smart-city technology instead. Check which description fits your startup before relying on either. Scale A 2017 plan aimed at 30 startups a year, on a non-cohort model with eight to ten working from Palava at any one time. The 2018 release reported six startups onboarded for the second cohort from 80 applications. It also said eight startups had been mentored since launch, and three of them became clients of Lodha Group, one of them UtopiaTech. These figures are self-reported, and the sources give different scales, so read them as rough figures. Who runs it Lodha Group is the parent. It funds the programme from its startup investment fund for real estate and smart cities. Sources differ on who operates it. The 2017 launch release points to Zone Startups India as the operator, while a 2018 release says Lodha established the programme in partnership with Zone Startups India. The launch release is dated September 2017, and the 2018 release says it was established in November 2017. Locations The 2017 launch release places the programme at Palava City in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The 2019 homepage gave an address in Dombivli, Thane district, which we could not confirm as current. Current status The programme's website no longer loads. The last dated intake we found was announced in November 2018. A 2026 Mumbai accelerator roundup still lists the programme, but it does not name a current batch.

Name: Parul University
Description: PIERC, the Parul Innovation and Entrepreneurship Research Centre, is the startup incubator of Parul University in Vadodara, Gujarat. It is a Section 8 company, and it takes founders from an idea through to a growing business with incubation, a six-month accelerator and an investor readiness programme. How the programmes work PIERC runs programmes for startups at different points. The Startup Incubation Program opens with a two-week pre-incubation training on design thinking, market research and business planning, then moves startups through the idea, prototype and growth stages over about two and a half years. GrowthPad is a six-month accelerator for startups that already have a product or early revenue and want to raise money from angel investors and venture capital firms. Startup Nivesh is an eight-week investor readiness and fundraising programme that ends in a demo day in front of investors. The HealthTech Accelerator, run with the university's hospital, takes healthcare startups through a six-month programme with clinical testbeds, and its applications are currently under review. Who can apply PIERC's pages say that applications are open to Parul University students and to external founders across India. The GrowthPad page advises a Private Limited company with DPIIT recognition, and it accepts unregistered founders who agree to register as a Private Limited company within three months. Startup Nivesh takes startups from any Indian state and any sector, provided they are Private Limited with active DPIIT recognition, and each cohort is capped at 30 startups. The HealthTech Accelerator takes a small cohort of healthcare startups that have a working prototype and some early validation. Facilities PIERC's centre sits in the BBA Building on the Parul University campus at Limda, near Vadodara. Its facilities include co-working space with work desks, meeting lounges and seminar halls, a Fab Lab for hands-on prototyping, and prototyping support for innovators who are building real products. Startup studios operate in Vadodara, Surat, Ahmedabad and Rajkot. Support on offer Beyond its programmes, PIERC offers startup counselling that helps students match an idea to real market needs. It assists founders with government schemes such as SSIP and the Startup India Seed Fund, supports IP and patent filing, provides legal compliance support, and helps startups reach markets through exhibitions and startup expos. It also runs the Vadodara Startup Festival and a women's startup festival. Founders can register for the Startup Bootcamp listed on the pierc.org site, and experienced people can register as mentors through the same site. Its startup events include pitch sessions, expos and demo days that bring founders in front of investors, mentors and government officials. Who runs it PIERC was registered in 2015 and grew out of Parul University's Entrepreneurship Development Cell. Its team includes a chief executive officer, incubation managers, and centre heads for its startup studios. Scale PIERC reports that it has incubated more than 210 startups, that those startups have created more than 1,200 jobs, and that they have filed more than 100 intellectual property applications. These figures are PIERC's own, carry no date, and have not been independently verified. One counter on the Startup Nivesh page renders as zero, so it is not used here. Locations The main centre is on the Parul University campus at P.O. Limda, Taluka Waghodia, in the Vadodara district. PIERC also runs startup studios in Surat, Ahmedabad and Rajkot, and the GrowthPad orientation is held at the Vadodara studio, with a separate contact address for each studio on the programme page. Who to contact The general enquiry address for the centre is pierc@paruluniversity.ac.in, and the programme pages list separate addresses for Startup Nivesh and the HealthTech Accelerator.

Name: PedalStart
Description: PedalStart is a founder-led startup accelerator for pre-seed and idea-stage startups in India. It says it invests at the inception, pre-seed and seed stages, in exchange for equity. Its office is at DLF Phase 1 in Gurugram, Haryana. What they support PedalStart works with founders from idea validation through to an MVP and their next raise. The site says it backs founders who bring clarity, execution and deep market understanding. Its stated audience is pre-seed and idea-stage founders building startups in India. Programmes The main route is the founder-led accelerator. The site does not state its length, format or any fee, and it gives no batch dates or intake status. The homepage shows an Apply Now button and nothing about when the next intake opens. Selected startups are called into structured programmes such as the Start-up Sprint, where the site says stage, clarity of problem and founder commitment are evaluated. The homepage reports that the 8th Start-up Sprint has concluded. The site gives no dates or fees for the next one. PedalInvest is a separate network for investors, not a programme founders apply to. Launched under the PedalStart ecosystem, it connects angels, high-net-worth individuals and venture partners with early-stage startups. Membership is invite-only, and the site says background checks apply. Equity and terms PedalStart's blog says its investment "is structured in exchange for equity" and that "exact terms vary based on stage and traction." An older press article, which we could not open, reports that founders can join on a subscription basis without giving up equity at the outset. That article is unconfirmed. Ask for the terms in writing before agreeing to anything. Track record The figures below are the site's own and are self-reported. The homepage cites more than 4,000 startups onboarded, more than 40,000 applications, more than 2,000 pre-accelerated startups and more than 20 funded startups. It also says 46% of its portfolio startups secured up-rounds. It cites more than 200 mentors. The site does not date these figures. A company-data listing that we could only read from a search snippet gives different counts: over 3,000 startups onboarded and 45 accelerated. The two sets of figures do not match, so treat the homepage counts as the site's claims rather than verified numbers. The homepage names portfolio companies including UpKraft, InsightAI and Flowatt, and describes a pre-seed round for each as led by or from PedalStart. Investor numbers also differ across the site. The homepage cites more than 1,200 investors. The PedalInvest page cites a community of more than 1,000 investors and more than 1,200 verified members. Those pages give different counts. How to apply Use the Apply Now button on the homepage, or the join-the-accelerator form on the blog, which asks for name, phone number, email and purpose. The site says applications are evaluated, and selected startups are then called into structured programmes. For PedalInvest, sign up on its own page. What the site does not say It does not state the accelerator's length, format, fee or team, and it does not list what a startup receives beyond the investment itself. It gives no founding year. Its pages also describe it two ways. The homepage says "we are not an accelerator on paper, we are a team that actually builds with you," while a blog post says PedalStart "does not position itself as a short-term cohort-based accelerator."

Name: Razorpay Rize
Description: Razorpay Rize is Razorpay's startup programme for early-stage founders in India, launched in 2021. It brings together three free founder communities, a few dedicated programmes and a company registration service. Razorpay is based in Bengaluru, and the Rize pages carry its registered office there. What Rize offers Rize has three parts. The first is the communities, where founders get tool credits, Razorpay product offers, expert knowledge sessions, mentorship, networking events, a founder directory, a marketplace of deals and a resource vault with investor lists. The second is a set of programmes, Rize for YC and Rize Pitch Perfect, that founders can use even if they are not in a community. The third is Rize Incorporation, which helps founders register a Private Limited company, an LLP or a One Person Company through partner firms. The three communities Rize Tech+ is for early-stage tech and AI founders. Rize D2C+ is for founders in D2C, eCommerce and retail, from early to growth stage. Rize Xport+ is for founders who build in India and sell to customers around the world, across tech, SaaS, D2C and services. Membership is free. A founder cannot join more than one community: every application goes through a selection process, and the team places you in the one that suits your startup best. Rize for YC Rize for YC helps founders prepare an application to Y Combinator. It has an AI-powered application review, learning sessions with YC alumni, a library of sample applications and guides, and mock interviews with alumni. The page says there is no selection criterion for the reviews and sessions, and that the programme costs nothing. Mock interviews are for founders who have received a call from YC. The programme runs for each YC batch, and the dates on the page change, so check which batch is open before you plan around it. Rize lists many founders from its community who were later accepted into YC, though its pages give different counts. Rize Pitch Perfect Pitch Perfect is described as a programme for learning how to tell your story, build a strong deck and refine it for investors. Rize does not show a separate intake page for it, so ask through the Rize team before relying on it. Company registration Rize Incorporation is aimed at early-stage founders who want to register a company at low fees. It covers Private Limited companies, LLPs and One Person Companies, and the pages also cover other forms such as partnership firms, sole proprietorships, public limited companies and Section 8 companies, with city pages for Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata and Kanpur. Registration is done through dedicated partners. The site also offers free tools: a company-name and trademark search, a company-type finder, document guides, startup templates and an investor list. Scale The pages give different figures for the size of the community, so treat any single number with care. They describe more than a thousand founders, large numbers of company registrations, and mentor hours and founder stories shown on the community page. Things to know Rize is a corporate programme run by a payments company, not a grant or a fund. It does not hand out money. Its value is community, credits, mentorship and services. Founders who use Razorpay products get extra offers through the community.

Name: Rebalance
Description: Rebalance is a private accelerator and angel investor network for early-stage Indian startups that have at least one woman founder. It calls itself India's first accelerator programme and angel community, and its stated mission is to get more women into startups and into venture capital, as founders and as funders. It runs no building and no lab: the accelerator is a semi-virtual, 15-week programme with two in-person bootcamps in Gurgaon or Bangalore, and the rest of what Rebalance does sits on the investor side. How the accelerator works The Rebalance Accelerator runs twice a year and takes fewer than 15 companies per cohort. Over 15 weeks there are roughly ten group sessions on Zoom plus a three-day in-person bootcamp in India, so founders keep running their company while they go through it. Weekly sessions work on market-product fit, market sizing, understanding users and growth strategy. On top of that there are one-to-one hours with mentors and with the Rebalance team, sector-relevant sessions curated for each batch, and pitch practice in front of a panel of founders and investors before demo day. The perks are the usual accelerator stack: cloud credits from Google and Amazon sized to what you actually use, and partner credits from WebEngage, Truecaller, Twilio, Amazon Activate and Freshworks. Rebalance also says it makes warm introductions to more than 150 VCs across India, the US, Europe and Asia, and opens co-selling conversations with corporate partners for pilots, research and investment. One thing it offers that most programmes do not is a founder wellness and performance strand, where it brings in experts to work with women founders on habits and endurance. Selected companies in a batch can receive investment through the Rebalance Angel Community at pre-seed or seed. Rebalance also offers to take the mandate for a founder's whole round and advise on structure and terms. Who can apply Three things are required, and the first is a hard gate: a diverse team with at least one female founder, minimum viable traction (a prototype, users, early revenue or pilots), and a tech-enabled, sector-agnostic idea that can scale. The FAQs are blunt that founders without a woman co-founder cannot join the accelerator, though the angel community evaluates deals separately and invests regardless. LGBTQ founders are explicitly welcome. Rebalance is sector agnostic and does not gate on funding stage. It says it has worked with companies from stealth up to pre-Series A, and from pre-revenue through to break-even and raising Series A, so having already raised early money does not disqualify you. No incorporation requirement and no state or city restriction is stated anywhere on its site. What it costs you This is the part worth reading twice before applying. Rebalance takes 1% sweat equity when you join the programme, and it takes a percentage of anything you raise through its network if you choose to raise. It is up front about both in its FAQs. It does not publish a programme fee. The investor side Two of Rebalance's three programmes are for investors rather than founders, which matters if you are trying to work out what it is. The Rebalance Angel Community is its angel network, which it describes as 60% women. There is no membership requirement and no minimum commitment. Members get an angel investing crash course run with experienced angels and fund managers, access to pre-screened deals, and seats at the accelerator's demo days where they meet founders directly. The community invests in companies regardless of whether they have women founders, even though most of what it backs leans diverse. The Diverse Investors League is the fund-side collective — VC funds, syndicates and family offices that want more diverse deal flow. Rebalance says more than 150 funds sit in it, and members get early access to accelerator founders matched to their thesis. For a founder, the practical point is that the accelerator is the only door in, and the two investor networks are the reason the programme can put you in front of capital. Track record Rebalance's own counters, which it does not date, report ten cohorts run, 30 investments made and 170 founders supported, with 85% of the portfolio women-led. Its Companies page gives the founder number differently, as "150+ founders", so treat the count as approximate. A figure of the same size appears three different ways across its pages — as follow-on funding, as what portfolio companies have raised at pre-seed and seed, and as what has moved through the investor collective — so we have not published it as any one of those. Named portfolio companies include Hyperface, Brainsight.AI, Darwix.ai (formerly Cur8), Vecros, Dnome, DreamFly Innovations, Pinky Promise, LearnTube, Stack, Tea Trunk, Accacia, Language Curry, Kinderpass, Myplan8, The Disposal Company, PowerSutra, Tilt, Nife, GoCodeo and Terra Bioware, among others. Who runs it The People page names Aishwarya Malhi and Vikas Kumar as the founders behind Rebalance, with Adrika Shukla on programme and investments and Meher Joshi on marketing and partnerships. Its mentor and speaker panel is large and drawn mostly from Indian operators and investors, including people from Google, Fundamentum, Kae Capital, Saama Capital, Bain & Company, Tata Business Hub, Nobroker, xto10x, Sirion Labs and Goodwater Capital. Where it is Rebalance publishes no office address. The only physical anchor on its site is the programme format: the two bootcamps run in Gurgaon or Bangalore. Everything else happens online, so where you are based should not decide whether you apply. The only contact route it publishes is hello@therebalance.com.

Name: SHINE FOUNDATION
Description: SHINE Foundation, short for Sahyadri Hub for Innovations and Entrepreneurship, is a Section 8 company set up by Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management (SCEM) to support innovation and entrepreneurship. It sits on the SCEM campus in Mangaluru, Karnataka, and runs an incubation programme and an acceleration programme for startups from the region. It is also the Mangaluru-cluster execution partner for the Karnataka Acceleration Network (KAN), a programme of the Government of Karnataka and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM). How programmes work SHINE's own site names two programmes of its own. The SHINE Incubation Programme is meant to give early-stage startups full support so they can validate their products. The SHINE Accelerator Programme supports entrepreneurs and industries from the region, to promote community-based innovation. Neither page gives an intake window, a duration, a fee policy or an equity policy, so write to SHINE before assuming a call is open. The programme with a clear structure is KAN, which SHINE delivers in Mangaluru under KDEM guidelines. It is a four-module programme covering strategy, validation, go-to-market and scale. Startups get one-to-one mentoring and group workshops, weekly mentor reviews against milestones, access to customers and partner institutions in the Mangaluru region for early validation, pitch coaching and investor introductions, and Demo Day preparation. Description: S.P. Jain Institute of Management & Research (SPJIMR) runs entrepreneurship programmes from its Andheri West campus in Mumbai. The best-known is Start Your Business, a four-month hybrid course for people starting a business and for early-stage start-ups. How programmes work The institute runs four entrepreneurship programmes listed on its site: Start Your Business (SYB), Sashakt, EnPower and Start-up Sprint. SYB is the core course. It combines expert sessions, mentoring and a business plan that participants present to a panel of investors, faculty and mentors. Sashakt is free and taught in Hindi for micro-entrepreneurs. EnPower is a two-month certificate for undergraduates and recent graduates. Start-up Sprint is a five-day on-campus programme. Who can apply SYB is for aspiring entrepreneurs and early-stage start-ups, preferably with an undergraduate degree from a recognised university. EnPower is for students and recent graduates. Sashakt is for entrepreneurs aged 25-30 who run micro-enterprises. Start-up Sprint is for undergraduates and fresh graduates from any discipline. Facilities SYB participants get access to incubation facilities at the Sardar Patel Technology Business Incubator (SP-TBI) after the programme. SP-TBI is located within the Bhavan's campus in Andheri. Access is subject to SP-TBI's own terms. Who runs it SPJIMR was established in 1981 by Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, a non-profit educational institution. Its entrepreneurship work sits in the Centre for Family Business & Entrepreneurship (CFBE). Locations The Mumbai campus is at Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan Campus, Munshi Nagar, Dadabhai Road, Andheri West, Mumbai 400058. Scale The site states that the FT MiM 2026 ranking places the institute at number 26 globally and number 2 in India. The site does not state how many startups or entrepreneurs the programmes have supported, so no count is given here.

Name: SVIF
Description: SVIF, the S V Innovation Foundation, is an incubator and accelerator for early-stage startups in Gujarat. Its contact address is at Kadi Sarva Vishwavidyalaya in Gandhinagar, and it describes itself as both a support-stage incubator and an early-stage startup accelerator. How programmes work SVIF runs four programmes. The Incubation Program is a 6–12 month deep-immersion programme that takes a startup from raw idea to a market-ready MVP. It combines co-working infrastructure, hands-on mentorship, milestone tracking and access to the wider SVIF ecosystem, and each batch takes 6 to 10 startups. The Acceleration Cohort is a 90-day cohort for post-MVP startups. Spots are limited to 6 to 8 startups, and the cohort ends with a Demo Day in front of investors. Mentoring gives one-on-one and group guidance from more than 15 industry mentors across technology, marketing, operations, legal and finance. Funding Support helps startups prepare to raise capital, with pitch preparation, financial modelling, grant navigation and introductions to SVIF's investor network. SVIF says a nominal equity agreement may apply to the Incubation Program and the Acceleration Cohort. Mentoring requires no equity. SVIF says it typically runs one or two cohorts a year. Who can apply The Incubation Program is open to founders based in Gujarat or willing to work from Ahmedabad. SVIF's programmes page says remote participation is available for select programmes for founders based outside the city, so check the individual programme before assuming you can join from elsewhere. The Acceleration Cohort is for post-MVP startups. Funding Support is available only to SVIF incubated and accelerated startups and to select applicants at advanced stages. Mentoring is open to founders who want one-on-one or group guidance from industry mentors. How to apply Each programme is applied for through SVIF's online application form. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, and the team says it will contact applicants within 5 to 7 days of applying. Applications for the next Acceleration cohort are open at the time of writing, and spots are limited to 6 to 8 startups, so founders who want that cohort should apply early. Once a mentee is accepted, SVIF says it will match them with a mentor within 7 days. Facilities The Incubation Program includes co-working infrastructure. SVIF's homepage also describes co-working space and meeting rooms in Ahmedabad's startup corridor. Its programme pages place the primary facility in Ahmedabad, not Gandhinagar, so ask which location your programme uses before you apply. Scale SVIF's homepage gives both a figure of 22 or more startups incubated and the line 'no startups published yet'. Its portfolio page shows zero startups. This page therefore gives no startup count. The site does say it has 15 or more expert mentors, has completed four or more cohorts, and maintains relationships with 25 or more active angel investors who focus on early-stage Gujarat-based startups. SVIF says 40 or more investors attend each Demo Day. It also says past cohort startups have closed seed rounds within six weeks of Demo Day, but it gives no count of how many. Who runs it SVIF's about page lists SVKM, GTU, EDII, DPIIT / Startup India, BIRAC, Gujarat iHub, the Wadhwani Foundation and the University of Alberta, Canada under 'Supported by and associated with'. SVIF does not say that any of these bodies recognise it as an incubator. SVIF also says it has strong institutional relationships with EDII Ahmedabad and GTU that give access to academic seed funding for eligible startups. Locations SVIF's contact address is Kadi Sarva Vishwavidyalaya, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. Its programme pages say its primary facility is in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. Founders should check each programme's location before applying, because remote participation is offered only for select programmes.

Name: Saksham
Description: Saksham is a national accelerator programme for startups working in assistive technology, run by SACC India, the Startup Accelerator Chamber of Commerce. It backs early-stage founders building inclusive, accessible solutions for people with disabilities. Information here is drawn from the programme's own site, which documents a single accelerator rather than a wider incubation operation, so this description is shorter than most. What they support Saksham is focused on assistive technology: solutions that address challenges in mobility, vision, hearing, speech, or cognitive disabilities. The current intake is run as Saksham 3.0. It looks for startups registered in India that are working to create accessible and inclusive products for people with disabilities, and asks that applicants already have a working prototype or a minimum viable product. The emphasis throughout is on assistive devices and inclusive technology rather than a general, sector-agnostic cohort. Programmes The accelerator helps founders move an assistive-technology product forward through mentorship, product testing and validation, and connections into the market, and it finishes with a Demo Day. Selected cohort startups can also receive grant support and introductions to investors; the grant is described as a staged process rather than a single payment, and the programme does not fix a specific amount on its page. SACC India has run the accelerator over more than one cohort, with earlier cohorts listing the startups they selected. How to apply Founders apply through the online application form linked from the programme site. Because applications run as cohorts, the window is open at some points in the year and closed at others; when it is closed, the site is the place to check for the next intake. SACC India, the Startup Accelerator Chamber of Commerce, is the organiser behind the programme and runs it as its assistive-technology accelerator.

Name: SanchiConnect
Description: SanchiConnect is a deep-tech enablement network founded in 2022 and headquartered in Noida, Uttar Pradesh. At its core it is a free-to-join community and matchmaking platform: startups, investors, enterprises and mentors sign up to find each other, rather than apply to be selected into a cohort. Alongside that network, SanchiConnect and its partners run a small number of named, application-based accelerator programmes for deep-tech and fintech founders, and it operates a physical co-working space for the community in Noida. What they support The network is open to deep-tech startups broadly — AI/ML, robotics, biotech, cleantech, space and quantum computing are all named as areas members work in. Its two accelerator programmes narrow this further: VELOCITY, run with YourNest VC, looks for DPIIT-registered deep-tech hardware and software startups with core IP, from MVP stage through to early revenue, across sectors including AdTech, AgriTech, BioTech, HealthTech/MedTech, SpaceTech, mobility, manufacturing and energy. Pulse, run with Thinkuvate, is narrower still: AI-driven fintech startups incorporated in India or South-East Asia, at proof-of-concept or early-revenue stage with a working MVP. A third programme, Leap to Unicorn, was open to India-based founders in any sector with at least an MVP or working prototype, and did not focus on deep tech specifically. On the network side, joining does not require being selected — any deep-tech startup, investor, enterprise or mentor can sign up, and SanchiConnect says there is no subscription fee to join. Programmes Pulse is a 24-week AI and fintech accelerator, run jointly with Thinkuvate. Selected startups get one-on-one sessions with industry leaders and functional experts, access to a pool of expert mentors, a demo day in front of investors, and investment on a term sheet issued after due diligence. SanchiConnect does not charge a programme fee, but reserves the right to take equity in each company it invests in. Its most recent intake closed applications in December 2025 after receiving 598 applications, with cohort selection due by January 2026. VELOCITY, run with YourNest VC, is a 60-day scale-up accelerator for DPIIT-registered deep-tech startups with core IP, aimed at near-commercialisation or early-revenue companies. Selected startups get mentorship from YourNest partners, a programme focused on go-to-market and global alliances, and market access, with investment again offered on a milestone-based term sheet after due diligence. Like Pulse, there is no programme fee, and SanchiConnect reserves the right to take equity. Its last published cycle drew 1,282 applications. Leap to Unicorn was a free, no-equity founder programme structured in phases: open registration, a shortlist of 400 founders invited into a 15-day virtual bootcamp of masterclasses and pitch coaching, a pitch-video round narrowing to 20, and a jury round selecting a final 5 for a studio finale. Participants who progressed got media exposure, investor access, expert mentoring and a feature in a top-100 startups-to-watch report, with IDFC FIRST Bank, Moneycontrol and CNBC-TV18 as partners. Its most recent published cycle closed registration in February 2024; SanchiConnect's homepage references a later season, suggesting the programme has run more than once, but no open or upcoming cycle was found on the programme's own page. All three programmes were closed to new applications at the time of this review — none had an open intake. Facilities and support SanchiConnect runs DeepTech Hub, a physical co-working space at the Delhi–Noida border, next to the Sector 16 Metro station, for founders, investors and domain experts to work alongside each other. Beyond the accelerators, SanchiConnect also offers Technology Investment Advisory, an investment-banking-style advisory service for deep-tech fundraising, family-office co-investment, cross-border capital raises and IPO readiness, aimed at founders and investors rather than being part of a cohort programme. It also lists a software platform for managing ecosystem data, and video-pitching tools that let startups pitch to investors directly through the platform. Who runs it SanchiConnect is led by Dr. Sunil K. Shekhawat as CEO and co-founder, with a leadership team covering growth, investments and technology. Its advisory panel includes Rahul Bhasin, Managing Partner at Baring PE Fund, alongside advisors with backgrounds at Global Logic and T-Hub. SanchiConnect's own homepage names Baring Private Equity Partners-India, Seafund and 8X Ventures as having funded the organisation. Locations SanchiConnect is headquartered in Sector 3, Noida, Uttar Pradesh, with its DeepTech Hub co-working space located separately at the Delhi–Noida border. Its accelerator partners include YourNest VC and Thinkuvate, and its broader partner list spans T-Hub, Nasscom and IIT Kanpur. How to apply There is no single application route into SanchiConnect: joining the free network is a straightforward sign-up, while each accelerator programme (Pulse, VELOCITY, Leap to Unicorn) runs its own online application form, taking roughly 15–30 minutes to complete, with the programme team explicit that applications sent directly by email will not be considered.

Name: Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology, Surat
Description: ASHINE, the Association for Harnessing Innovation and Entrepreneurship, is the technology business incubator of Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology (SVNIT) in Surat, Gujarat. It sits on the institute campus at Ichchhanath and works through the institute's Research Park. How the programmes work ASHINE runs incubation for technology-based startups. It also gives funding to student teams and innovators who are still building a prototype or proof of concept, and it runs an accelerator with the Wadhwani Foundation for early-stage ventures that are ready to scale. Incubation and funding are tied to state schemes for startups in Gujarat, so the funding calls follow those schemes' rules as well as ASHINE's own. Who can apply The incubation route is open to startups. The institute's startup policy says ASHINE gives incubation support to external startups where SVNIT faculty, staff, research scholars or students act as consultants or mentors. Proof-of-concept funding is open to innovators and student teams. Intellectual property support is open to innovators who need to protect a creative or technological outcome. The Wadhwani Liftoff accelerator has no open call on the programme page at the time of review, and interested founders are told to watch ASHINE's announcements. Facilities and services ASHINE offers pre-incubation and incubation support, co-working space, a product launch space, seminar and conference rooms, a fablab for product design and prototyping, IP support, mentoring and handholding, alumni connect, legal support and funding support. The co-working space is also rented to freelancers and professionals who are not in the incubator, and meeting rooms are charged by the hour. Scale ASHINE's home page lists 200 startups supported, 29 startups under incubation, 51 startups under pre-incubation and 72 proof-of-concept projects supported. These are the figures the incubator reports about itself, and its pages do not state a date for them. Focus areas ASHINE's thrust areas are engineering and technology, materials and manufacturing, and energy and environment. The institute's startup policy makes ASHINE the single body at SVNIT that carries out the institute's startup and entrepreneurship policy, so it also coordinates innovation work across departments. Who runs it ASHINE is a not-for-profit Section 8 company set up by SVNIT. Its board is made up of institute leaders, and it has faculty in charge of incubation, the SSIP cell, co-working and industry interaction.

Name: Sharda University
Description: Sharda Launchpad Federation is the innovation and entrepreneurship arm of Sharda University in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. It is a Section 8 company registered under the Companies Act 2013, set up by the university as a centre for entrepreneurship development. How the programmes work Sharda Launchpad runs a permanent incubation programme for ventures at the idea and early stage, a food and beverage accelerator for startups at prototype, early-traction and scale-up stages, and a government-supported technology business incubator called DST i-TBI Sharda Launchpad. It also offers a paid certificate course in new age entrepreneurship. Who can apply The incubation programme is open to student entrepreneurs of Sharda University, and its overview says it also supports startups and innovators from across India and abroad. The food and beverage accelerator takes startups in cloud kitchen and QSR, B2B food supplies, food products, and food logistics. The DST i-TBI focuses on agritech, rural health, women empowerment and rural livelihood. The certificate course takes graduates of any discipline. Support on offer The pages list co-working space, legal and regulatory support, IPR support, government grant assistance, mentoring, industry expert connects, weekly startup clinics, and access to university labs. Funding is described as available to budding entrepreneurs, with the amount given on the page. Startups incubated there are listed on the incubates page. Who runs it The leadership, advisory board and in-house and industry mentors are listed on the About page of the Launchpad site. Location Plot No. 32-34, Knowledge Park III, Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The Launchpad pages give the postal code as 201306; the university's main site gives 201310.

Name: ShelterTech
Description: ShelterTech was an accelerator for for-profit, scalable start-ups working on gaps in India's affordable housing value chain. It was not a standalone organisation but a co-branded programme, organised in a partnership between Habitat for Humanity's Terwilliger Center for Innovation in Shelter and the Centre for Innovation Incubation and Entrepreneurship (CIIE). It was run across two bases: CIIE at the IIM Ahmedabad new campus in Vastrapur, Ahmedabad, and Habitat for Humanity at the IITM Research Park in Taramani, Chennai. The programme is not currently open. Its website states that applications are now closed, and every dated milestone on the site belongs to a single 2018–2019 cycle, with an application deadline of 6 March 2019. The description below records what that programme was and how it worked; a founder should not expect an open intake unless the organisers announce a new one. What it supported ShelterTech looked for start-ups with for-profit, scalable business models addressing affordable-housing challenges or adjacent markets, whether B2B, B2C or B2B2C. Start-ups with pilots, early customer traction or sales were preferred, though idea-stage teams could apply if they backed their claims with detail on their intellectual property, background and team. To apply, a start-up had to be registered in India with at least one co-founder based in India; the organisers stated they could not support start-ups based outside India through the programme. How the programme worked ShelterTech ran as a non-residential accelerator in two phases, each with its own cohort of start-ups. The first phase kicked off in December 2018 and the second from April 2019, and the programme ended with a demo day in July 2019, when start-ups from both cohorts pitched. Its own pages describe the length inconsistently: one page calls it a year-long initiative, while the about page and other answers describe it as a four-month programme run in two cohorts. Each phase was expected to accelerate a cohort of four to five start-ups. Selected companies could receive financial support through the programme, in the form of equity investment, grant support, or both, with a route for start-ups that reached a higher scale to pitch the Terwilliger Center's global venture fund. The number of start-ups that would receive this support is stated differently in different places on the site, so it is best read as a small handful rather than a fixed figure. Beyond funding, the programme offered problem-solving support, access to partner and founder networks, and connections to the wider affordable-housing sector. Who ran it The accelerator was organised in partnership between Habitat for Humanity's Terwilliger Center for Innovation in Shelter and CIIE. CIIE was set up by IIM Ahmedabad with support from the Government of India and the Gujarat Government to provide seeding and incubation support, with a focus on technology and mass-impact areas. The programme also named sector partners working in affordable housing, including Brigade Reap and Mahila Housing Trust. Locations and contact ShelterTech was co-run from two sites: CIIE at the IIM Ahmedabad new campus, Vastrapur, Ahmedabad 380015, and Habitat for Humanity at the IITM Research Park, Kanagam Road, Taramani, Chennai 600113. General queries went to a programme inbox, support@sheltertech.in.

Name: Silver Ridge Accelerator
Description: Silver Ridge Accelerator is a privately run accelerator for founders who already have a working product and early revenue and want to build for markets beyond the one they started in. It is led by a single named partner, Dhiraj Shah, whose background is in venture capital at Venture Catalysts and in operations at Castler. It is a young and deliberately small operation: its whole public presence is one page, and several of the endorsements on that page were written while the accelerator was still being set up. How the programme works There is one programme. Silver Ridge describes it as partnership rather than a taught course, and says it works alongside founders on business development, mentorship and access to capital. The published list of what a selected company gets covers eight things: access to a global partner ecosystem, help with market expansion, access to capital, support in putting together investment collaterals, mentorship, structuring, legal and compliance support, business development support, and support on the follow-on round. What the site does not publish is as relevant as what it does. There is no cohort, batch, intake window or deadline anywhere on the site, so applications appear to be read as they arrive rather than in rounds. The programme's length is not stated. Whether it runs online, in person or as a mix is not stated. Whether Silver Ridge takes equity is not stated either way, and neither is whether the founder pays anything to take part. A founder should settle all four of those in writing before committing, because the site will not answer them. Three organisations are shown as growth partners: AngelList India, Recur Club and MG & Co. Legal. The site names them but does not describe what each partner does for a participating company. Who can apply Silver Ridge publishes four screening parameters, and all four are about the company rather than about who the founders are. It wants a product that is already built and solving a real problem; early revenue traction at an annual recurring revenue threshold it names on the page; a digital-first, tech-driven and scalable business model; and a clear differentiator in a crowded market. There is no stated restriction by sector. There is no stated requirement that the company be incorporated, and no stated restriction by country, state, founder category or company age. Nothing on the site limits the programme to Indian-registered companies, and nothing confirms that it is open beyond them. Everything visible about the operation points to Indian founders — its partner's background, the partners it names, and every company and founder it shows — so an Indian startup with revenue is plainly the kind of applicant it is built around. A founder outside that description should ask before applying. How selection works Silver Ridge publishes a weighting rather than a process, and it is unusually explicit about it. Its "60/40 Rule" puts sixty per cent of the decision on the team and forty per cent on the idea, on the reasoning that markets and technologies change while strong teams keep finding a way through. On the team side it names six things: resilience, decisiveness and boldness; integrity and trustworthiness; clarity rather than jargon; the ability to navigate ambiguity; technical proficiency backed by a track record of execution; and skin in the game. On the idea side it names six more: a unique proposition; a strong competitive advantage; a frugal and clear business model; serviceable and achievable revenue potential; a plan for how capital will be used; and a path to profitability. No interview stage, screening call, diligence step or decision timeline is described, so a founder cannot tell from the site how long a decision takes. Who runs it One person is named on the site: Dhiraj Shah, Partner. His profile describes a focus on ethical investing, experience in venture capital at Venture Catalysts and in operational growth at Castler, and an investor network he says spans four geographies. No other staff member, adviser, board member or mentor is named, and no fund, vehicle or parent company is named either. Nine testimonials appear on the page, from founders at Delhivery, Castler, Lorien Finance, SalesAgents.ai, Basic Home Loan, Ensuredit, D'Moksha Homes and Zingbus. Almost all of them are about working with Dhiraj Shah personally rather than about going through the accelerator, and two of them describe the accelerator as something he was about to launch. What the track record on its site refers to The page carries a block of figures — startups evaluated, startups fundraised for, follow-on rounds, exits and a mortality rate — under the heading "Founding Team Track Record". These are the founding team's record from before Silver Ridge, not results the accelerator has produced, and they are self-reported and undated. The page also ships two versions of the same block that label the same figure differently, one as startups fundraised for and the other as startups funded, which are different claims. A row of eighteen company logos sits under the heading "Previously Backed Companies" and is likewise not presented as a Silver Ridge portfolio. Where it is based The site states no address, city, state or country, and gives no phone number. Its only contact route is a general email address and the application form. How to apply Every "Apply Now" button on the site opens the same online application form. There is no deadline to work to and no application fee is mentioned. The form asks the applicant to sign in with a Google account before it will open. Questions can also go to contact@silverridgeaccelerator.com.

Name: Social Alpha
Description: Social Alpha is a not-for-profit innovation and venture-development platform for science and technology start-ups working on social, economic and environmental problems. It is run by the Foundation for Innovation and Social Entrepreneurship (FISE), launched in 2016 and sponsored and supported by Tata Trusts. Rather than one incubator building, Social Alpha operates as a network of labs, challenge programmes and seed funds spread across several Indian cities. Locations across India Social Alpha's main lab is the Social Alpha Lab in Yeswanthpur, Bengaluru, Karnataka. In the same city it also runs mach33.aero, a joint initiative with CSIR's National Aerospace Laboratories (CSIR-NAL) for aviation, aerospace and space-tech start-ups, housed inside the Industry Interface Building at CSIR-NAL on HAL Old Airport Road, Kodihalli. In Delhi, it runs a lab inside Tata Power-DDL's Smart Grid Lab in Rohini, home to the Clean Energy International Incubation Centre (CEIIC). A separate clean-energy challenge, run through the Clean Energy Innovation and Business Incubation Centre (CEIBIC), has used testing and office space at the Energy Management Centre in Trivandrum, Kerala, alongside the Delhi CEIIC facility. Beyond these physical labs, Social Alpha runs challenges and accelerators with partner institutions in other cities, including one with NIPER Ahmedabad. What they support Social Alpha looks for founders building science- or technology-based solutions in climate and clean energy, agriculture and rural livelihoods, health and wellness, assistive technology, waste management and the circular economy, and space technology. It works across the founder journey, from an idea or lab-stage innovation through a working prototype to a start-up that is ready to scale, and it explicitly favours ventures whose technology needs a longer development runway than typical venture-backed software. Programmes Much of Social Alpha's work happens through named challenges and accelerators rather than one standing programme. Techtonic is its recurring scouting platform, run in themed editions such as Techtonic: Innovations for Sustainability (covering energy transition, new materials and natural resources) and past editions on clean energy, agriculture, animal husbandry and circular economy, several run with partners such as the M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation and the U of T India Foundation. The Atal Incubation Centre at Social Alpha, set up under NITI Aayog's Atal Innovation Mission, focuses on climate, health and livelihoods and has onboarded start-ups through grand challenges including the India Clean Air Challenge and Pfizer INDovation. The SpaceTech Innovation Network (SpIN), supported by ISRO, accepts applications on a rolling basis for foundational space technologies and downstream applications. mach33.aero runs a similar lab-to-market model for aviation and aerospace start-ups. On the funding side, Social Alpha hosts a Department of Science and Technology NIDHI Seed Support Scheme seed fund for start-ups already in its incubation programme, and it has run agriculture-focused accelerators such as Krishi Mangal with Cisco CSR. Facilities and support Entrepreneurs get access to Social Alpha's own innovation labs for product development, iteration and testing, along with specialised facilities such as the Tata Trusts PATH Impact Lab for healthcare technology and 3D printers at discounted rates. Support goes beyond lab space: seed capital and connections to follow-on capital, go-to-market strategy help, design and manufacturing support for turning a prototype into a manufacturable product, mentorship and knowledge-sharing sessions, and shared back-office services such as accounting, legal, IP and HR so a start-up can keep its own team lean. Health-focused ventures also get support with clinical validation and regulatory readiness. Track record Across 2016 to 2024, Social Alpha states it evaluated more than 20,000 innovations and supported more than 300 start-ups, making over 90 seed investments and more than 100 catalytic grants, with more than 60 follow-on funding rounds for its portfolio and over 65 patents granted to portfolio companies. Named portfolio companies include Phool, Kamal Kisan, Padcare Labs, Voxelgrids, Bionic Yantra, Tactopus, Himalayan Rocket Stove and Strawcture. How to apply There is no single always-open application for all of Social Alpha; each lab, accelerator and challenge runs its own call and its own timeline. Some, like SpIN, accept applications on a rolling basis with a quarterly review; others, like the Techtonic editions and the Atal Incubation Centre's grand challenges, open and close around specific cohorts. Founders typically apply through the individual programme's own page, and NIDHI Seed Support Scheme applicants can reach the team directly for guidance.

Name: Soma
Description: Soma is a deep tech accelerator and SaaS platform based in India, operating under the broader India Accelerator ecosystem. It was designed to address a specific gap in the Indian startup landscape: the lack of structured support for startups rooted in scientific research and engineering innovation. Soma brings together government agencies, industrial partners, academic institutions, and venture capital to create an integrated support system for deep tech founders. Role in the Startup Ecosystem Soma operates as a hybrid model that combines a digital platform with hands-on acceleration. The SaaS component connects deep tech startups to relevant resources, partners, and funding opportunities, while the accelerator component provides structured mentoring and milestone-based support. The platform has partnered with MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), the nodal body under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, to support technology-driven startups in India. Programs Soma Deep Tech Accelerator: A structured program that takes deep tech startups from concept validation through to scaling. Participating startups receive mentorship from domain experts, access to prototyping and testing infrastructure through academic and industrial partners, and introductions to investors focused on science-driven ventures. MeitY Partnership Program: In collaboration with MeitY Startup Hub, Soma supports technology startups with government-backed resources, including grants, mentorship, and market access. Platform Services: The Soma SaaS platform provides tools for startup management, milestone tracking, and ecosystem mapping, enabling startups to navigate the deep tech support landscape more efficiently. Who Benefits Deep tech founders working in scientific research, engineering innovation, hardware, and frontier technologies. The program is designed for startups that require longer development timelines and specialized infrastructure, which are common in deep tech but poorly served by standard accelerators. Strategic Impact Soma addresses one of the biggest structural challenges in Indian deep tech: the fragmentation of support across government, academia, and industry. By building a platform that connects these three pillars, Soma reduces the friction that deep tech founders face when trying to access labs, grants, and domain expertise. Its partnership with MeitY gives it institutional credibility and access to government resources that are otherwise difficult for individual startups to navigate.

Name: Sparknext
Description: Sparknext is a startup accelerator that works alongside founders to help them build and grow their companies. On its own pages it describes itself as a hybrid startup accelerator, though it is worth noting a mixed signal: a founder testimonial on its startups page instead calls it an incubator, so you will see both words used about the same organisation. Alongside the accelerator, Sparknext runs a second, separate line of work: it designs and teaches startup education and works with colleges and institutes in India and abroad. These are two different offerings — one for founders building a company, one for educational institutions — and they are described separately below. What they do for founders Sparknext's pitch to founders is to help them grow faster and limit failures. It says it gives founders a set of practical advantages to survive, disrupt and succeed: experience, resources, access to experts, help reaching product-market fit, the first customers, the first hires, processes, a working network and hard-won wisdom. In other words, the support is hands-on and operational rather than purely advisory — the team works with a founder on the real problems of getting a company off the ground. The accelerator does not publish eligibility rules such as a required stage, sector or location on the pages read, so the specifics of who it takes and when are not stated. What is clear from its own description is the kind of help on offer and the outcome it aims for, rather than a fixed curriculum or timeline. Startup education for colleges Separately, Sparknext designs and teaches startup education, and says it helps some top colleges in India and abroad. This is a business-to-business offering aimed at educational institutions rather than an open application route for individual founders. The pages read do not state a fee, a schedule or a format for this work, so if you are a college or institute the practical next step is to get in touch to discuss what it would involve. Who runs it Sparknext was founded by Ahmed Aftab Naqvi. On its own pages he is also described as the CEO and co-founder of Gozoop, a digital agency whose client list it says includes a range of well-known Indian and international brands. Beyond the founder, the pages read do not name a wider team. Startups Sparknext's startups page features Aceblend, which it describes as a fast-growing nutraceutical startup and a category leader in plant protein. The page refers to other names too, but Aceblend is the one its own copy actually describes, so it is the only one carried here. What is not stated It is worth being precise about what Sparknext's own site does and does not say, because some widely repeated details are not on its pages. The site publishes no postal address, no city and no contact email — all contact runs through web forms. It also states no founding year and no single sector focus. A founding year, a Mumbai base and an ecommerce focus appear on third-party company directories rather than on sparknext.com; treat those as reported elsewhere, not as the organisation's own statements. Whether the accelerator takes equity, charges a fee or is currently running an intake cannot be confirmed from the pages read.

Name: Startup Jharkhand
Description: Startup Jharkhand is a non-government, Section 8 not-for-profit startup accelerator for founders in Ranchi and across Jharkhand, run by I-Hub Startup Jharkhand Foundation. It began as a foundation team in November 2023 and has since run three completed Saksham accelerator cohorts and a growing calendar of founder events. Its work is organised around three things: fundraising readiness, market access and capacity building. Fundraising readiness means equipping founders with the metrics, narrative and connections to raise institutional capital. Market access means opening doors to enterprise clients, government procurement and strategic pilots. Capacity building covers the accelerator, masterclasses and the mentor network. The site lists 15+ mentors, an advisory board that includes former and current startup CEOs, and 25+ portfolio startups across sectors such as AgriTech, FoodTech, DeepTech, SaaS and Health and Wellness. Programmes Saksham is the flagship accelerator. Saksham 1.0 selected a cohort of 5 startups from 100+ applications, Saksham 2.0 onboarded 12 startups from 100+ applications, and Saksham 3.0 selected 14 startups from 200+ applications. Saksham 4.0 is the current round: a 6-8 week mentorship programme for startups that already have an MVP or working product and early customers, users or pilots. It is listed as free to apply and does not promise funding; it prepares startups to be investment-ready and creates introductions. NIRMAN 1.0 is a pre-accelerator for aspiring founders and early builders, from a solid idea to an MVP in progress, open to founders in any sector who are solving a real-world problem. It offers mentorship, workshops and masterclasses, peer community and help building, testing and launching an MVP. Alongside these, Startup Jharkhand runs a monthly Startup Mixer in Ranchi and Jamshedpur, an intimate founder roundtable of 15-20 entrepreneurs, plus the annual Entrepreneurial Connect summit and IGNITE, a campus ecosystem builder programme. Who it is for Saksham is primarily designed for startups in the Startup Jharkhand ecosystem, but startups from other states are also eligible to apply. A founder with only an idea should look at NIRMAN first and Saksham once there is a product and early customers. What it is not Startup Jharkhand is an accelerator and community, not a grant-giver. Its pages describe mentorship, workshops, networking and investor readiness, and state plainly that participation does not guarantee funding.

Name: Startup Reseau
Description: Startup Réseau is a Mumbai-based company that designs and runs accelerator, incubation and market-access programmes. It was established in 2012 by a team from India's startup ecosystem, and it is led by founder and chief executive Ajay Ramasubramaniam. Most of what it runs is built for someone else — a corporate, a state government or a university — alongside a smaller set of its own programmes that founders apply to directly. What it actually is Startup Réseau describes itself as a consulting organisation working across technology, innovation and digital entrepreneurship in emerging markets. It organises its work around four pillars: Enterprise, Capital, Markets and Services. The Enterprise side sets up industry-themed accelerators, corporate venture capital programmes, innovation challenges, demo days and round tables for large companies. The Markets side runs structured market-entry programmes in both directions — helping Indian companies look abroad and helping foreign companies understand India. The Capital pillar has its own page, but at the moment it says only that it is coming soon. That matters for a founder reading this page. Many of the programme names attached to Startup Réseau are engagements it delivered for a client and then finished. Games24x7, Sanofi India, MSD India, Delhivery, Saint-Gobain India, Aditya Birla Capital, DP World, LenDenClub Alpha and RNFI have all had programmes built and run for them. Those are real pieces of work, and the alumni page groups participating startups by which of them they came through, but none of them is an open door today. The programmes listed below are the ones with a route in. Who can apply There is no single application. Each open programme has its own form, and the live ones are advertised as banner slides on the home page. The clearest open intake is the Integrated DeepTech Accelerator Program, run with the investor Unicorn India Ventures. It asks for a working prototype, minimum viable product or validated technology rather than an idea; a founding team with the technical skill to build and scale it; proprietary technology or a defensible technical moat; and a clearly defined customer problem with a credible path to commercialisation. It is also geographically gated: the startup must be registered in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana or Odisha. It charges a participation fee for the bootcamp stage, refunded to the startups selected into the incubator cohort. The own-brand GrowthX programmes are for business software and enterprise tech companies that have been operating for under three years and are still early on revenue. GrowthX WE Sprint is the women-founder version, open to founders across South and South East Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Torque is for business software and enterprise tech startups wanting customer introductions in India. EarthLab is for early-stage climate, sustainability and agriculture startups, and is run without taking equity. Two of the youth programmes are for students rather than companies. The Founder Development Bootcamp is a seven-day programme for aspiring student entrepreneurs aged 18 to 25 and is open to students from all backgrounds. Kettle is a six-month incubation programme taught inside a partner college — currently École Intuit Lab — for final-year undergraduates, and carries academic credit, so it is not an open intake. Some programmes on the site are not for Indian founders at all. The GIA Mumbai Acceleration Programme, run with Enterprise Singapore, is for Singapore-based companies expanding into India. Gateway 91 is an India immersion programme for global founders, investors, corporate executives and government representatives. Startup Bridge Canada runs the other way, for growth-stage Indian business software, enterprise tech and deep tech companies that have raised institutional funding or have steady revenue and want a North American strategy. Facilities Startup Réseau names one space of its own: Startup Réseau Labs in Mumbai, which gives a selected Torque team room for up to three people. It publishes no laboratory, prototyping or open coworking offer, and no postal address. Scale Its home page carries counters claiming more than 600 startups accelerated, more than 45 corporate partnerships, more than 65 programmes run, reach in more than 15 countries and more than 30 sectors. All five are self-reported and undated. Its stated vision of reaching 10,000 startups and 100 enterprises is an ambition, not a result. Who runs it Ajay Ramasubramaniam is founder and chief executive. Jagruti Bista is managing director for programmes, Anshul Ajay manages international programmes and Adithya Binoy leads the youth programmes. The team page also lists a regional lead for Africa, reflecting programmes the company runs outside India. Events Startup Réseau runs NeXTT, a corporate innovation and venturing summit, the Mumbai AI Summit, and a TechTalks series of thematic sector events. It also publishes landscape reports, including one mapping central and state grant schemes in India and a NeXTT report on corporate innovation. There is no careers page on the site.
