Name: Startup Stairs
Description: Startup Stairs (Startup Stairs Private Limited) is an incubator and seed-stage accelerator based in Gurugram, Haryana. It says it is DPIIT-recognised and an NSDC International investee, and that it supports startups from idea to scale. Its homepage names five core sectors: drones, electric vehicles, AI, PCBs and defence. How its programmes work Startup Stairs runs several separate offers, and they ask different things of a founder. The Idea to Funding Accelerator is a 30-day programme for early founders. The Startup Validation Sprint is a 3-day, in-person programme. Both charge a programme fee, and its refund policy says all purchases on the platform are final and non-refundable. The Growth Partner Programme is a partnership in which Startup Stairs takes equity in two of its three tiers and works for a fixed retainer in the third. Startup League is a startup discovery, evaluation and investor-pitch platform that runs in cohorts. The only offer that takes equity is the Growth Partner Programme. The accelerator and the sprint do not mention equity on their pages. Startup League Startup League is its best-known programme. It describes itself as a platform that connects startups with investors, mentors, incubators and corporates. Cohort 1 finalised 30 startups. Cohort 2 is a hybrid event, held in Haryana and online, with a three-stage evaluation by domain experts and investors, a pitch day and a demo day. The page gives the pitch day as 24 September 2026 and the demo day as 1 October 2026, both of which have now passed, yet it still says applications are open. Another page on the same site gives a different start date and submission deadline for Cohort 2. Treat the status of Cohort 2 as unclear and check with Startup Stairs before relying on it. A third cohort is listed as upcoming, with dates to be announced. The page says Startup League is backed by Startup Haryana and DPIIT and advertises a pooled funding opportunity for qualifying startups. It does not say who provides that funding or on what terms. The site also describes the League two ways: one page calls it sector agnostic, covering deep tech and AI, fintech, consumer tech, health, climate, edtech, logistics and agritech, while another calls it a deep tech platform focused on AI, EVs, drones, defence and PCBs. Idea to Funding Accelerator This is a 30-day programme with 10 expert sessions, 4 one-to-one mentor reviews, 2 masterclasses and an investor demo day. It is built around investor-readiness and execution work, and the page says it is not an online course. It is for idea-stage, prototype, first-customer and early-revenue founders, including working professionals building a startup. Applicants are reviewed for stage fit, and shortlisted applicants may be invited to a short programme-fit discussion. The page states that taking part does not guarantee investment or investor meetings, and it lists people who should not apply, such as those who are joining only because they expect guaranteed funding. Startup Validation Sprint The sprint is a 3-day, offline programme that combines mentoring and tasks and ends in a validated roadmap. It is aimed at idea-stage and early-stage founders, including first-time founders, technical and non-technical founders and small co-founder teams. The venue is not stated. Growth Partner Programme The Hybrid Partner tier is for early-stage startups building an MVP and going to market, and it takes 1 to 2 percent equity. The Anchor Partner tier is for scaling startups, takes 5 to 10 percent equity and is limited to 10 startups a year. The Retainership tier is a fixed retainer fee with no equity. The site is inconsistent about whether the Hybrid tier is open: one page marks it as coming soon, and another describes it as an active model. Partners and support The homepage lists AVPL International, Drone Tech Multi-State Co-operative Society Ltd., Drone City Haryana, Drone Planet and NSDC among its partners. It says these partnerships give selected startups access to technology expertise, AI support, prototyping, testing, manufacturing guidance, industry networks, field deployment and market access. It does not say which partner provides which support. Startup Stairs also supports selected startups that come through DroneThon 2026, a national drone product competition. DroneThon is run by Drone Tech Multi-State Cooperative Society, not by Startup Stairs. Rural entrepreneurship work Startup Stairs acted as the execution and activation partner for Yuva Udyami Yatra, a rural entrepreneurship mobilisation drive aimed at bank-linked micro-enterprises at panchayat level. Its Uttar Pradesh cycle ran from 20 March to 30 June 2026. This is work with rural micro-entrepreneurs rather than a startup programme, so it is not a route for most founders reading this page. Who runs it The homepage names Deep Sihag Sisai and Dr. Preet Sandhu as co-founders and promoters. Location The site footer gives the address as Plot no. 251, Ground Floor, Phase 4, Udyog Vihar, Sector 18, Gurugram, Haryana 122015. Its terms of use give a different registered office at Unit No. 840-42, Tower B3, Spaze IT Park, Sector 49, Sohna Road, Gurugram, Haryana 122018. We have not found any statement of when the company was founded on its own pages.

Name: StartupBay
Description: StartupBay is an online accelerator and venture studio for technology founders, run by StartupBay Pte. Ltd. It has an India office in Pune and group entities registered in Singapore and in Prague, Czech Republic. It describes itself as a startup accelerator, venture studio and global market entry platform, and works with founders across Asia, South Asia and the Middle East rather than from a physical incubation space. What they support StartupBay is built for technology-first founders, from idea-stage teams through to companies ready to scale into new markets. Its programmes are delivered online. It works with first-time and early-stage founders through its accelerator, with deep-tech and AI builders through its venture studio, and with growth-stage companies through its market-entry work. It does not present itself as a campus incubator and does not offer desks or lab space to outside startups. Programmes The JumpStart Program is StartupBay's execution-focused accelerator. It is delivered fully online and moves founders from an early idea toward an investor-ready startup through structured learning modules, weekly execution sprints, founder reviews and mentor checkpoints, with an emphasis on market and investor readiness. StartupBay runs an India-facing enrolment of JumpStart, JUMPSTART INDIA, described as a twelve-week, 83-step programme built around nine core modules, available online and through a mobile app. StartupBay's pages describe the programme's length in different ways in different places, so a founder should check the current programme page for the intake they are joining. StartupBay Studio is a venture studio that co-builds companies with founders rather than only advising them. It is organised in three stages: an Idea Lab for opportunity validation and early prototyping in deep tech, a Build Pod for co-developing an MVP with a shared team, and a Spin-Out Engine for legal formation, early funding rounds and team scaling. It is a selective, partnership-based engagement aimed at deep-tech and AI founders, domain experts and operators ready to lead a venture, not an open public intake. The Global Market Entry Program helps scale-ready companies expand internationally. It runs in five steps: market orientation, market entry strategy, business-plan localisation, customer pilots and business expansion. It offers local partners and operators, market-entry playbooks, and introductions to investors and enterprises across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and the United States. Track record StartupBay's own pages give different counts of the startups it has worked with: parts of its site refer to hundreds of startups built, scaled or accelerated and founders mentored across more than fifteen countries, while another part of the homepage invites founders to join a much smaller group, and the only live counter on its JUMPSTART INDIA programme page shows a small number of participants. Because these figures do not agree with one another, they are best read as the company's own claims rather than settled totals. How to apply Applications are made programme by programme on StartupBay's website. Founders enrol in the JumpStart accelerator, including the JUMPSTART INDIA instance, directly online, with the India instance also available through a mobile app. The venture studio is entered by applying to be co-built with, and the Global Market Entry Program by requesting access to its markets. For general queries, StartupBay lists a contact address on its site. StartupBay is a registered trademark of StartupBay Pte. Ltd.

Name: Startupbootcamp India
Description: Startupbootcamp India is the India arm of the Startupbootcamp accelerator network, and its about page names Kamal Bansal as its co-founder. It runs industry-specific accelerator cohorts that connect early-stage founders with corporate partners, mentors and investors, with its cohort pages placing the programmes in Ahmedabad. Its pages date the network to 2010. How programmes work Programmes run as fixed-length cohorts rather than open-ended residencies. Both cohorts described on its site are 12-week accelerators, and both have finished: the site says no cohorts are active right now and that the next application window is being prepared. The 2026 cohort, the SBC Sprint2Frontier Acceleration Program, is an investment-focused accelerator for pre–Series A startups taking proven technologies from validation to scale. It covers deep tech, defence and aerospace, climate and sustainability, and AI for enterprise. Selected startups take part in mentorship, investor-readiness sessions, tailored matchmaking with investors and clients, repeated pitch opportunities and facilitated meetings with stakeholders, and some of them receive strategic funding. Its pages give different accounts of the programme itself: the length is 12 weeks on the programme page and 13 weeks in its downloadable brochure, with the published cohort dates running from June to August 2026. Terms are described in two ways as well, with one page speaking of founder-friendly, SAFE-style terms and the programme details saying that terms vary by cohort and are shared during the application process. No equity share is published anywhere. The 2025 cohort, the SBC Idea to Launch Energy Transition Acceleration Program, worked with a cohort of 10 early-stage energy transition startups in climate tech, energy transition and renewable energy. It took them from idea and early validation to investor readiness, working on core business fundamentals, and it ran from September to December 2025. Applying to either programme costs nothing. Nothing on the site states a fee for the startups that are selected. Its named ecosystem partners include Microsoft, AWS, IBM and Mercedes, and it describes a wider corporate and ecosystem partner set across finance, mobility, consumer goods and technology. Each process ends with a selection day, where startups pitch in front of ecosystem partners. Who can apply For the 2026 cohort the programme asks for pre–Series A startups with a tested or proven technology, ideally above TRL 6. Pilots, proofs of concept, market trials or early paying customers are desirable. Prior external funding is not mandatory: bootstrapped, angel-funded and institutionally funded startups are eligible. At least two committed team members must actively take part, and founders are expected to be open to mentoring, coaching and structured feedback, and comfortable with investor-facing discussions and strategic reviews. Its general pages describe a wider fit than any single cohort does. One speaks of early-stage startups with a working product or strong prototype, and another of pre-revenue startups with clear market validation. No page says the programmes are closed to founders based outside India, and the portfolio companies it lists are from Indian cities. Scale Its pages print several different sets of counts. The portfolio page counts 200+ companies and says 76% of them go on to raise after the programme. The homepage counts 1600+ global alumni, 150 cohorts, 10+ companies and 39+ corporate and ecosystem partners. The about page counts 150+ mentors, 200+ portfolio companies and 20+ countries. The contact page counts 150+ programmes run, 300+ active mentors and 50+ partners. The India portfolio listed on the site is 10 companies, all from the 2025 energy transition cohort. These are the network's own published figures, and most of them are printed for the global network rather than for India alone. Who runs it Its about page names Kamal Bansal as co-founder of SBC India and Pratham Bansal as programme manager of SBC India, and its programme materials give Kamal Bansal the title co-founder and CEO. The same pages name Trevor Townsend as co-founder and chair of SBC APAC and Richard Celm as managing director of SBC APAC, while the programme materials give Richard Celm the title executive program director. The site refers to the wider Startupbootcamp ecosystem and to SBC APAC leadership, and names no separate legal parent. Its careers page lists no open roles. Locations Both cohort pages give Ahmedabad, India as the programme location. The contact page invites visits by appointment and gives a general contact email and phone number, but no street address or pincode.

Name: The Asia Pacific Low Carbon Lifestyle Accelerator
Description: LowCarbon.Earth is a climate-tech accelerator run by the Massive Earth Foundation, a Section 8 non-profit based in Gurugram, Haryana. It was launched in 2021 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and it works with early-stage founders across India and the Asia-Pacific region who are building sustainable goods and services. How the accelerator works The programme runs as a virtual, equity-free accelerator over twelve weeks. It is built to help early-stage climate-tech startups strengthen their investment readiness and scale their impact through expert-led mentorship, exposure, and access to investors and corporates. It also returns as a recurring annual cohort, so founders who miss one intake can look out for the next. Past editions have run bootcamps, workshops, mentorship, networking sessions and investor pitch opportunities, and have closed with a demo day where shortlisted startups pitch to investors. Who can apply The accelerator is open to early-stage, revenue-positive startups based in India and the wider Asia-Pacific region that are solving for climate. It covers sectors such as renewable energy, mobility, air quality, sustainable agriculture, the circular economy, water security and plastic recycling. The stated entry criterion is being a revenue-positive startup based out of Asia-Pacific working on climate. Scale Since it began, the accelerator reports that it has evaluated over 3,000 startups and supported more than 180 through its bootcamps, workshops, mentorship and investor sessions, and it says it evaluates over 500 startups a year from the Asia-Pacific region. These are the organisation's own published figures, and its pages do not always agree with one another: a separate page describes a cohort of more than 1,000 startups, so the supported count is best read as an order of magnitude rather than a settled number. Who runs it The accelerator is an initiative of the Massive Earth Foundation, a Section 8 non-profit organisation, which it runs in collaboration with UNEP. The Foundation operates from an office on Golf Course Road in Sector 43, Gurugram, Haryana, while the accelerator itself runs as a virtual programme and has held demo days in the region, including in Bangkok. How to apply Applications are made online through the programme's own application form, which asks for founder and startup details, sector, location, stage, a pitch deck and a product video. When a cohort is open it accepts submissions on a rolling basis; between intakes, founders can watch the official site for the next annual call. To follow the programme, look up LowCarbon.Earth and the Massive Earth Foundation, and watch for its events and demo days.

Name: The Gain
Description: The GAIN is a Section 8, not-for-profit accelerator based in J. P. Nagar, Bengaluru. It describes itself as a global accelerator for innovative technology startups, and it works with founders who already have early revenue or traction and are aiming at the growth stage. How programmes work The GAIN runs a small set of acceleration programmes rather than one open intake. Its pages describe support in three areas: go-to-market strategy, customer connects and access to funding. Mentoring, investor connects and introductions to partners are part of the offer across programmes. The programmes on the site are StartupToScaleup, Access To India, Global Immersion Program and the Elevate WomEN Acceleration Program. Each has a different audience, so check the programme page before applying. Who can apply StartupToScaleup is aimed at technology-based startups that graduated from the TIDE and CoE schemes of the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY). Access To India is aimed at startups from across the world that want mentors, partners and customers in India, so it is not a programme for Indian founders. The Elevate WomEN Acceleration Program is for women entrepreneurs in Karnataka, and its acceleration track takes existing startups at the growth and scale-up stage. What the programmes give StartupToScaleup gives acceleration support through workshops and one-on-one sessions with experts and mentors. Startups are also helped to reach relevant global markets, which are chosen by sector, and the programme says it charges no fee and takes no equity. Access To India combines mentor sessions, workshops, corporate visits and clinical validations, and helps startups test their technology and build local partnerships. The Elevate WomEN track runs for six months with a small group of selected startups and covers MVP development, fundraising, global connections, branding, pitching and investment readiness. Track record By its own account, The GAIN has supported over 50 startups since 2018. It says it has run two cohorts of StartupToScaleup, in association with MeitY and MeitY Startup Hub, across EdTech, healthcare, FinTech, AgriTech and Industry 4.0. It also says it supported 11 South Korean startups through its Access2India programme, and that six of them later raised follow-on funding. The site says its partner network covers 13 or more countries. These are the organisation's own figures, and the pages do not date them. Its portfolio page lists startups in areas including healthcare, medical technology, energy, EdTech, FinTech and industrial technology. Who runs it The GAIN describes itself as a Section 8 company. Its team page lists an evaluation and investment team, and it says its accelerator is supported by the StartupXseed venture platform. Its listed events and blog posts date mostly from 2021 and 2022, so check the site for the current status of any programme before applying. Name: Together Fund
Description: Together Fund is a venture capital fund based in Bengaluru that backs AI-native startups in the US-India corridor. It describes itself as an operator-led, AI-first fund, started in 2021 by founders who wanted to be the kind of investors they wished they had. It has offices in Bengaluru, Chennai and Palo Alto. Who it backs Together Fund invests only in AI-native companies. Its site names horizontal applications, vertical solutions, healthcare, infrastructure and consumer products. It also backs deep tech at the edge of AI and hard science, including robotics, autonomous systems, semiconductors and quantum technologies, and says it welcomes defence and aerospace founders. It looks for early-stage companies, typically at seed and Series A, and says it makes 8-10 investments a year. It builds for global markets or uses Indian talent to scale abroad. SwarmSpace: the programme side SwarmSpace is Together Fund's community, AI studio and research lab for builders in India. It has three parts. The Community runs AI talks, roundtables and founder salons, and is open to founders, researchers, operators, open-source contributors, indie hackers and students. The AI Studio is a 12 weeks programme for selected startups, covering the path from idea to product-market fit and scale, with a US immersion included. The Research Lab does frontier AI research through hands-on programs and industry initiatives, but its page gives no programme detail yet. How the AI Studio works Selected startups receive flexible equity funding from Together Fund, so this is an investment and not a grant. They also get founder mentorship, credits from partner AI providers, research support, cloud and compute credits, and office hours. Dedicated office space is available in Bangalore and Palo Alto. Together Fund strongly encourages AI Studio startups to build from the Bangalore office, because that is where the community, events and founder salons happen. The Bangalore space is 5,000 sq ft in Indiranagar. The Chennai site is described as a deeptech garage for frugal innovation and full-stack experimentation. Who can apply The fund's gate is the product, not the founder's background: you should be an AI-first startup. The AI Studio is for exceptional AI founders. There is no stated requirement for incorporation, city or institution, but the fund focuses on the US-India corridor. The site publishes no application dates and no selection criteria; check the apply form for current intake. Scale On its own pages Together Fund reports 35+ portfolio companies and says more than 40% of them have had follow-on funding. These are self-reported and undated. Its listed portfolio includes Composio, Emergent, Hunar, Metaforms, Presentations AI, Runable and Wispr Flow, among others across applied AI, AI infrastructure and healthcare. Who runs it The fund describes itself as operator-led: every partner has built and scaled companies before becoming an investor. Manav Garg and Girish Mathrubootham are its co-founders and managing partners. Its team page also lists Lakshmi Shankar and Shubham Gupta as general partners. Contact Together Fund is at 299, 6th Main Road, HAL 2nd Stage, Indiranagar, Bengaluru 560038. Questions about investments and SwarmSpace go to the deals inbox on its site, and general enquiries to the hello inbox.

Name: Udhmodya Foundation
Description: Udhmodya Foundation is the business incubator of the University of Delhi. The University set it up in 2022 as a Section 8 not-for-profit company, and it works out of the 5th floor of Maharishi Kanad Bhawan on the University's North Campus in Delhi. Its own pages explain the name: the word Udhmodya stands for the rising Sun setting out on a journey to success through innovation. The Foundation runs incubation, pre-incubation and virtual incubation, and it is open to people from outside the University as well as to its own students, faculty and staff. Its stated mission is to support and nurture innovators and new and early-stage enterprises so they become successful and sustainable. How incubation works The incubation programme is called UDIT, short for Udhmodya Incubation and Training. It is described as a hub for people who want to ideate, collaborate and turn an idea into a sustainable venture, with mentorship, networking events and access to capital behind it. You apply through an online application form linked from the UDIT page on the Foundation's site. The University's Innovation and Startup Policy 2023, published in full on the site, sets out how the rest works. There are three routes. Pre-incubation runs from six months to one year and is meant for founders who arrive with an idea or an early prototype. Incubation runs for 24 months and can be extended to 36 months on the Foundation's recommendation. Virtual incubation follows the same steps remotely, with an online interview or pitch session and an onboarding and orientation stage, for founders who cannot be on campus. The Foundation takes a minority equity stake in companies it incubates. The size of the stake is decided by its Finance Review Committee and depends on what the startup actually uses — brand, faculty time, space, infrastructure, mentorship, seed support, accounting, legal and patent help, and any University intellectual property. Where the equity model applies, startups get a three-month cooling period during which they can use incubation services on a rental basis and decide whether to continue, so equity is not issued on the first day of support. Intellectual property developed using the Foundation's facilities, funds or support is jointly owned by the inventors and the Foundation, and is licensed jointly, with the inventors having the primary say. Who can apply The policy defines four categories of incubatee. Category I is students enrolled in any University of Delhi programme. Category II is faculty, including former, emeritus and visiting professors. Category III is non-teaching staff, current and former. Category IV is "others" — any individual or group of prospective entrepreneurs who do not fall into the first three, and all University of Delhi alumni. So this is not a students-only incubator: an outside founder with no connection to the University applies under Category IV. There is an incorporation requirement. Registration requests are accepted only on behalf of registered unlisted businesses as defined by the Companies Act 2013. If the company is not yet incorporated, the promoters or founders can still apply, but they must register the firm within three months of the application being approved. The majority of the founders, shareholders or core team must hold Indian citizenship. At the point of seed support, the venture must be registered as a partnership firm, LLP, private limited company or one person company. Students get specific concessions. A student can work on a startup instead of a minor or major project, seminar or summer training, can earn academic credit for building a venture, may be allowed to sit examinations with lower than the minimum attendance on the Foundation's recommendation, and may take a break of a year or more to work on the startup and return to their course afterwards. Facilities Incubation is offered in hybrid mode. The Foundation provides shared office space and labs in physical mode, and the same support virtually. Startups get dedicated desks and office equipment, private meeting rooms for investor, partner and client meetings, and high-speed internet. Pre-incubation facilities are described as tailored with expert input for the earliest stage of a venture. The policy adds that startups may get access to prototyping labs and testing facilities, depending on the nature of the business and on what the Foundation and the University have free. Incubatees may also use the Foundation's address for their company with prior permission, and on-campus accommodation may be considered for a limited period subject to availability. Beyond space, the Foundation offers mentorship and coaching, legal and financial services such as accounting, legal advice and tax consultation, and shared services covering IT support, administration and marketing. It says it has partnerships with venture capitalists and angel investors, and that it runs networking events, workshops and ideathons through the year. Scale and track record The Foundation's startups page lists 23 ventures: 7 at incubation stage and 16 at pre-incubation stage. They include Riding Rangers in hyperlocal delivery, Bio-Mandii in climate tech, Kabad Hatao in e-waste and waste management, Nirikshakk in IT and health tech, and DU Buddy, an app for college students. The page gives no total and no date, so treat it as the current list rather than a cumulative count. Wadhwani Foundation is the Foundation's startup training partner and runs a 14-week acceleration programme that Udhmodya startups can apply into to get pitch-ready. ICICI Bank is listed as a startup support partner for banking. The Foundation has also worked with the Delhi Development Authority on a national hackathon, with the Indian Council of Social Science Research on a seminar for startups and faculty, and with the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell and AICTE on a faculty development programme. Who runs it Prof. Yogesh Singh, the Vice Chancellor of the University of Delhi, is the Chairman. Dr. Abhishek Tandon, an Associate Professor in the Department of Operational Research at the University, is the Joint CEO. The board has eleven directors, all drawn from the University's senior faculty and administration. Day-to-day incubation is handled by a small operations team. The Foundation advertises its own staff vacancies as notices on its home page rather than on a careers page. Events The events page carries both upcoming and past events, and is the best place to see what the Foundation is running now. Past items include faculty development programmes on innovation, entrepreneurship and design thinking, Startup Accelerator Program awareness sessions run with Samarth Bharat at several Delhi University colleges, a cyber security workshop, an entrepreneurs' summit and a paid internship scheme for University of Delhi students. The internship scheme has run in several rounds, is part-time at 10 to 12 hours a week for up to six months, carries a monthly stipend, and can be taken only once in a student's entire course.

Name: Upaya Social Ventures
Description: Upaya Social Ventures is a nonprofit that invests in early-stage, for-profit companies that create jobs for people living in extreme poverty, in India. It was founded in 2011, and its India office is in Bangalore, Karnataka. Alongside its investments, it runs an accelerator, a facility for textile waste enterprises, a cohort in the ClimaFii Alliance and a community of practice on job quality. Who it invests in Upaya focuses on what it calls the missing middle: businesses too large for microfinance and too small for traditional bank financing. Its investments page describes them as mission-aligned, early-stage, for-profit companies that create jobs for people living in extreme poverty. Upaya says it is often the first institutional investor in these businesses, and that it gives hands-on advisory support alongside its funding. Its pages describe its money in two ways. The investments page says seed funding, and the approach page says loans made from a pool of recoverable grants. The site does not say which applies to a given business, or whether equity is taken. Programmes Catalytic Investments is Upaya's direct investment work. The Dignified Jobs Accelerator runs in cohorts for early-stage social businesses. The Textile Waste Management Technical Assistance Facility supports sanitation worker-first enterprises. The ClimaFii Alliance is a five-year initiative anchored by Shell Foundation with Accion, in which Upaya is the India partner. The Dignified Jobs Collaborative is a community of practice, and it is not a funding programme. Accelerator cohorts The accelerator's two listed cohorts each focused on one sector and each had partners. The 2024 cohort covered the allied sectors of agriculture, ran for six months, and worked with Yunus Social Business Fund Bengaluru. Upaya may select up to three businesses from it for investment. The 2025 Circular Innovation cohort covered plastics and textile and fashion waste management, ran for nine months, and worked with Global Business Inroads and rePurpose Global. The 2025 cohort ran in two levels. Level 1 is a three-month virtual programme for 60 businesses. Level 2 is a six-month, hands-on programme for 10 businesses. Funding is not part of the accelerator. ClimaFii Alliance ClimaFii is a five-year initiative anchored by Shell Foundation in partnership with Accion, with co-funding from UK aid. Upaya joins as the India partner, and BFA Global joins as the Sub-Saharan Africa partner. Its India cohorts include a no-interest loan, and every selected business receives its funding through that loan. The alliance is for mid-growth stage businesses registered and operating in India, with a potential to reach 3,000 to 5,000 micro-entrepreneurs. Its pages list companies in the 2025 and 2026 India cohorts. Scale Upaya's homepage gives 153 businesses accelerated and 64 investments made. Both are its own counts, and the site does not define them. Its homepage and careers page give 126,308 dignified jobs created by portfolio companies since 2011. Other pages on the site give different totals for the same measure, and the site does not say which is current. On gender, its impact page says 41% of jobholders are women. Its gender page says nearly half of the jobholders at its portfolio partners are women. The two figures do not match. Who can apply Each programme sets its own eligibility. The Dignified Jobs Accelerator takes early-stage businesses in India that create dignified jobs for people in extreme poverty, and it strongly encourages women-led businesses to apply. Catalytic Investments backs mission-aligned, early-stage, for-profit companies that create jobs for people living in extreme poverty. The ClimaFii Alliance takes mid-growth stage businesses registered and operating in India. The Dignified Jobs Collaborative has no eligibility test. It is a community that invites thought partners, funders, data contributors and amplifiers. Locations The site lists an India office on Sri Krishna Temple Road in Indiranagar, Bangalore, and a second office in the United States. It describes itself as a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, which is a United States designation.

Name: Upekkha Accelerator
Description: Upekkha is an AI-focused startup accelerator based in Bengaluru. Its main programme, the Upekkha AI Accelerator, is for founders building AI-first B2B software companies, and it describes itself as 'for Global Indian Founders'. Upekkha also runs Up Advisory, a programme for B2B software companies that are scaling. How programmes work The Upekkha AI Accelerator offers one-to-one mentorship, cohort sessions, a founder community and cloud and AI credits from AWS, GCP and Anthropic. Upekkha takes equity in the startups it accepts. Its terms are a baseline equity stake plus a success fee on milestones, which can be paid in equity or in cash. Applications for the current round closed on 6 September 2026, and the site does not say when the next round opens. Up Advisory is separate. It offers personalised advisory to B2B software companies focused on scaling. The page organises its offer around six pillars of growth acceleration, and it sets no deadline or intake date. Upekkha's press page describes a pre-seed fund, and an older homepage listed a SAFE note as funding. Its current application page says the company does not invest and takes equity instead. The site does not explain how a founder would apply to any fund, so this page does not list one as a programme. Who can apply The accelerator is for founders building or moving toward an AI-first B2B business. The application page asks for early revenue, bootstrapped or angel-funded teams, deep technical or domain expertise, and a wish to stay in control of the company. It describes early revenue as signals of product-market fit that are not yet repeatable. The site does not say whether a founder must be based in India. Up Advisory is for B2B software founders who are focused on scaling. It asks founders to check whether the programme is right for them, and it sets revenue-stage thresholds that this page does not repeat. Scale The company's own figures do not agree with each other. Its application page gives 170-plus startups across the community, while its press page gives a portfolio of 200-plus startups. Its homepage and press page give 300-plus founders in the community, and its application page gives 350-plus. The homepage also says more than 100 AI mentors are part of the network. The application page says ten of its startups have exited, and names SocialPilot among them. These are the company's own claims, not audited totals, and the site does not reconcile them. Community and events Upekkha holds an annual gathering for its founder community, where founders share experiences and grow their businesses together. The 2026 edition took place on 16 January 2026 at The Paul in Domlur, Bengaluru. The 2025 edition was held on 6 March 2025 at the Grand Mercure Hotel in Bengaluru. Both events have passed. Who runs it Upekkha's advisory page introduces its team with short bios. Prasanna Krishnamoorthy is described as ex-CTO-in-Residence at Microsoft Accelerator India, who has worked hands-on with more than 120 startups and is a two-time startup founder. Shekar Nair's bio lists one IPO (Xylan, USA) and three exits (Xylan, Allegro and Elina), and a former role as India Head and APAC OEM at NetApp. Gokul KS drives the accelerator programmes and founder community engagement across 300-plus founders, according to his bio. Locations Upekkha's legal pages give an address in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. The site does not describe an office where founders work, and it does not say where accelerator sessions are held. The fallback email address uses the domain upekkha.in, while the website is at upekkha.io.

Name: We Founder Circle
Description: We Founder Circle, usually written WFC, is an angel investor network based in Surat, Gujarat. It pools money from member investors into seed rounds for early-stage Indian startups, and it runs a cohort accelerator, EvolveX, branded EvolveX by WFC. We Founder Circle Private Limited was incorporated on 22 September 2020 and publishes its annual returns on its own corporate governance page. Two different doors lead in, and they work very differently. EvolveX is a three-month accelerator with numbered cohorts, published eligibility and an application form, and it is the route most founders will want. The angel network itself is a rolling deal pipeline: startups that sign a term sheet with WFC are presented at online pitch sessions to member investors, and the round closes only if enough of those investors commit. How the accelerator works EvolveX is a cohort-based accelerator that invests in startups in exchange for equity and puts them through a three-month programme. Its own pages describe the programme slightly differently in two places, one calling it hybrid with online and in-person sessions and the other calling it virtual, so expect mostly online sessions with some travel possible. Sessions are led by industry experts and CXOs and are chosen around what the startups in that cohort need, and every startup also gets one-to-one mentoring from the EvolveX team and its mentor bench. EvolveX says it typically selects five to seven startups per cohort. The published cohort start dates run from January 2022 through January 2025, and applications were open for its eighth cohort when we last checked. It takes equity, and it also charges a programme fee, which it says covers the legal work and due diligence, the expert-led sessions, the one-to-one mentoring and the demo day. Both of those are worth weighing before you apply: this is a paid, equity-taking accelerator, not a grant. Beyond the three months, EvolveX says it helps its stronger startups raise a follow-on round: pitching to outside investors at a demo day, a profile on Invstt, the group's own investment platform, and introductions to VC funds and angel networks. It also offers corporate introductions through WFC's corporate innovation partnerships. Who can apply EvolveX is sector agnostic. The sectors it names are AI, clean tech and sustainability, deep tech, consumer brands, SaaS, agri tech, health tech, sports and gaming, and its own answer on sectors adds fintech and ed tech. It asks applicants to be DPIIT-recognised and to be raising a first cheque or a pre-seed or seed round. On stage, it says it suits pre-revenue startups that have a proof of concept or a working MVP, and that startups already making revenue can apply too. One of its pages also admits startups at the idea stage, which the other does not, so if you are pre-prototype it is worth asking before you spend time on the form. Nothing on its pages restricts applicants by city, state, age or category, and there is no host-institute or student gate. Because the investment is made for equity and closed with share subscription paperwork, you will in practice need an incorporated company. How selection works Applications are screened first, then EvolveX holds three to four rounds of discussion with the founders before putting the startup in front of its investment committee. It puts the whole evaluation at four to six weeks on one page and seven to eight weeks on another, so plan for the longer end. It says the decision rests mainly on the founding team, the product or idea and the size of the opportunity. Founders who are turned down may apply again to a later cohort, and EvolveX asks that you only do so once you have made real progress since the last attempt. The angel network route The network side of WFC is built mostly for investors, and its founder-facing pages explain the process rather than offering a form. Once a deal arrives, an in-house team screens it, shares an information checklist, and holds calls with the founders. The deal is then circulated to the community members with relevant expertise for their view. Once roughly half the round is committed, third-party agencies run legal and financial due diligence and the report goes to the investors. A shareholders' agreement is signed, committed investors are given fifteen days to transfer, and share certificates follow. Startups that cannot gather commitments close to their full raise are dropped rather than part-funded. WFC also states plainly that it does not sign NDAs with founders, because it shares the plans it receives with its members. Be aware that the buttons for this route do not currently work. Join The Community, Join Our Portfolio and the Founders link in the footer all lead to a missing page, and two of the three items in the site's own Programs menu, InvestorX and Startupx, have no page behind them either. The accelerator is the only intake we could verify. Scale and track record The numbers WFC publishes are self-reported and undated, and they do not agree with each other. Its portfolio page headline says it has funded more than 120 startups while the same page's browser title says more than 150, and the home page carries both figures. It also reports a community of more than 25,000 angel investors across more than 80 countries, more than 6,000 startups evaluated, and that a third of its portfolio founders come from tier 2 and tier 3 cities and just over a quarter are women. EvolveX reports seven cohorts and 38 startups, while its written answers say 30 or more from five cohorts in one place and 28 or more from four in another; its portfolio page itemises six. Name: YES BANK
Description: YES BANK is a private sector bank founded in 2004 and headquartered in Mumbai. It operates 1,255 branches. YES BANK operates 1,255 branches. Founded in 2004, it was built from the outset around corporate and business banking rather than retail branch expansion, and its network remains concentrated in metros and larger cities. Its role in the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups. YES BANK is one of 40 institutions registered with the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company as a CGSS Member Institution (NCGTC MLI ID 46, classified as a private sector bank). Member Institutions are the lenders that actually extend credit under the scheme: you borrow from YES BANK, and NCGTC guarantees YES BANK against your default. That guarantee is what allows the facility to be extended to a DPIIT-recognised startup without collateral, with cover of 85 percent of the amount in default on smaller loans and 75 percent above a set threshold. What this means in practice. Its recent history is a matter of public record and founders should factor a conservative credit posture into their expectations, particularly for larger or unsecured facilities. Where it remains useful is in its corporate banking orientation: the desks are set up for business lending rather than retail cross-sell. Confirm current appetite for your facility size before investing heavily in documentation. The terms are the bank's, not the scheme's. This is the point founders most often miss. CGSS fixes the guarantee, not the loan. The interest rate, tenure, moratorium, repayment schedule and how the Annual Guarantee Fee is passed through to you are all set by YES BANK under its own credit policy, and they differ materially between Member Institutions for an identical borrower. Nor does registration oblige YES BANK to lend: it appraises you on its normal credit standards first and applies the guarantee second. Approaching more than one Member Institution is almost always worth the effort.

Description: build3 is a startup studio and venture builder for impact-driven founders, operated by BIRUDO3 FOUNDATION. It backs startups that push progress on the UN Sustainable Development Goals or benefit people and the planet, and it works across sectors rather than being limited to technology. Its pages list addresses in Candolim, Goa and in Pune, along with a startup ecoāshrām at Ekundrawadi in the Sindhudurg district of Maharashtra. build3 describes itself as a startup studio rather than a campus incubator, and most of what it offers runs online. Its main programme is the build3 Impact Accelerator; alongside it, build3 runs a Fundraising Bootcamp for founders preparing to raise, and an online Impact Startup Academy course. The reach it reports spans more than one programme, with a wider community it puts at well over a thousand people building startups for both profit and purpose. What they support build3's focus is impact-driven startups, meaning ventures that push progress on the UN Sustainable Development Goals or benefit people and the planet. Its accelerator is pitched at founders at the earliest stages, from an idea through to a functional early-stage business. The programmes are open across sectors, and non-tech startups are welcome. The accelerator is primarily India-focused, though international startups aligned with the mission may apply. Programmes The build3 Impact Accelerator is a 10-week virtual programme that aims to take impact-driven startups from the earliest stage toward product-market fit, built around coaching and workshops, a cohort and mentor community, and investment for selected startups, with a venture-builder phase following for some. In exchange for its support, build3 takes a small equity stake in participating startups. The build3 Fundraising Bootcamp is a 30-day sprint that helps early-stage founders prepare to raise. It is structured in three steps: a two-day in-person networking bootcamp in Goa, four weeks of live online sessions on weekday evenings, and an offline pitch event where selected startups pitch to investors, venture capital firms and family offices in Delhi, Bangalore or Mumbai. It is a paid programme, and founders are supported by an investment banker, a deal team and a dedicated relationship manager who match investors and set up meetings. The Impact Startup Academy is described as a five-week, online-only, step-by-step course on building startups that tackle an important societal problem and are self-sustainable, led by instructors. Track record build3 reports that its Impact Accelerator has completed eight cohorts, accelerated more than four hundred startups, built a founder community of over a thousand, and funded dozens of startups. Its Fundraising Bootcamp pages report founders supported across several cohorts. These are build3's own figures. Who runs it build3 is operated by BIRUDO3 FOUNDATION, a non-profit entity registered in Pune. build3 also states that it is a B Corp-certified business. How to apply Applications are made per programme through forms on the build3 website. For the Impact Accelerator, the process is a three-stage evaluation: an application form, then an interview, followed by a reference check, assessing a startup on compatibility, capability and commitment, alongside factors such as the founder's fit with the problem. The Fundraising Bootcamp is applied to through a short form on its page. The Impact Startup Academy is joined online from the build3 homepage.

Name: herSTART
Description: herSTART is an incubation and accelerator programme for women-led startups in India. It is run by the Gujarat University Startup and Entrepreneurship Council (GUSEC) from Ahmedabad. It is aimed at women who have an innovative idea, a prototype or an existing business and want to take it to the next stage. How programmes work herSTART runs in editions. Each edition picks a cohort through an application and shortlisting process. Shortlisted startups then take part in a bootcamp, expert-led sessions, one-on-one mentoring and industry connects. The fifth edition, herSTART 5.0, describes a virtual accelerator programme, a residential programme with a demo day, and an offline programme for the cohort. Its cohort members pitch to a panel of investors for feedback and funding. The herSTART site publishes the shortlisted startups for each edition. The fourth edition was launched in October 2024 with UNICEF and SBI Mutual Funds. It focused on founders from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. In July 2025 it held a three-day offline accelerator at Gujarat University. herSTART also runs an Angel Investment Certificate Program for women who want to become angel investors. It is jointly issued by herSTART and GUSEC and run with India Accelerator. Who can apply For the fifth edition, the business must be 50% women-owned, the idea must be innovative and original, and the applicant must be an Indian citizen. A female applicant may apply with more than one idea, but only one idea per applicant is selected. Earlier editions used different rules. The 2021 edition asked for at least one woman as a promoter, with the primary applicant female and an Indian citizen. Check the terms of the edition you are looking at before you apply. The Angel Investment Certificate Program is for women HNIs and ultra-HNIs, business leaders, CXOs, senior professionals and aspiring women angel investors. No prior angel investment experience is needed. Facilities and support The fourth edition lists mentorship, guidance and networking, up to two years of incubation support at GUSEC, access to government and private funds, a dedicated co-working space for women, cloud credits and single-window startup support. The fifth edition lists a technology resources and prototyping facility, a community of founders, and industry connects for business expansion. The site describes access to government grants and funds. It does not say every startup receives a grant. Scale The fourth edition page shows the following counters: 530 women-led startups supported, 2000 jobs created by startups, 15000 women sensitised, and 85 IPR filed. These are the organisation's own figures, and the page does not date them. Past editions The second edition held a herSTART Summit on 8 March 2021 and closed its application window on 4 April 2021. Name: iStart Rajasthan
Description: iStart Rajasthan is the Government of Rajasthan's startup platform, run by the Department of Information Technology & Communication (DoIT&C) from the IT Building at Yojana Bhawan, C-Scheme, Jaipur. It is the single door to the state's startup support: recognition as a Rajasthan startup, incubation at Techno Hub in Jaipur and at the district iStart Nest centres, the QRate assessment, and the funding incentives written into the Rajasthan Startup Policy. Its own words for what it is: an integrated startup platform conceptualised by the Department of IT&C. How it works Everything starts with registration. A founder creates the firm's SSO ID on the Rajasthan Single Sign On portal, logs in, searches for iStart and completes the registration, uploading the documents that match the entity type — a self-declaration for a sole proprietorship, the partnership deed for a registered partnership, the LLP agreement for an LLP, or the eMoA for a private limited company. Once the startup is recognised, the other schemes open up from its dashboard. The assessment that sits under most of the money is QRate. A recognised startup submits a business plan online, using the template published on the portal, and gets back a scorecard with an assessment of strengths and weaknesses within fifteen working days. Assessors look at the concept, product and service; revenue streams, pricing and business model; the priority market and expansion plan; customer experience management; product and service design; market potential and size; cost structures; the business case; and marketing and sales planning. The result is a band — Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum or Signature — and that band decides which slab of state support a startup qualifies for. A startup that disagrees can apply for re-evaluation, and a startup that improves its band can come back for more. Who can apply The entity must be registered in Rajasthan, or have a branch or sales office in the state. It can be a sole proprietorship, a private limited company or OPC, an LLP or a partnership firm. Beyond that, iStart follows the DPIIT definition: not more than ten years from incorporation, annual turnover within the DPIIT ceiling in every financial year since incorporation, working on the development or improvement of a product, process or service or running a scalable model with real potential for jobs and wealth, and not formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business. There is a separate route for student and rural startups — an individual or a group with a workable business idea but no legal entity yet. Selection is sector-agnostic. The state names social and clean tech, mobile and information technology, the Internet of Things, IT applied to garments and crafts, mining, SME manufacturing and services, and disruptive ideas in any sector as the areas it is looking for. Support for startups State support is staged. Pre-seed startups can apply for an ideation grant, with more for startups where women founders hold most of the equity. Seed-stage startups can apply for a viability grant, sized by QRate band. At growth stage a startup chooses between a Scale Up Fund, given as debt that can convert to a grant and capped at a share of what the startup has already raised, and a Startup Equity Fund, where the state's alternative investment fund matches money raised in exchange for equity. Extra boosters sit on top for employment generation, product-based startups, startups in thrust sectors, and startups founded by women, transgender people, people with disabilities, SC-ST founders and rural founders. Older policy benefits are still published too: a monthly sustenance allowance for a year at idea or prototype stage, seed funding, and marketing and commercialisation assistance at MVP stage as a loan or convertible equity. Every one of these goes to an evaluation committee, which invites the startup to present before the nodal institution approves and disburses. Around the money sit the services. A Patent Information Centre handles patent searches, filing help for patents, copyright and designs, and awareness workshops. The Rajasthan MSME Act 2019 route lets a new enterprise file a declaration of intent on the Raj Udyog Mitra portal and skip certain approvals for its first three years. Bootcamps and mentoring clinics work on product, strategy, business plan and pitch. Investor Connect handles introductions to angel investors and venture funds. iStart Spotlight takes capacity-building training on operations, human resources, marketing and promotion out to the districts. An internship scheme places people inside partner companies with a government stipend. Benefit partners include Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud credits, preferential room rates from OYO Rooms, and TiE Rajasthan. Incubation and locations Techno Hub in Jaipur is the flagship. The state describes it as a hundred thousand square feet of incubation space with seating for more than seven hundred startups, offering free space, connectivity, mentoring and advisory support, co-working, video conference rooms, individual and shared offices, committee halls and tinkering labs. The district centres are branded iStart Nest, and the site publishes addresses for Kota, Udaipur, Bharatpur, Bikaner, Jodhpur, Pali and Churu, with Ajmer listed as under construction. iStart Nest describes itself as providing free incubation. A Virtual Incubation Program exists so a startup anywhere in Rajasthan can be incubated without moving, with the same components delivered remotely plus webinars, events and introductions to mentors, investors and accelerators. Students The iStart School Program covers students in classes 8 to 12 in any registered school in Rajasthan, college students in any recognised college in the state, and anyone working on or planning a startup. It is free. There are two tracks, one for aspiring founders and one for founders already building, and a suggested team size of one to five with a designated leader. Launchpads — innovation spaces inside schools and colleges with dedicated corners, materials, hackathons and mentoring sessions — are the physical half. A learning platform carries bilingual video courses with assessments and government-branded certificates, and TalentConnect links college students to startups and employers. Scale, and what iStart does not run itself The home page counters report 9,404 startups, 49,492 jobs and 134,766 students. The incubation programme is separately described as having supported more than 650 startups, and mentoring is said to run through 66 Launchpad coordinators and mentors at nine incubation centres on a hub-and-spoke model — the site's own numbers for centres vary between pages, so treat them as its claims rather than a count. The portal also hosts a section for partner incubators and accelerators, among them AIC Banasthali, Startup Oasis, Software Technology Parks of India, Marwari Catalysts and Startup Chaupal. Their programmes are their own, not iStart's. How to reach iStart The help desk numbers are 0141-2921337 for technical support and 0141-2922286 for general queries, and the portal inbox is helpdesk.istart@rajasthan.gov.in. There is no careers page. The events page is live but listed nothing upcoming when we last checked.
